in writing. between the "putin effect" and the "trump effect", we find ourselves in a complicated context. we europeans do not believe in national solutions but in cooperative solutions. european solidarity is fundamental to us and this must be reflected in an ambitious road map to be signed in rome on 25 march. for the union to be a social, economic and democratic powerhouse, we need that roadmap which reconnects us with our citizens. a road map which not only strengthens security and defence in europe as set out in the bratislava road map, but which is an agreement for a social europe, thus ensuring that the strategy for growth and employment is accompanied by increased investment. as regards migration, it is essential to address development problems with third countries. the maltese presidency must establish a genuine european asylum system and not the shame we are experiencing these days with the cold wave. we are waiting for a commission white paper which will, among other things, provide european migration policy with effective mechanisms with a tailor-made budget. only then will we be prepared for the future.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, 14 years ago, when i was a member of the basque parliament, we passed a resolution calling on the spanish government to include the defence of the tobin tax in the spanish presidency's work programme for 2002. spain is now one of the states involved in an enhanced cooperation operation to introduce a financial transaction tax. we started here in 2011. in 2013, france and italy already started to apply their own tax. on 22 january 2013 it was agreed that ten countries would do so together in 2014. and the last ecofin of 2015 promised it for ten by mid-2016. i hope this time it's the right one. i say this because today's debate reminds us that we need to return to a world in which the financial system returns to its instrumental role and is simply devoted to mediating between saving and productive activities. i say this because we need that money to drive innovation, to drive growth, to consolidate the social pillar, to rescue people from the margins. a useful and didactic way of doing this is to move from words to deeds. just raising the debate is useful because it recognises that these operations must be taxed. the introduction of this tax should help to prevent and avoid some merely speculative operations which do not create jobs and only enrich those who practice them; activities which do not boost the economy. this tax will not harm users of banking services; it is intended to tax the buying and selling of financial assets on a medium and large scale, an operation which is not exactly an everyday occurrence for the vast majority of europeans. i believe that this approach, if it is established at community level, would also enable the commission to achieve a degree of economic and financial independence from the member states, which would make its task of promoting and coordinating policies which bring european added value much more effective. humanism, redistribution and solidarity are also european values, principles which are completely alien to greed and speculation.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, the truth is that in our group this seems to us to be one of the most important projects that should be put forward. we are a little concerned that this very ambitious proposal, on which we have been working since 2011 and which parliament has asked for, is starting to be diluted like a small lump of sugar, in the sense that, well, we already have enhanced cooperation with only ten countries, and we are also concerned that there are things that are slowly being diluted. i mean, we have a smaller and smaller tax base. we are concerned that, for example, futures derivatives, interest rate derivatives, are being excluded. secondly, there is talk of extremely low rates, which would, if that were the case, obviously undermine the two objectives which i believe this tax has, namely to raise money (and the figure of 35 000 million which has already been mentioned would be very important) and also to curb some of the speculative activities. in this respect, i think that both the council and the commission should try to insist on two points: firstly, that this should finally come to fruition. we are also concerned about the timetable because we had negotiations on 5 december which were postponed, and we are already very late in implementing it, but also that the commission and the council insist, even if only in enhanced cooperation, that this tax really has the capacity to perform its function. we should not have a formal financial transaction tax, but one which is either too little or too weak to fulfil its function. i would urge you to do that. we would like to have a legislative text tabled next month, if possible at the ecofin meeting on 27 january; that would be very positive. and i would also like to remind you - and with this, i conclude - that the monti report on own resources which came out this week points to the financial transaction tax as one of the key measures for own resources, and it is probably one of the easiest to put on the table, so please do everything possible to get this through and please make sure that the backlogs are closed and that it is put into practice at once.
mr. president, many colleagues say this will cause the money to march. i would ask you: what happened when, over a hundred years ago, corporations had to pay a labor tax and created social security? the greatest social genius the world has ever invented. somebody started it. somebody started it. someone has to start with taxation to financial movements. someone has to start, and europe has to be. europe must be the one to start by setting out a path which is a wonderful sign to the world, which is a wonderful sign to the social justice that is expected by millions of europeans who are waiting for europe to give progressive signals and to allow a tax collection for the european union and for social redistribution. someone has to start and we can do it, because we can overcome the technical problems. you can, you can.
in writing. the spanish socialists have been advocating for many years the need to introduce a financial transaction tax which would penalize speculation and improve fiscal justice, and we have therefore been supporting the commission's original proposal and its approval through the enhanced cooperation procedure. the tax must also be european, so that it becomes an own resource of the union (with the necessary adjustments as long as there are non-participating member states) and the commission's financial and political autonomy is reinforced, making it a real executive power of the federal court. it is therefore disappointing that the council comes to parliament and says nothing, because it does not explain what elements keep the discussion open, nor when it is expected to be adopted. i therefore call on the council to adopt the broad-based and collectable financial transaction tax before the end of the maltese presidency.
in writing. the commission had promised that the tobin rate would be a reality by the end of 2015; after the difficulties in the negotiations, it seems that we should be satisfied with it remaining on the council's agenda in 2017. we cannot delay a decision any longer and we hope that the maltese presidency will finally respond to a historic demand of the social movements against financial speculation. we believe that the main potential of the tobin rate is to reduce financial volatility by taking a toll on the purely speculative activity of funds and financial markets. however, let us not forget that this type of activity, although harmful, is not the main cause of the current economic crisis, which has structural causes in the increase of inequalities, the fall in wages and the reduction of the role of the state in the economy as a result of the increasing financialization of its operation. that is why we deplore the fact that the tobin rate is being used by the commission to conceal its real commitment to deepening this path, through initiatives such as the banking union or the capital union, which we continue to reject.

member of the commission. – madam president, thank you for this timely debate. migrants and refugees in europe are facing the harshest winter conditions we have seen in decades, from the aegean islands to the north of europe. in some parts of europe, this was not expected. we have all seen the images in the press of many of the refugee camps and let me be clear: nobody should feel proud of this situation. our moral obligation is to offer these people dignity. today. not next week. not even tomorrow. we are therefore assisting the authorities in their response on all the urgent actions that need to be taken by greece in order to accelerate the winterisation of the camps. both my dear colleague commissioner avramopoulos and i are in regular contact with the greek authorities. on the greek islands, where the situation is most serious, we are exploring all possible solutions to assist the government and the local authorities in these extraordinary times. commissioner avramopoulos was in lesbos earlier today, to assess the situation on the ground and, of course, to discuss and find immediate solutions. we welcome the quick response of the greek authorities to deal with the difficult situation on the islands. first, to move the most vulnerable to winterised reception sites. second, to transfer to the mainland asylum applicants – especially vulnerables – who cannot be returned to turkey and who therefore have been referred to the regular asylum process. third, to deploy a navy ship to accommodate those in need, especially in lesbos, during the harsh weather conditions. having said this, for the medium term, we are discussing with the greek authorities the creation of appropriate shelters, including closed facilities on the islands, as well as the improvement of existing infrastructure. as my dear colleague dimitris avramopoulos mentioned to me and said today in lesbos, this solution will only work in cooperation and with the support of the local authorities and, of course, of the local populations in the islands who have demonstrated immense generosity to hundreds and thousands of refugees and migrants in the last two years. we stand ready to provide available funding to create this additional accommodation capacity and we have communicated this to the national and local authorities. we did so in the mainland, in partnership with unhcr and other humanitarian actors and other humanitarian partners. the european union humanitarian aid partners – un agencies, international organisations and ngos – are also on the ground assisting. over 200 000 winterised items have been distributed to the refugees and migrants – sleeping bags, blankets, and clothing appropriate for cold weather. these are not of course long-term solutions, but these extraordinary times require extraordinary responses. we are monitoring the situation on the island closely and we will keep doing whatever is needed to support the greek authorities for as long as it takes. on the mainland, the situation is very different. winterisation can be considered to be under control. thirty-one sites are already winterised with the help of the emergency support instrument. this is my responsibility, through the emergency support instrument, and thank you so much for your support in establishing this emergency support instrument, which is managed by my services and dg echo. eur 200 million were allocated last year in the humanitarian field alone, and 25% of this amount – more than eur 50 million – has been provided to humanitarian aid partners for winterisation activities in greece, in particular on the mainland, and of course to repair and improve existing shelters, to construct new ones, to improve sanitation conditions and to provide heating – the list is long. this is in addition to the funds already available. since the beginning of 2015, eur 352 in emergency assistance from the home affairs funds were made available for greece. this assistance, provided either directly to the national authorities or to eu agencies and international organisations, is aimed at directly supporting migration management in greece, including its reception capacities and, of course, improving the camps on the mainland and islands. this emergency funding comes on top of the eur 509 million already available to greece under the national programmes for 2014-2020. here, let me remind you that, overall, the european union has made available over eur one billion for greece under the home affair funds and the new emergency support instrument. greece is the biggest beneficiary of these eu funds. let me now turn to serbia and to the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. the commission is using all possible tools to help the authorities cope with the refugee crisis, not least because these two countries are candidate states. here we are also providing significant financial and technical support. i am aware of the huge difficulties due to the cold weather and heavy snowfall, especially in serbia. i will be going to serbia this weekend to assess the situation on the ground and to discuss with the authorities, meet with the refugees and express once again tangible european union solidarity. expanding the reception capacities and ensuring that existing centres are adequate for the winter has been a priority for us. with more than eur 43 million allocated to serbia since october 2015, both through humanitarian aid and pre-accession assistance, the european union is the largest donor. (eur) 19 million of humanitarian assistance was granted to improve reception conditions, to winterise facilities, and to provide a warm meal and medical help. a further eur 24 million financed through the instrument for pre-accession is also helping serbia to host these refugees and migrants and at the same time to reinforce its capacity to control its borders. this is part of over eur 118 million in eu financial and technical support for serbia in this field since 2007. of course, more needs to be done to provide safe and humane conditions for migrants, including through the expansion of reception capacity. we stand ready to help and this is why i am going there at the weekend to negotiate and discuss matters with the serbian authorities in order to improve the situation on the ground. the former yugoslav republic of macedonia is hosting around 200 refugees. since the crisis broke out in 2015, the commission has allocated eur 19 million specifically to help the former yugoslav republic of macedonia cope with the refugee crisis, including in humanitarian assistance. this is part of over eur 50 million in eu financial and technical support for the country since 2007 in the field of border, migration and asylum management. we will consider additional funds as needs arise. this is the situation in the three countries referred to – greece, serbia and fyrom – and course i would like to say again that we are not proud of this very painful situation. the european union allocated enough money, but through some weaknesses on the ground this money was not utilised in the best way in order to deal with this unprecedented situation.

the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank all the alternative rapporteurs from the various groups for their cooperation and for the good ideas they have given us to improve the text by means of amendments. i would like to say that it has been a long time since the commission has had occasion to put forward a proposal relating to the need to analyse and assess the situation of freight transport within what is now the general situation of mobility, infrastructure and european transport, which is more concerned with the passenger part of the transport than with the freight part. in this sense, at the present time, when there is growth through the opening up of panama and suez, and above all, let us say, the various aspects of electronic commerce and the rise of the new social masses, which are precisely demanding a path to exports in europe, we need, of course, to make an assessment of the current situation. and here we are, in relation to the free movement of persons, goods and services, with the emergence of national rules which tend to create new obstacles, without the commission having so far succeeded in establishing a clear and obvious framework to avoid such obstacles and problems for mobility. we also need a strategy with a whole series of points to make national and european union legislation more coherent, where the importance of urban nodes and specific urban logistics also appears, and to ensure that the financing of the new financial framework that will start to be negotiated in 2017 recognises all these needs. we also need, and we are watching with interest, how the commission is also interested in improving them, in improving crossborder transport and, above all, in particular, the links that are missing in my region - for example, everything related to the canfranc crossing - and also to improve rail links to sea ports, river ports or airports. in the case of spain, i would also be interested in the cantabrian-mediterranean corridor. and above all, facilitating the capillarity - one of the industry's demands - of the global network towards the core network and corridors, and the fundamental role of multimodal platforms in trans-european networks. a series of ideas or attempts at a solution: in the european semester, the need to make national plans more consistent with the plans that the member states themselves have signed in brussels, and which often do not correspond; the proposal for the golden rule, that is, that the obligation to co-finance european infrastructures does not lead to public debt, specifically. i would also like the coordinators to concentrate on the freight aspects of their respective corridors, and we can assess with the commission on a biannual basis what is being done in those corridors in relation to the improvement of intermodality in the field of freight transport. we are also concerned about the need for investment in the maintenance of these infrastructures, not just the construction of new infrastructure, and that is why we also thank mr katainen for agreeing in parliament that all investment in the maintenance and upgrading of motorways and roads could be part of the new efsi. we certainly support the continuation of the digital transport and logistics forum, especially with all aspects of innovation, digitisation, simplification, and above all to avoid that redundant legislation again that is adding layers to the national, regional and local with the new proposals for european directives and standards. we certainly want to facilitate the development of ports and the systems that link them and improve safety, especially those like galileo and egnos, and to ensure that they are financed so that we do not always have to worry about their continuity. we therefore ask the commission to provide specific funding for freight transport and a specific call for proposals, which we hope will be launched in 2017, for logistics projects. the commission is also proposing that projects in urban nodes, specifically those relating to much-needed urban logistics, which avoid pollution, noise and congestion, be supported and facilitated through good practice. we also stress the need for new technologies such as automation, drones, etc., which are to be integrated more and more rapidly into logistics and freight transport, to have a fluid relationship with conventional vehicles and also with users, who are increasingly vulnerable. we complement our report with a proposal for green corridors, with the need to improve data and, as a conclusion, with the need to restore the dignity of employment and working conditions to make them more attractive to the new generations.
mr president, i would like to congratulate mrs ayala sender and hope that the contents of this report will oblige the states to fulfil the commitments they have signed. the first incentive is the idea of not counting these investments as debt. the second is that we need an integrated system of mobility of people and goods, fully intermodal, with no bottlenecks between states and low emissions. thirdly, this logistics revolution is fundamental to combating climate change, improving our global competitiveness and activating an interesting employment corridor based on knowledge and the intensive use of new technologies. so when a state does not fulfil its part of the bargain and delays investments in a priority project like the so-called 'basque y', it is hurting all the partners in the european project. that is why we must find the means to relaunch this list of essential priority projects, so that we can talk seriously about transport, mobility and logistics in the european union.

in writing. the european social pillar was announced by president juncker to the european parliament on 9 september 2015. the european pillar of social rights sets out a set of key principles to support fair and well-functioning labour markets and social protection systems for the euro area. the areas of action of the pillar are grouped under three main strands: equal opportunities and access to the labour market, fair working conditions and adequate social protection. the report highlights that persons in vulnerable situations or who are more frequent victims of discrimination, such as women, ethnic minorities, the long-term unemployed, senior citizens and persons with disabilities may need complementary measures aimed at promoting their participation in the labour market and ensuring decent living standards throughout their lives; in this regard, it also highlights that the report insists that the rights of persons with disabilities must be integrated into the whole social pillar with a human rights-based approach that is in line with the obligations of the union and its member states under the crpd.
in writing. european citizens have long called for europe to focus on social aspects, and i therefore welcome this report, which will help to better balance economic policies and social needs, support fairer labour markets and protection systems, and strengthen the european social model, helping to achieve upward economic, social and territorial convergence. the eu is facing important current and future challenges, such as the digitisation of the economy and the consequent emergence of new jobs and forms of work, demographic challenges and the scourge of poverty, which unfortunately is still very much present in our society. the reduction of poverty and social exclusion must be one of the pillars of the social pillar, as current growth can only be sustainable if it includes all citizens. to achieve this we must work together in the short term, through policies that alleviate existing poverty and promote entry into the labour market, and in the long term, through policies that break the cycle of poverty, mainly focused on education and reducing school dropouts.

member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank everyone for their participation and remarks in the debate. both the critical and the supportive remarks are very useful to us in building up the project for the years to come and the upcoming multiannual financial framework. indeed, the erasmus programme, which started its career 30 years ago as a student mobility programme, transformed into a very complex programme with higher education aspects. it is no longer only about student mobility, but strategic alliances among higher education institutions, the exchange of ideas and best practices, and a strong and institutionalised cooperation among higher education institutions. it has a chapter on volunteering which can be very useful for young europeans to gain experience and skills in volunteering which can be used on the labour market. we have some funding programmes for sports, especially for grassroots sports, and we have projects in youth policy as well. this means that erasmus+ is today much more than a student mobility programme. it is a complex programme for the future because it not only helps young people to find their own place in today’s and tomorrow’s societies, but it also helps them to develop a complementary european identity which is not antagonistic to local, regional or national identities, but complements them. it adds to their personality and thereby hopefully helps european integration in this very critical period. there is, of course, a lot of room for improvement. that is why i thanked you for all the remarks which raised the issue of funding. the structure of the erasmus+ budget is an incremental one, which means that from 2017 until 2020, there is a 10% increase in the budget, which means wider opportunities madam president, commissioner, in 2003 we adopted the emissions trading directive so that emission reductions could be made in a flexible, efficient way and without exposing our industry to unfair competition from third countries. this third element is particularly important in the mediterranean basin, which is much more exposed to maritime traffic and competition from third countries. to give you an example, we can put cement. the important thing is not to create comparative disadvantages between industrial sectors because of a design flaw in the system. i know that this is not an easy matter, but it is necessary that the same conditions, burdens and privileges exist for sectors which have to compete in the same economic field. the question of over-allocation is resolved in the report by a more dynamic mechanism of adjustment to production levels. i think that the cooperation between the itre and envi committees has been good. i would like to congratulate mr duncan and also thank mr belet for the great effort he has made within the epp group.
madam president, what we are debating today and voting on this week is the key to the vault of the system for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, polluting emissions. the cde should be an ambitious instrument to meet the objectives of combating climate change; it should serve as a stimulus for industries to develop cutting-edge technologies for reducing emissions; it should serve to reinforce european leadership in the fight against global warming. yes, all of that is true. but our duty is to promote rules that ensure a level playing field for the industrial sectors concerned; our duty is to promote economic activity, employment and the competitiveness of our industry, while encouraging its innovative capacity to reduce its emissions. so, ambition and balance. and that, of course, was the purpose of some of the amendments i tabled in the itre committee. if we recover any of them, we will also recover ambition and balance.
on behalf of the alde group. – madam president, i would like to thank the commissioner, colleagues and the rapporteur for their cooperation. this report talks about many things – airports, state aid – and asks us, as in other years, for more financial and human resources for dg competition because there is a lot more work to be done. but i want to focus here on the google case because, seven years after the commission announced allegations of antitrust violations by google, we have a spent a lot of time on this. certainly, eu regulatory time does not correspond to the necessity and urgency of the companies in the real economy. i am aware, commissioner, that a lot of time was lost by your predecessor, mr almunia. these years of unproductive settlements, discussions and delays in the still-ongoing investigations have left competitiveness in the online search market severely damaged. but, at a certain point, a decision has to be made one way or another. that is why, in this report, we call on the commission to finish all google antitrust investigations. let me recall two recent facts. last december, foundem, the first complainant in the shopping case, had to close its shopping comparison website, and yelp also closed its european businesses. this is how the behaviour of google impacts on companies. ms vestager, may i suggest to you that your provisional decision, which i hope will come in the next weeks or months, should impose a record—breaking fine on google. you need to show companies that they cannot be rewarded for losing time because, in the last two years, google’s attitude and behaviour has caused more damage to complainant companies. when it comes to remedies, may i suggest that all companies sit down with their technological experts, together with the commission, to try to find non—discriminating future-proofed remedies. thank you very much. let me remind you that time helps monopolies and damages smes.

member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the honourable members for their very substantial comments. unfortunately i will not be able to give each and every one an individual answer. one of the important things for me is for our rules to be an enabler. for instance, when mr schwab calls for tourism in state aid we will be more than happy to give guidance on where state aid is absolutely allowed, where it is no economic activity but allowing people to be acquainted with the region, to know what to do to find the businesses who do have the economic activity. that, i think, is the important thing. i also very much look forward to the debate with the committee on agriculture and rural development because i think that we can meet one other to ensure jointly that we have a very competitive sector in which we use the means of competition and, at the same time, allow for a more balanced approach in sectors where many, many small suppliers are facing very heavy-duty negotiators on the other side of the table. i look forward to addressing these issues. some of you have mentioned the tax issue. it is, of course, obvious that every member state is sovereign in setting the level of their corporate taxation. if we want european tax legislation it will be through the front door, via the council, with unanimity. in the same treaty that gives member states the serenity to set their own tax level, we have very strong rules that say you cannot give a company, or group of companies, selective advantages. selective advantages, paid for by taxpayers, ruin fair competition and, in particular, do not give small and medium-sized businesses a fair chance of making it in the market. therefore, obviously, the commission will also continue its work in relation to fiscal aid – a.k.a. tax and state aid. some of you have been asking about the ongoing merger control procedures in two of three mergers in seeds and pesticides, or ‘crop protection’ as they call it. we will, of course, be as firm and as insistent as always to make sure that we have competition in this sector both for seeds and for pesticides. this is the very basis of our food chain and obviously we need competition there as well, and we will thoroughly investigate these mergers, including that of bayer and monsanto if we are finally notified of this. on the google case, i very much appreciate the insistence, because these are important cases. we are dealing with fast-moving markets and, as was mentioned, we have companies which suffered while the investigation was ongoing. therefore, we are doing our utmost to deal with the responses that we now have had to the statement of objection, and to examine them in detail to make sure that we give this company, like others, the right to defend itself, because that is important. as was mentioned, there is, of course, also a need for checks and balances when it comes to the commission competences in enforcing competition law, and for the court to be able to overrule our decisions. therefore, our work should be thorough and expert, while, of course, speed is a very important challenge for us, precisely because, as was mentioned, these are fast-moving markets. last but not least, we hope that the digital single market will not keep being mentioned as a separate part of the single market, but will come to be seen as a fully integrated part of the single market, because it offers a lot of choice for consumers. as you may know, we have opened three new cases in the field of digital business in order to make sure that every business has a fair chance of making it. these are in video games – part of the holiday business – and our aim is to make sure that consumers get the choice they should have. i will leave the detailed comments for now, but i assure you that we are using our best efforts to enforce competition law, and i very much take on board the things mentioned today – in particular by the rapporteur and in terms of the draft report’s recommendations for our future work.
the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner vestager, i would like to express my sincere thanks to the alternative rapporteurs, their assistants and the political group advisers, because they have helped to take this report much further than i originally intended. it's been a great joint effort for equal rights. when we talk about gender inequality, we tend to think about the skyrocketing pay gap, the ridiculous presence of women in decision-making positions, or the great scourge that we are ashamed of: gender violence, whether physical or psychological. but we rarely think about how this inequality affects our daily lives, our well-being, our health and especially our mental health. did you know that biomedical research and clinical trials on drugs and treatments don't take into account that half the population is female? that they don't take into account the biological, physiological and psychological differences between men and women, beyond their reproductive systems? i became aware of this problem some time ago when, on a visit to a hospital, a nurse told me of her experience. hospital staff were concerned because they could not understand why so many patients who had survived a heart attack returned to the hospital after a year and died shortly thereafter. the same hygienic conditions, the same tracking mechanisms -- medical history, family history, other risk factors had been taken into account. but it took them a while to realize that most of the patients who relapsed and died were women, because cardiovascular disease is more common in women than in men, and previous research lacked that approach. mental health is a very well-observed problem. there are considerable gender differences in patterns of mental illness, especially the most common ones: depression and anxiety, for example, mood disorders that any of us knows firsthand, have a prevalence almost three times higher in women than in men. one in ten workers in the european union, for example, has taken a leave of absence for depression, which costs some 92 million euros a year. mental health is also linked to employment and investment. the report we are debating today boldly addresses these and other equally relevant issues, such as the devastating and lifelong effects that gender-based violence has on the mental health of victims, the prejudices that still exist about lgbti people and that condemn them to deteriorated mental health, or the urgent need to implement the guidelines on protecting and supporting the mental health and psychosocial well-being of refugees, asylum seekers and migrants in europe. but when we talk about gender equality and health, it's imperative that we talk about abortion openly. conscientious objection by doctors cannot endanger the health and freedom of a woman who requests a voluntary termination of pregnancy. it is simply unacceptable that in italy, for example, more than 70% of doctors refuse to practice it today, despite being protected by law. we want to ensure that there is a minimum number of health professionals available to carry out these medical interventions, guaranteeing access to sexual and reproductive health services in all countries of the union in accordance with the legal standards in force. the european union is bound by its treaties to ensure the protection of human health as part of all its policies and to work with the member states to improve public health, prevent disease and eliminate sources of danger to physical and mental health. in short, it is the legal and social responsibility of all policy-makers to fully integrate the specific needs of women, half the population, in defining public health and health-care services policies at european and national level.
madam president, last saturday's actions around the international day of women and girls in science brought to light a real thing: the gender gap in research. i mean, the universal pattern for research is the young white male. that is why we greens consider this report essential to reduce gender inequality. but as a member of the committee on development, i would like to stress that we must go further, from a north-south perspective. first, investing in research and development on a global scale is necessary to achieve universal health coverage. secondly, we need to require transnational pharmaceutical companies to respect human rights when conducting clinical trials. and third, we need to reduce poverty, ensure access to education and social protection to end the gender gap in mental health once and for all.
madam president, i would also like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr de jong, and to point out to the commissioner - who i know is also particularly sensitive to these issues - that just as we have lobbyists' registers and also the code of conduct for commissioners - which could be improved, but which have served as an example and a guide for the member states which are lagging behind - we also need a code which protects and gives a legal framework to whistleblowers at european level, which would be the mark and the guide so that, in national areas - for example in my country, where there are and where there are real hardships and situations, very conflicting ones - we could at least serve as a guide to give them that protection. so: legal framework, of course, for these whistleblowers, with their rights and with the obligations as well. but above all, a legal framework that would give them protection at the moment when they enter a kind of limbo where they lose their jobs, they are in a really terrible psychological situation... and of course, all the help to the common good and the common interest that they are carrying forward is beyond appreciation, and they must be protected. please, madam commissioner, help us with that.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, first i would like to thank the honourable members for today’s discussion. i think it clearly showed that the broad majority in this house shares the commission’s view that we need to move towards the completion of the second review of the greek programme without undue delay. the question raised by mr bullmann and reiterated by several other colleagues is this: what exactly prevents us from doing so right now? i would say that there are some elements. first, agreement is clearly within reach, so if all sides make the final push, we can do it in a short time. on the fiscal pass: as i said, greece has overperformed on the 2016 fiscal targets and is on track to meet the target of 1.75% primary surplus this year. a small gap remains as regards reaching a 3.5% primary surplus in 2018, but measures have already been pre-identified which could cover a substantial part of this gap. on structural reform implementation, once again substantial progress has been made. there are some outstanding issues, but certainly with a push from the greek authorities, those can be closed very quickly. the issue we are currently discussing is to ensure imf participation in the programme, because, according to the esm treaty, we work in liaison with the ecb and, wherever possible, in close cooperation with the imf. we also know that the imf has a more cautious growth and fiscal forecast with regard to future greek performance, and correspondingly a certain gap is emerging vis-à-vis the european institutions’ and imf forecasts. so we are also working to bridge that gap, but once again, if there is a push and a constructive attitude from all sides, it is certainly doable. with the current state of affairs with the greek economy finally recovering, and with quite a strong rebound expected in the economy this year, it would be a shame now not to make this final push and keep the programme on track. so the commission will continue to work to ensure that the programme is on track, that we reach an agreement, and that we can ensure that the greek economy is finally returning to sustainable economic growth and job creation.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, thank you for organising constantly on the situation in ukraine. presidents juncker and tusk met last week with prime minister groysman and commissioner stylianides will travel next week to the eastern part of the country. the eu foreign ministers focused once again on ukraine during the latest foreign affairs council on 6 february and high representative mogherini recently met with president poroshenko and with deputy prime minister klympush-tsintsadze, and after the exchanges in the mini plenary in brussels i am glad that this plenary session offers yet another opportunity to discuss this issue with you. ukraine remains at the top of our agenda, because the illegal annexation of crimea and the destabilisation of eastern ukraine challenge the foundations of our international system and the security of our continent. but also and foremost because we must urgently stop the suffering of our ukrainian friends. the deaths of innocent civilians trapped in a conflict area are unacceptable. and the upsurge in fighting in the avdiivka area has claimed the lives of numerous people on both sides. hundreds of civilians have been forced to leave their homes. critical infrastructure ensuring the delivery of water, electricity, heating and gas has been affected and many civilian homes have been damaged. the dire humanitarian situation has been worsened by the current harsh winter conditions. today, the level of fighting has decreased somewhat. the citizens and the authorities of ukraine have mobilised, together with humanitarian actors. this has helped prevent a humanitarian catastrophe. however, let us not forget that since the beginning of the conflict more than 10 000 people have died. tens of thousands have been injured and over 3.8 million people remain in need of humanitarian assistance. next week commissioner stylianides will travel close to the contact line and deliver a strong message of european support to the local population. we should all put pressure on all the relevant actors to respect the ceasefire, grant access for humanitarian actors to the areas not under the control of the government and ensure the free movement of people and goods across the contact line. the tireless efforts of the organization for security and co—operation in europe (osce) special monitoring mission and the special representative of the osce chairmanship in office were key to avoiding a more serious crisis. they have our constant and full support, along with our support to the efforts undertaken within the normandy four format. after two-and-a-half years we still see that the minsk agreements have not been fully implemented. a high number of ceasefire violations, views of proscribed weapons including artillery and tanks, restrictions on the osce’s monitoring activity and lack of progress on the disengagement of forces and military hardware continue to be reported on a daily basis. there are still many hostages and illegally detained persons awaiting release. a reverse positive trend is needed. the granting of full, safe and unhindered access for the osce special monitoring mission and then ensuring full humanitarian access in accordance with international humanitarian principles must be a priority. we have said this and will continue to underline it. russia bears a direct responsibility in helping to achieve a solution to the crisis. we will continue to call on russia to use its considerable influence over the separatists it backs to meet the minsk-related commitments in full. we also remain deeply concerned about information on the presence of russian military equipment and personnel in separatist held areas. on 3 february federica mogherini had a phone—call conversation with the russian foreign minister, sergey lavrov, where she stressed precisely the need to ensure an immediate and complete ceasefire to pave the way for the implementation of the other parts of the minsk agreements, including the political strand. ukraine was also at the core of the high representative’s talks with the new us administration last week in washington. she took the opportunity to state once again the european union’s common position, including on sanctions. we do not see sanctions as an objective but as a tool. we have repeated time and again that when the minsk agreements are fully implemented the related sanctions will be removed. this also means that as long as the agreements are not implemented the sanctions will remain in place. consequently, the high representative also discussed with her american interlocutors how to best support the implementation of the minsk agreements. the european union stands ready to step up its support for the implementation and we have increased our financial and technical support to the osce special monitoring mission. we are preparing a substantial new programme for government controlled areas near the contact line and we want to support economic development, social cohesion and job creation. the rapporteur. mr president, i greet the vice-president of the european commission, mr valdis dombrovskis, and all my colleagues here. we are discussing the governance of the single market today. we value all that we have achieved, which is not little, and all that remains to be done in this unique political project which is the european union. regardless of the political storms that may be shaking us, brexit, new nationalisms, or rather, populist political opportunism on the right and the left, there is something that we can be undeniably proud of, europe's greatest achievement, which is its single market. a market of 500 million people that, over the last 50 years, has generated economies of scale unimaginable for european businesses, helping us to create transnational competitiveness, new business opportunities and new jobs. a single market which has contributed, more than any other policy adopted in this house or in the council, to better integrating european companies by offering them international value chains and, therefore, global competitiveness. the european single market has increased consumer supply, offering lower prices, and has enabled citizens to live, work and study wherever they want. the changing environment of the union, the external effects of globalisation are permanent challenges for the single market, to which it has to adapt. we, as legislators and in fulfilling the political mandate given to us by the citizens, must continually optimise policies to consolidate economic recovery and to encourage convergence towards those who achieve the best results. the obstacles identified in the markets for goods and services are a brake on the productivity and competitiveness of the european economy. companies are often suffocated by outdated and overly burdensome rules. in my report i have stressed the urgent need to remove barriers to the single market and to create the right environment for the growth of our economies. at the same time, we need to be especially attentive to innovation and global value chains that are creating new and important opportunities. digital technologies are transforming many industrial sectors, enabling more efficient production and new and innovative business models. increasingly, services and industry are coming together in clean and smart business offerings that bring greater added value to their customers. however, this innovation also challenges traditional business models and consumer-business relations. in this respect, and to improve the european economic model and restore competitiveness, a comprehensive combination of public resources, structural reforms and targeted investment is required. all the institutions and member states of the union must act together if a sustainable recovery is to be achieved and the convergence process is to be revitalised. this requires close involvement of the european parliament and national parliaments, the social partners, national, regional and local authorities and civil society as a whole. the investment plan is now operational, aiming to mobilise at least eur 315 million in new investment over three years and return investment to sustainable pre-crisis levels. the plan, announced and implemented in record time, aims to stimulate investment finance, remove obstacles, increase innovation and deepen the single market. europe is putting the money in, but as always the member states play a key role in achieving these objectives, and i must say not always successfully. the report of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, for which i was rapporteur, presents a text agreed by the pro-european political forces, who identify themselves with a better and more efficient europe. in this respect, imco focuses on three key areas: strengthening the single market pillar within the european semester process, unlocking the potential of the single market in key areas of growth and strengthening the governance of the single market. we call on the european commission to strengthen the pillar of the single market through a system of regular monitoring to identify country-specific barriers to the single market and to assess integration and competitiveness in the single market. we call for the potential of the market to be harnessed by collecting and working on the information obtained from the member states, to reshape, incorporate, implement and enforce the single market regulatory framework with the ultimate aim of delivering very concrete results to citizens. we believe that the european commission should systematically monitor the implementation and enforcement of single market rules through country-specific recommendations, especially when these rules contribute to structural reforms. in this context, i would remind you that the objectives of the investment plan for europe, the juncker plan, include the removal of obstacles, the increase of innovation and the deepening of the single market. i would stress in this connection that improving the investment environment means strengthening the single market by increasing regulatory predictability, strengthening the level playing field within the union and removing obstacles to investment within and outside the union. despite the removal of tariff barriers in the single market, a large number of various non-tariff barriers remain, and i believe that strengthening the single market requires urgent action at national and union level to remove such barriers. i would like to thank my colleagues and the other rapporteurs for the good work they have done. i think our committee is proud of the work we are doing in this direction.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, there are two ways of talking about minimum incomes: as an individual and subjective right to a decent life so that no family is left below the poverty line an objective to which the european union can contribute by upward harmonisation of social protection, for example through a minimum income framework directive, as the eesc is calling for or we can talk about minimum incomes by linking them to the dismantling of labour rights, without fighting economic inequality and the neoliberal policies that cause it, but by legitimising an unfair system by concealing its most serious effects. this is what the european semester is all about and its purported social recommendations, which are designed to strengthen the power of capital over the economy, from privatisation to deregulation. it's a debate that i illustrate with the minimum income, but it's transversal to all the debates on european governance and constitutionalism that we've had today, whether it's better to add a social pillar to the eurozone or to rebuild europe on elements like the social charter, for example. social democracy continues to advocate neoliberal economic policies in exchange for minimal progress in social protection, but the two objectives are incompatible in the long term. we know, however, that without putting social rights ahead of economic freedoms, there is no room for improving the lives of europeans.
mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, i am very pleased with the excellent work done by the rapporteur, mrs yana toom, and of course by her colleagues in the working group, because this report, which deals with the social aspect of the european semester, is absolutely essential from a political point of view, and more so at this moment. and it is essential because it is the report that puts the european citizen back at the centre of policies and in the policy objective, because everything that is done in the european semester, including the sacrifices, is done for the european citizens, and that is where it is worth getting right. let us not miss the mark; this is the analysis of a series of short-term policies 'one semester' and, in particular, of macroeconomic policies and their effectiveness on a series of values which i shall now say. this is not a debate about the ideal labour market or some absolutely arithmetically insane figures or some structural targets for how to get to pensions. what we have to do is to see what the consequences of the policies have been on employment (in a very general sense: quality, where the unemployment funds have gone), on inequalities, whose dynamics must be broken at once, because they are being exaggerated and because they even harm economic growth, and not only socially, but also in the financing of social policies: how they have gone, how we have evolved. in this field, and in the fight against poverty and gender equality within inequalities, there are some excellent ideas, suggestions, even demands, in the text we will adopt tomorrow.
mr president, i have to say... commissioner, if there is a general consensus in this house, it is that europe is in an exceptional situation. the refugee crisis, the brexit, the rise of populisms. but in the face of this exceptional crisis, the response from the european commission is practically ordinary, as if nothing had happened since 2014. and i believe that a change is needed, a change in social policy and a change in economic policy too, precisely to combat the problems that are afflicting us today in the european union as a whole. we need a more social europe. we need to focus on raising wages, not only to make the recovery fairer, but also and fundamentally to make the recovery more sustainable over time. we need to support the longterm unemployed more. we need to support more, too, youth employment. and we also need to push the expansionary policy forward not only with the juncker plan, not only by betting on public-private initiative, but also by allowing member states to invest in strategic areas, to increase public investment. we believe that in this situation we must not only contribute with good words and good intentions, but we must find strong solutions to prevent 2017 from being another year of political deficit and the european commission's political response to the problems that afflict citizens.
mr president, first of all i would like to thank the commission for the tone of this annual growth report, because it is probably the first time that the commission has taken up the need for a global approach to the euro area. until now, in recent years, there has always been a country-by-country analysis, and that prevents or prevents you from having a global view of what economic policy should be for the euro area as a whole. this time it's done. and that overall reflection leads the commission to assume that a different fiscal policy is needed, an expansionary fiscal policy for the whole of the euro area, which will probably have to be combined with different approaches in each of the countries. but this global approach is very necessary because monetary policy is not enough to revive growth, and we need a serious expansionary fiscal policy, which is also linked, by the way, to what my colleague sergio gutiérrez was calling for: the need to build the social pillar in the european union.
mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to congratulate mr hökmark on the work he has done. the coordination of economic and budgetary policies within the european union is the key to the european semester and it is our responsibility to contribute to ensuring convergence and stability in the european union, to contribute to ensuring sound public finances, to fostering economic growth, to preventing excessive macroeconomic imbalances and to implementing the europe 2020 strategy. it is true that the exit from the crisis is becoming a reality and the latest data are positive, as evidenced by the fact that unemployment continues to fall and is already at 2009 levels, inflation is approaching the european central bank's targets, and growth gained strength in the last quarter of 2016. but it is no less true that there is still a long way to go. the european central bank has done its part. monetary policy alone is not enough to stimulate growth. investments in strategic sectors are needed, as are structural reforms. the way out of the crisis requires a tightening of economic governance and continuing reforms at the national level. that is the only recipe and spain is a good example. spain leads the european union in economic growth and job creation. structural reforms are the key to overcoming the crisis. let's face them without fear.
mr president, we have been discussing for some time issues of great current and future importance, such as the demographic challenges of ageing and economic and social cohesion, especially in relation to employment, the fight against poverty and social exclusion. however, despite the need to make further progress in these areas, i believe that we are leaving in the background the territorial aspect necessary to achieve a harmonious development of the union. i come from aragon, a region where, in addition to the ageing of the population, a large part of its territory suffers from depopulation and dispersion problems. in this respect, over the past few years i have tabled many amendments with a number of colleagues which have been adopted both within and outside the european semester, and now it is time for them to be translated into concrete measures. like aragon, there are many regions in spain and the rest of europe with the same problems. it would therefore be appropriate for europe and the member states to consider the development of a european plan to meet this challenge. mr dombrovskis, if we do not act soon and make sure that these regions are able to establish a population and, in particular, encourage young people to stay in their territories, we risk condemning many of these european areas to extinction.
on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, the banking union is an eu project after the creation of the euro and it is fundamental for the future of our currency. the absence of european financial supervision was one of the reasons that brought us to the financial crisis. national financial supervision is less effective as banks globalised their activities. the ecb has been reliable and has won strong credibility. the contrast with some national central banks is huge. yesterday, for instance, the former president of banco de españa, miguel ángel fernández ordóñez, as well as his supervisory team, were indicted by the spanish justice on charges of allowing irregularities in bankia’s initial public offering in july 2011. bankia’s ipo was done, even though banco de españa knew that it was close to bankruptcy. it was just done because of the close relations between the banco de españa and bankia’s director, rodrigo rato. thousands of people lost their savings and bankia was bailed out for eur 23 billion, paid thanks to a european bail—out. this is why the banking union is so important: to say goodbye for ever to the bad practices of many national supervisors in many national central banks in europe. i would like to call attention to the amendment to be tabled with the greens and ecr: the use of public money to bail out banks has to be only in exceptional cases. if the rules of the banking union are not followed, as may happen now in italy, our future will be full of more public deficits and a new banking crisis will put the euro at risk. only if all member states comply with banking union legislation will it be possible to create a european deposit guarantee to complete our project and give extra assurance to citizens and investors. answer to a blue-card question. i have to say, mr president, that if the small savings banks in germany are not subject to european supervision, if there are losses, only the german taxpayers, the germans, will pay for the mistakes that the bundesbank may make and there will be no effect of these losses on the whole of europe. i should also say, for example, that in the case of bankia the spanish prime minister rajoy always said 'it's too big to fail', but that is not true because the former commissioner for the european union, who was also spanish, said that in germany there are banks bigger than bankia which were closed down so as not to cause losses for the taxpayer. i have to say that, in this sense, if italy is to be consistent, it cannot sign the banking union in 2014, as renzi did, and then say that now we will do a bailout as we have done all our life because there are losses for investors.
mr president, i should first like to congratulate my colleague, mrs danuta hübner, on her report and say that banking union is an indispensable component of monetary union and a fundamental pillar of a genuine economic and monetary union. but banking union is not only necessary to ensure stability and restore confidence in euro area banks; it is also essential to increase financial integration, to reduce european banking risk and moral hazard, to help break the link between banks and sovereign debt, and to promote risk sharing within monetary union. the banking union plays a key role in financing investment and thus in fostering growth and job creation in the union. we then committed ourselves to banking union in response to the financial crisis and we have already achieved the first two pillars: the single supervisory mechanism and the single resolution mechanism. we must continue to move in this direction, ensuring that sharing and risk reduction go hand in hand. that is why we must move forward in the negotiations to create a european deposit guarantee fund to complete the banking union and to ensure that taxpayers' money is protected against possible future crises. economic and monetary union is in much better shape today than it was before the financial crisis, but completing banking union is a necessary step to continue moving towards a genuine economic and monetary union of the member states.
mr president, we are discussing today an important report which we will be voting on in the coming days, which clearly aims to close the banking union model. in the first half of 2012, the euro area was very close to the abyss. we believed for a moment that the euro could disappear and it was the commitment in the summer of 2012 to create the banking union that saved us from disaster. and i have to say that since then the crisis first started to slow down and now we are in a situation that is a little more optimistic, but with problems. but that banking union which was launched in 2012 needs to be completed, and we need to approve a european deposit guarantee fund now. we cannot wait, we cannot continue to follow the council's instructions to delay, to delay the negotiations. and in parliament we need to move quickly, with a backstop prosecutor that closes the model once and for all.

member of the commission. – mr president, last year on 19 april the commission launched the european cloud initiative with the ambition of ensuring that science, businesses, public services could reap all the benefits of the so-called ‘big data revolution’. today we produce 2.5 billion – billion – bytes of data per day. that is, as someone once put it, four eiffel towers of blu-ray discs per day, so the fundamental question for us tonight is really how we should deal with it, and the cloud initiative is part of the answer to this question. the communication proposed the creation of an inclusive, european, open science cloud, deploying an efficient european data infrastructure to address such enormous data flows and opening up the user base to the public sector and industry. as commissioner for research, science and innovation, i have followed very closely the work of this house and it culminated with the adoption of the report in front of us today. let me say a word of gratitude to the chair, jerzy buzek, for stepping up as a rapporteur, and to mr boni and ms maydell for their work in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe) and the committee on the internal market and consumer protection (imco). i knew from the beginning that the contribution of this parliament would be a valuable support for our strategy for an open and trusted cloud-based data environment geared to the scientific community. we are now deeply committed to engaging with all relevant stakeholders to ensure that the european cloud initiative can achieve its objectives. we are now discussing sustainable funding and implementation instruments with the member states, research infrastructures, scientific communities and other key players. but let me assure you that we are here to tell you that your advice will be followed, that the commission has already started to implement the initiative very much along the lines that you suggest. first, on the european open science cloud the commission is preparing a roadmap for governance and financing to be presented to, and discussed with, the member states in the course of 2017. our aim is very simple. we want our 1.7 million european scientists to have the best services for text and data mining, the best data management plans and the best training programmes. we made open data the default in horizon 2020, starting in 2017. in other words, we kind of transformed an exception into a rule simply because we intend and we believe that the commission should lead by example. we will fund a pilot project on the european science cloud to ensure that the governance in the european open science cloud is truly representative of european science, that it create synergies amongst existing and future initiatives of this kind. over the year, we will do more. we will define a governance board before the end of 2017 and we will work on making all our research data fair; findable, so scientists can identify each piece of data in a unique way; accessible, so it can always be obtained freely; interoperable, because science is today at the intersection of disciplines; and reusable, because you cannot lose important data after you have used it, you have to be able to use it in different disciplines at different times. so if we want better research, if we want better science and if we want better innovation, it is essential to be able to set these fair principles of data as the global standard, so we all speak to same language and we can advance in science. after addressing you on the science cloud, let me now give you some information about the european data infrastructure, a european high performance computing strategy under development with member states and european industry. this includes a pooling of the necessary investments at all levels to create a world-class pan-european high performance computing and big data ecosystem by 2023. we want this ecosystem to be built on two exascale computers. that means a billion operations per second, which is basically one thousand times faster than today’s supercomputers. the commission agrees that the take-up of high performance computing services by businesses, consumers, public administrations and scientific sectors requires seamless user-friendly access with appropriate levels of data protection, security and services to ensure trust and confidence in their use. i believe the key for the future in terms of data is about exactly these two principles: trust and confidence. and so in this context, on 10 january last, the commission adopted the communication on building a european data economy. that deals with additional big data issues. it advocates reducing barriers to the free flow of data. it looks into questions of ownership, access to data, liability in the context of data-driven processes and autonomous systems. it puts emphasis on measures necessary to ensure an open and competitive economy without unjustified lock-in effects. as regards widening the benefits of the european cloud initiative to industry, the commission is considering several proposals on the supply and demand side and on the extension to smes. let me finish by reiterating that the commission is fully committed with you to supporting science, industry and public authorities in europe, access to world-class data infrastructures and cloud-based services as they become the decisive factors for success in this digital era. in a recent visit to heidelberg i saw how the institute of bioinformatics generates more than eur 1.3 billion per year of value just by having made one very simple choice: scientific information freely available to the global science community. that is the way we are going. that is the way we will have to go, thanks to your report.
