mr president, i have to say... i'm sensing a bittersweet taste at the end of this commission of inquiry. there is no doubt that the new regulation introduced will allow for more effective testing and monitoring of emissions, but we must admit a certain failure to require liability and compensation. the fact that mr tajani is now president of this parliament, that the infringement proceedings have not yet resulted in sanctions against the member states, that consumers still have to go to court for redress, that our cities still have polluted air and that the car companies, which have become rich at the expense of the health of europeans, now want to burden the workers with the transition from diesel to electric vehicles, is proof of this. dieselgate has demonstrated the corruption of a regulatory system in the hands of the big producers. even if we breathe a little cleaner air in the future, i have the feeling that little or nothing has changed in the relationship between the european union and big business.
mr president, commissioner, over the past year the committee of inquiry has received technicians and experts from all over the european union to find out what has happened to the polluting emissions from vehicles. at this point, we all have a fairly approximate idea of what happened: the text gives an adequate answer to our questions. the priority must be to preserve the environment and the health of the citizens, of course! the european union's legislation must evolve to promote less polluting fuels. it is also desirable to avoid the installation of deactivation devices similar to those detected in the case of the fraud in question and to include polluting emissions in the scope of the environmental liability directive. our legislation must offer greater protection and redress to the consumer in cases like this, because consumer protection is essential in this single market we have created. finally, i am not in favour of creating a new ad hoc agency. we have many agencies in the european union, and i don't think that's the solution to prevent cases like this. we just have to lay a solid foundation for it and stick to it. the text we are voting on today clearly points the way forward and we must also consider whether we are not being too demanding with some industrial sectors which have to compete with the rest of the world.
mr president, it is already clear that the european parliament has done its job. the european commission and the member states have not done so. by action or omission, they have failed. the commission has already taken action, because the prevention and control mechanisms failed, and it has failed to act, because when the first alarms were sounded, the european commission and the member states looked the other way. and yes, we must take the decisions for the future that this european parliament is proposing. of course we need to create an agency, an agency that has the capacity to prevent, that has the capacity with broad powers to impose fines, that has the capacity to recall vehicles. there is no administrative burden left over, as they say, what is left over is bad practice and, for that, the agency has a very specific mechanism to deal with it. of course, the people who have been deceived - the users and consumers - must be compensated. of course, we must be consistent and meet the objectives we have set. and as rapporteur for the future renewable energy directive, i too will be advocating greater decarbonisation in the transport sector.
mr president, when the volkswagen scandal broke, we talked about three types of messages: we talked about responsibility, we talked about restoration or rectification and we also talked about trust. the clearing of liability is still going on in the european courts, but what will really restore consumer confidence in the car industry is the amendment we are introducing today in european legislation. it is true that the extreme left will not support it because it is insufficient and is thus once again joined by the extreme right, which will not support it either because it thinks it will place an excessive burden on industry. but they don't realize that what really hurts the company is the shadow of doubt about its social and environmental responsibility. this regulation therefore improves the capacity for control, avoids conflicts of interest between manufacturers and type-approval authorities and increases the penalties for those who are found to be in breach. we socialists are concerned about the environment. that's why we want the laws to be clear and enforced. that is why we are calling for the introduction of a european agency with responsibility in this area. we are concerned about citizens, their health and their confidence, and that is why we are putting in place greater fraud prevention and compensation mechanisms. and we are concerned about the workers, who are exemplary in the collective bargaining model, and therefore we want to send them a message of thanks and reassurance, that we are with them and that their concerns and their way of acting have also been in the work of the s&d group.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the forests of sumatra and borneo in indonesia are crying out for the destruction they are being subjected to. two million hectares of forest are lost every year, the irreplaceable habitat for many animal species such as the great apes of borneo. this is unsustainable production for an uncontrolled market, where transnational corporations act without control, burning the forest and then installing illegal palm oil plantations. and the european union is no stranger to this reality: we are the second largest consumer of palm oil in the world. that is why we have supported this report which urges the european commission to act, to abandon the use of vegetable oils by 2020 and to increase control of imported palm oil, to finally increase the traceability of these products. it's time for these institutions to protect the planet and its people and to rein in corporate power and enforce human rights in every corner of the planet.
madam president, until two years ago, there was no awareness in spain of the ubiquity of palm oil in our food, but the fact is that the obligation to indicate on the labels the type of vegetable oil used as an ingredient has made it possible to make a small revolution. this week, the major food distribution chains in my country - alcampo, eroski, mercadona, lidl - announced that they were withdrawing their linear products made with palm oil. social pressure is growing because people want to protect the environment and they also want to know what they are eating. both the environment and the right to food go hand in hand. the public knows this and is telling us and demanding that we take note. but taking notes is not patching. the objective of this report is to phase out palm oil from biofuels by 2020. that's why we've supported it, because it's a start to start tackling the paradoxes of fighting climate change. but we understand that we need to go much further: we need to rethink the global food distribution system. otherwise, we will continue to patch up one of the greatest challenges facing humanity.
madam president, when we talk about the wage gap or the glass ceiling, we think of offices, large companies and cities, but inequality is even deeper in rural areas. there, women suffer a multiplied discrimination: in their decision-making capacity, in their pay and in the recognition of their contribution and ownership. i met maribel sanchez vadillo the day she took her first flight. he was coming to brussels to collect an award for his goat farm in candeleda (spain). maribel is an example of what women can achieve in a traditionally male world: success, recognition and business ownership. i call on the spanish and european authorities to guarantee women full access to ownership and management of farms and holdings. women transform entire communities when they participate fully in the economy, especially in the agricultural sector, and multiply exponentially the benefits for the whole society.
madam president, i too wanted to make an explanation of vote on this report which i consider to be a step forward. it is only an own-initiative report, but it is good that we give visibility to rural women. women in rural areas have particular difficulties. there are quite a few of them here, but i wanted to highlight especially that role of invisibility that they have, especially in working capacity. we are seeing how in these rural areas, 50 percent of the population are women. however, 40% of women are unemployed. what's the matter? what's the matter? many of them do not even register or register themselves in the unemployment systems. there is therefore a double invisibility: their lower contribution to the labour system - which then leads to their having fewer rights at the time of a pension - and their lack of recognition in the role of agricultural activity.
madam president, the common agricultural policy has historically turned its back on the crucial role of women. for example, in spain it is difficult to find a single line in rural development plans that specifically addresses the situation of invisibility and gender inequality in rural areas, let alone in the agricultural sector. it is time for the cap to put on the purple glasses, the purple glasses, because they are the ones who have supported and are supporting the rural world, the ones who have worked the hardest, the ones who have fed us, who have taken care of everything and everyone. they, who never had time for themselves, are the great forgotten ones. one of these women recently said in a newspaper in my country that "the countryside is dying, every year a small part of the space i live in dies; and it dies because we are killing it all together". the future of rural areas depends on policies that put women at the centre. let us not forget that the exodus from the countryside is primarily a female exodus. so to ensure that they stay is to guarantee a tomorrow. let us also put on the purple glasses to look at the countryside and, above all, let us put on the purple glasses to look at the primary sector.
madam president, the dieselgate is the symbol of what we might call 'the european fabric'. for two years, the european commission knew that vehicle emissions tests were being manipulated and did nothing, as if the puff was going to solve itself. in fact, the former commissioner for industrial policy, antonio tajani, was aware of this, but instead of punishing him, the european people's party has rewarded him with the post of president of this house. dieselgate is not only a consumer hoax but, because of pollution, it is also a very serious public health problem and a threat to climate change. despite this, both the european commission and the member states decided not to act, to stick their heads in a hole. why would you do that? because the revolving doors keep turning around the commissioners, the lobbyists and the car companies. this web of interests endangers health and endangers democracy itself.

mr president, one of the great problems we are having with regard to bailouts of countries is precisely that of democratic legitimacy. and the fact that the president of the eurogroup has failed to heed the call of this parliament today only increases the feeling of democratic illegitimacy in this whole process - one more reason why he has to resign. but it is true that we are here today to discuss greece, and greece needs to bring the spirit of the european semester into its rescue programme, i.e. fiscal responsibility - not this excessive austerity that we are imposing with primary surpluses of 3.5%, with a debt burden of 181% - greater flexibility so that they can get out of the economic crisis in which they are, and socially fair structural reforms that also facilitate investment. and to that extent, we call for them to be able to get back to collective bargaining, so that they can increase their minimum wages. in greece, the total wages have been devalued by 40%. because we also need to send them a strong message of social responsibility, of maintaining the social model; that these economic improvements are also affecting all the workers and citizens of greece. we therefore call for a message of responsibility, yes, but also of socially just responsibility for all citizens.
in writing. the greek public debt stock remains one of the key challenges for the euro area. its long-term sustainability is called into question by the international monetary fund, which is pointing towards the solution of a restructuring by reducing interest rates, increasing grace periods and amortization periods. the eurogroup should take this analysis into account in the framework of the negotiations for the renewal of the financial assistance programme. in particular, cross-compliance needs to shift the emphasis from labour market reform to regressive reform (collective bargaining needs to be reinstated) and fiscal adjustment. as for the setting of budgetary balance targets, they must be moderate and realistic, otherwise social conditions and political instability will worsen and the rate of economic growth will be damaged. in any case, other countries such as spain, portugal and italy are at or above the threshold of 100% sovereign debt to gdp. the use of the european stability mechanism as a debt redemption fund could help to solve this problem for the euro area as a whole.

the rapporteur. the commission is also responsible for the implementation of the this is a very important debate because we are talking about our external response to the phenomenon of migration and refugees, but it is actually a debate that speaks a lot about us, about what we want the european union to be, about what we think the european union should be. i really think it's not the time for rhetoric anymore. a lot has happened. president steinmeier was talking about courage today. we should probably move away from rhetoric and instead deal with courage. the european union is undoubtedly at a critical juncture and is in danger of becoming even more introverted. with the phenomenon of migration and refugees, it has been completely overwhelmed. overwhelmed by something we call crisis. but it's not a crisis, because it's not going to end anytime soon. we must stop calling the movement of people fleeing the most absolute horror a refugee crisis, and they have only one thing, and that is their right to be protected. we must stop calling the arrival of thousands of people a migration crisis, when they do not choose to leave their homes, their countries and their families on a whim, but flee because they have no other choice. we can talk about another crisis. the crisis of european solidarity that is a crisis. we have to be very careful not to let the commission and the council get involved in this. we can also speak of an institutional crisis, because the european council has been unable to fulfil its own commitments, which were already minimal commitments in the area of refugee reception. and we can also talk about moral crises, because we are more concerned with blocking the access of these people to our borders, even if it is through spurious agreements, such as the agreement adopted with turkey, or more interested in encouraging returns than in alleviating the dramatic situation of all these people inside and outside our borders. what europe is receiving is a tiny fraction of the harsh reality of the displacement of people around the world, from countries much poorer than ours, which are hosting five times and ten times as many refugees as we call them. our reaction has been, to say the least, irresponsible. especially that of national governments. he's been short-sighted, myopic, they don't want to see that this phenomenon is here to stay. the report we are presenting is an own-initiative report and therefore does not oblige the council and the commission to act. but it is a voice, the voice of the european parliament, the voice of the representatives of the citizens in the european union. and this voice is saying that the phenomena of migration cannot be understood as a threat, that we need a paradigm shift, a narrative shift, to make it something beneficial, as it has been throughout history. this is a battle that we democrats cannot lose and that we must fight without any qualms against a rising far right and a populism of both left and right that is clearly on the rise. to do this, the report says, we must move beyond a security-only approach to dealing with human rights, to dealing with integration, to dealing with these people having legal pathways to our countries. and not to always transfer responsibility to third parties. we are asking many countries which are in much greater difficulties than we are to take on something which we are not prepared to take on, and this parliament cannot be ignored in this whole new strategy of agreements with third countries. we are facing a very serious problem of credibility with our citizens and we have to respond to them to the extent that our values require us to respond. i think it is a great step forward that the european union's external action is also dealing with the phenomenon of migration and refugees. that's good news we have to follow very closely.
the rapporteur. mr president, first of all i would like to thank mrs valenciano for her cooperative and rigorous work and her spirit of consensus. i want to start by addressing the issue of the report correctly: we are talking about the challenges posed by the flows of migrants and refugees and the external role of the union. it is not, therefore, a report which focuses primarily on the internal dimension. an external dimension, mr president, is of paramount importance in dealing with irregular migration and addressing its root causes, as was stressed at the valletta summit and in the recent european councils. migration is a powerful tool for development and can therefore contribute to socioeconomic progress, as it has historically done. moreover, it should be addressed as a unique opportunity to transform migration into a key driver of sustainable and inclusive development. i therefore consider it essential that a positive narrative is used that promotes an authentic and objective understanding of the issue and the associated common benefits. i therefore wholeheartedly support the 'together' campaign launched by the united nations to reduce negative perceptions and attitudes towards refugees and migrants. i call on the institutions of the union to cooperate fully with the united nations in support of this campaign. i would like to stress that the union must respect its values and principles in all its common policies and promote them in its external relations, as stated in article 21 of the treaty on european union, which i am going to quote specifically, since i consider it of the utmost importance for our purpose: 'the union's action on the international scene will be based on the principles which inspired its creation, development and enlargement and which it seeks to promote in the rest of the world: democracy, the rule of law, the universality and indivisibility of human rights and fundamental freedoms, respect for human dignity, the principles of equality and solidarity and respect for the principles of the united nations charter and international law.' the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i have specifically mentioned the solidarity of the union and of all its policies to emphasize that the union's aid and cooperation must be unconditional and designed to achieve development and growth in third countries, thereby also fostering growth within the european union itself, and all the more so as the union is the world's largest donor. it is true that the humanitarian aid system is absolutely overwhelmed and therefore we need a comprehensive and more durable approach to migration that includes promoting closer links between the humanitarian and development arenas to address this challenge, while remembering that the primary objective of humanitarian aid is poverty eradication. i would also like to stress the empowerment of women and their greater participation in decision-making processes at all stages of migration. in addition, i call for greater protection for the most vulnerable, such as the aforementioned women, children, people with disabilities, older people and lgbti people, and in particular that all of them be granted one-off assistance and increased humanitarian protection and facilitated access to residency status and basic services, including health care and education. in line with the doctrine of the united nations at the september high-level summit, i consider it essential to achieve safe, orderly and regular migration. to do this, we must intensify our cooperation with the united nations, giving a key role to unhcr, the new resettlement programme of the european union. we also need to fight smugglers who profit from the vulnerability of migrants, and it is important to strengthen the protection of the union's external borders. i would like to condemn and denounce the terrible death toll at sea, and i would like to express my concern about the missing children and to call on the union and the states to assume their responsibility to achieve a global and multilateral response based on international cooperation and synergies to respond to these present and future challenges.
on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank the two co-rapporteurs, mrs elena valenciano and mr agustín díaz de mera garcía consuegra, for this comprehensive report which puts the european union and its partners in the spotlight. faced with this unprecedented scale and complexity of migration, europe must respond with clarity, efficiency and coherence. this report focuses on several aspects of the union's external action which i consider to be essential. first, the european union and the member states must confirm their political commitment to tackling the root causes of migration and forced displacement. we need to strengthen our commitments with our partners, for example on the emergency trust fund, and focus our action on, among other things, economic resilience, poverty reduction and security in third countries. secondly, as regards the union's international partnerships, we must step up our support for the first-receiving countries which play a key role in responding to migratory pressures, such as the western balkans or lebanon and jordan. socio-economic and judicial cooperation with countries of origin and transit should also be encouraged, in the framework of a balanced dialogue. in this context, monitoring the operational implementation of the rabat and khartoum processes is of paramount importance. on the other hand, we must continue our work in collaboration with the multilateral bodies and ngos that contribute their expertise and support european action at global level. it is essential to continue to involve all stakeholders in the management of this phenomenon. finally, i welcome the fact that this report gives a great deal of importance to the fight against the human tragedies faced by refugees and migrants. human trafficking, violence and abuse are too many to mention when we talk about all these victims who are forced to move. we must react to it. answer is "blue cardboard". first, in the interpretation, there was only one question: is the european union credible when dealing with migrants? i would like to say one thing: credibility implies making commitments in brussels and then implementing them at national level, taking joint and common action by all the member states, and speaking with one voice on the international stage. if we have more concrete and adequate instruments to meet this challenge, then we will gain credibility. yes, the european union has everything to gain if this credibility is accompanied by the elements i have just mentioned.
i would like to thank the two rapporteurs, mrs valenciano and mr díaz de mera, not only for the report but also for the speech they made this afternoon. to assess the report, i think it is good to put some facts in context. last week we learned that there have been about five million syrian refugees, a very significant part of the population of this country. but there are 60 million refugees in the world as a result of conflict. if the syrian war is resolved - and hopefully soon - we will still have tens of millions of refugees in the world. the european union was to be taken over by 28 countries and half a billion people. lebanon, which is the size of the alsace region where we are meeting today, has one and a half million refugees. so the crisis is not the number of refugees that have arrived. the crisis is the management of the hatred, of the indifference with which we have treated those migrants or refugees who flee from war or hunger. the report has medium and short-term answers. and the first is to change the narrative: migration or refugee is not a risk. it's a risk to mismanage. and to manage it badly is to respond exclusively with walls, with fences, with repression, with the neglect of human rights. to manage it well is to contribute to the development of those countries that force them to emigrate for lack of opportunities and not as an option to improve their lives. to manage it well is to offer legal channels and humanitarian visas. and to manage it well is to respect their human rights in all their aspects when they arrive on union soil.

mr president, i thank mrs valenciano and mr diaz de mera for their report. the crisis experienced over the last two years at europe's borders has shown us some of the inadequacies of the union's migration policy. important efforts are being made - for example, the creation of the european border and coast guard or the initiatives on asylum and visas - but we all know that the union's migration policy requires a global approach that strengthens its external dimension. arrivals have decreased substantially on the eastern mediterranean route, but in the central mediterranean they are increasing year by year. stabilisation of libya, the main country of origin, is of vital importance. so is the materialization of long-term cooperation with other of our african neighbours, where a major 'youth bubble' is being generated. a strong partnership and comprehensive collaboration with countries of origin and transit is essential to channel migration flows, tackling, as far as possible, the problems at their source - poverty, insecurity, lack of horizons, etc. i therefore welcome the valletta action plan and the launching of the 'senegal, mali, ethiopia, niger, nigeria' partnership frameworks, as well as the proposal for the external investment plan, which the commission has put forward. mass movements of people are a challenge that affects us all: there is no individual solution. i hope that the work begun at the high-level meeting on the large movements of refugees and migrants in new york last september will be followed up seriously and that the european union will be given a prominent place. our proximity to africa certainly demands it.
mr president, commissioner, the challenge of migration and refugees is not just for the council of ministers of the interior, is it? no, of course not: it has an outer dimension. and so we welcome the report by our colleagues, but many socialists demand that the dignity and human rights of refugees be respected regardless of their legal status, and we also say that it is not acceptable that conditionality is a mechanism to determine that only countries that commit themselves to readmission or control policies can be helped, and that the criminalisation of humanitarian aid, now permitted by the so-called 'facilitation directive', should disappear. we demand safe passageways, humanitarian visas, humanitarian corridors as a legal way of entering the european union, and that the european parliament be involved in defining and implementing policy, as well as in its budget calculation. but above all, we want to change the negative and prejudiced view of immigration policy. we reject the agreement with turkey. we demand a change in this prejudiced view and a full demand that the council fulfill its commitments on resettlement and relocation, finally changing this security approach to a humanitarian approach.

on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, commissioner, president-in-office of the council, the s&d group has on many occasions expressed its concern about the structural shortcomings and the scarcity of resources available in the context of the current financial framework. during the negotiations on this financial framework, we were already aware of the terrible consequences of the reduction in resources compared with the previous framework, and we opposed it. and thanks to this opposition, we were at least able to achieve some achievements: greater flexibility, a mandatory mid-term review, a roadmap for the reform of the union's revenue system, and even some new priorities such as, for example, the european youth guarantee. and it is good that we have achieved these improvements, because to the multiple crises facing the union today we should have added the budgetary crisis. in these first years we have used up all the room for manoeuvre we had to finance new needs, such as the launching of the european investment plan, the care of refugees, humanitarian aid and the fight against youth unemployment. but let us not be mistaken: this has had important budgetary consequences, especially in areas such as competitiveness, research or transport. that is why this review is so important, because we have no room for manoeuvre; we cannot continue to cut programmes to finance new needs, because these needs are still there. and that is why we also value this revision positively: it represents a potential increase of eur 6 billion between now and 2020, and this will allow us to strengthen key programmes for the future of the union in research, transport or education. it will also enable us to give greater support to smes, to double the european investment plan and to refinance the youth employment initiative at once. and this will also give us the opportunity to launch new investment and development plans for the countries around us, to provide resources for the european asylum support office or to develop a genuine european policy for the management of our borders. but, unfortunately, once again the 'creation' council has not been ambitious enough or courageous enough to dare to make a real review based on a rigorous analysis of needs and priorities and putting all the necessary means in place. but we in this parliament do not lose hope. as soon as we have adopted this revision, we shall get down to work - the commission will do the same - without wasting a single minute on a new proposal for the future. we know very well that changing the dynamics - and the council reminded us of this - and the decisions in the council is a task that requires a lot of patience. we know that we have to keep pushing and that we have to prove, day by day, that things can and should be done differently and better. but that's why, as einstein said, we did it because we didn't know it was impossible.
mr president, the multiannual financial framework 2014-2020 has been overtaken by events. the brexit, the investment crisis, the banking crisis, the poverty generated in the periphery and the border crisis show that the corsets that this framework forces us to have failed. it is not enough to engineer budgets to move small numbers or to resort to private investment schemes and guarantee funds that escape democratic control to patch up the problems we face. we need a policy that strengthens the union's own resources, a policy based on direct and progressive taxation, together with national contributions based on economic capacity and weighted by the per capita income of each country; a multiannual financial framework that, in terms of spending, is able to stimulate a new and ambitious plan of public investment for europe, socially ecological and job-creating, in initiatives committed to the change of model and to the energy transition.

chief negotiator. mr president, greetings to each and every one of you, ladies and gentlemen. thank you, mr president, for allowing me to speak directly to your parliament today, as a negotiator and alongside president juncker, who first of all trusted me with this mission, and i thank him. i would like to commend the very important work you have already done together under the aegis of president tajani with all the groups and committees and, of course, behind guy verhofstadt and his team. dear guy, we have started working constructively and efficiently and i am sure that this will continue until the end of the road. so, ladies and gentlemen, your resolution today will be the first political statement by a european institution in response to theresa may's letter to the president of the european council last week. with this resolution you will set the tone by addressing, of course, the british government, the governments of the 27 countries of the european union, but also and above all the european citizens. i am sure that i understand the message you are trying to convey to me. our common objective is to make this negotiation a success, that is to say, to reach an agreement. there are three conditions for this, which i would like to recall briefly. the first condition, which has just been underlined by jean-claude juncker, is unity. it is by remaining united that we will best defend together the interests of the 27 countries of the european union and their citizens and, at the same time, as each of the group chairmen has stressed, the fundamental principles and values on which the european project, which was reiterated in rome, has been based since day one. unity is essential not only for the union but also for our british partners. at the end of the road - and i would like to say this so that everyone is convinced - if the union were disunited, we would simply run the risk of not reaching an agreement. but failure to agree - as philippe lamberts has emphasized very strongly earlier - would have very serious consequences. of course, first and foremost for the united kingdom, but also for the union. that is why i repeat that the scenario of no deal is not ours. our ambition must be to succeed, not against the united kingdom but with the united kingdom. not against the united kingdom but with the united kingdom. mrs helga stevens, i have heard your appeal. to do that, we will need to explain not only what we are doing but also why we are doing it. we have a duty to the citizens to tell the truth. perhaps we should finally say objectively, without aggression and calmly what brexit means, what simply leaving the european union means. may i also say that this negotiation should have an educational dimension for all of us? it will be an opportunity to recall, or even rediscover, day by day all the progress we have made together and often forgotten: progress for the daily lives of citizens, consumers and businesses. ladies and gentlemen, our unity will be all the stronger if it is built on transparency and public debate. this extraordinary negotiation - which must remain extraordinary - which we will conduct in transparency will not be a secret negotiation. the second condition is to remove uncertainties. where the united kingdom's decision to leave the union creates uncertainty and insecurity, our role is to restore certainty and legal certainty, first for citizens, but also for beneficiaries of the european budget, in the united kingdom and in the other countries of the union as well as at the union's borders. to remove this uncertainty, the principles i will be defending on your behalf must be perfectly clear. for european citizens in the united kingdom and vice versa, the continuity and reciprocity of the rights they currently enjoy, until the day of brexit, will have to be effectively guaranteed and without discrimination, as president pittella has just said forcefully. i have of course listened to what the group chairmen have said in turn. the letter from theresa may also calls for a swift agreement on this issue. but, ladies and gentlemen, and i can say this in the light of the work i have been doing with our team for the last six months, the devil is in the details. we will have to ensure, beyond an agreement in principle, that this agreement provides effective guarantees for the citizens, as president juncker has just said, and it will also be the role of parliament to be vigilant. for the budget, a single financial regulation will cover all the commitments that the united kingdom has made to us, and we to it, as a member state. again, your resolution is unequivocal. we will never seek to punish the united kingdom. i never will! we will ask the united kingdom to pay simply what it has committed itself to as a member state. ladies and gentlemen, mr farage, we simply have to settle the accounts, no more, no less. no more, no less than that! (applause) i would like to thank finally, for the frontiers, particularly in ireland - as mrs gabriele zimmer has pointed out - arrangements will have to be found which never call into question the existing fragile balances, dialogue and, in particular, the good friday agreement, while naturally being compatible with eu law. the third condition is doing things in the right order and putting them into perspective. the uk letter makes clear that the uk government will push for parallel negotiations on withdrawal and on future relations. this is a very risky approach. to succeed, we need, on the contrary, to devote the first phase of negotiations exclusively to reaching an agreement on the principles of the exit. we are not proposing this to be tactical or create difficulties for the uk. on the contrary, it is an essential condition to maximise our chances of reaching an agreement together within two years, which is very short. it is also our best chance, as manfred weber mentioned very clearly, to build trust before proceeding to the second phase of negotiations. this second phase will be devoted to scoping our future relations and to discussing the necessary transitional arrangements. in other words, the sooner we agree on the principles of an orderly withdrawal, the sooner we can prepare our future relations in trade: obviously, a free and fair trade agreement, a level playing field, but also in security and defence. it is on the basis of these three conditions - unity, lifting uncertainty, and phasing of negotiations - that we can succeed, and your resolution will set the tone. i hope that the european parliament will make these three conditions its own. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, mr president, i would just like to say a word about our joint work from now until the end of the road. as president juncker has said, your role in these negotiations will be essential from start to finish. the beginning is today's resolution, and the end will be your vote on the draft withdrawal agreement that we will be negotiating for two years. with this vote, you'll have the final say. the democratic debate on this negotiation, which is not and will not be a negotiation like any other, will take place first of all in the european parliament. this public debate, here and in each of your countries, is essential to the success of brexit, but also to reaching an agreement on other future relations, which, i remind you, will have to be ratified by your parliament and also by the national parliaments. all along the way, we're going to work together, every step of the way, every moment. that is why i am pleased to be here today, to have had the opportunity to speak alongside president juncker and the council, and that is why i will continue to work in confidence with president donald tusk and his team on the eve of the extraordinary european council on 29 april. i shall remain available for your conference of group chairmen, for the conference of committee chairmen and, as far as i am able, for each of your groups. in conclusion, i simply want to confirm that throughout this long and extraordinary negotiation, my team and i will always be at your disposal.

madam president, to this point almost everything has been said on brexit, even if nothing has been done so far. i will just underline four ideas that seem to me of the utmost importance on the subject. firstly, the resolution on which this parliament voted today sets the framework for any future negotiation. five parliamentary groups have, happily, presented it. secondly, both sides have to concentrate on fair and discreet negotiations, conducted in a spirit of good faith and political rigour. thirdly, we will have to learn to divorce, since we have not been able to learn to live better together. that means we have to prepare a future that can make it possible to combine distance with collaboration. fourthly, and finally, as chair of the efa group, i wish to express my conviction that both parts will be able to give fair treatment not just to the territories that have expressed their will to remain: scotland, northern ireland and gibraltar, but also to wales. we have a long way in front of us. let’s honour each other at least with two virtues: loyalty and courage.
madam president, i want to start by telling you, ladies and gentlemen, that there have been interventions this morning that have seemed to me gratuitously aggressive. i don't think the path of this negotiation is that important to us. firstly, i would like to say that we need to have a tough negotiation on the conditions for withdrawal. europe has the right to establish a requirement that leaving the club is not free, that it is not better to leave than to stay. it is a cost-based pedagogy that europe must establish as a condition of its own continuity. secondly, i think it is important to point out to mr barnier that it might be important that at the same time as we negotiate the exit from the european union, we have a framework that ensures the rights of the four million british and european citizens who live together, because it is important that that agreement is simultaneous with the exit. and thirdly, i would like to reclaim what i believe is the end of this process. we must seek an agreement, but, ladies and gentlemen, an agreement which must also be the fruit of a desire to live together, also with gibraltar. spain does not intend to make a war of sovereignty, it does not intend to make a war of sovereignty with gibraltar, but spain has a pending historical dispute and wants to live with gibraltar. but we cannot accept that there is a colony in europe in the 21st century either: you have to understand that. this is the will of spain.
mr president, what was asked of the european parliament today was to be high-minded in the face of the united kingdom's decision to leave the european union and to take a clear position on the recognition of acquired social rights, of residence, of mobility, of social security for british people residing in the european union and europeans living in the united kingdom. but we have fallen into a confrontation that will strengthen british nationalism. a cart on which the spanish government has signed up, for whom the sovereignty of gibraltar is a more important issue than the rights of the 12 000 workers who cross the fence every day. we must not lose ourselves in abstract discourses which hide, under the cloak of nationalism or a hollow europeanism, the neoliberalism shared by the european union and the united kingdom. we believe that future relations with the united kingdom must be based on solidarity and mutual recognition of fundamental rights, because there is another europe, the europe of the european social charter, the europe of the european convention on human rights, of which we will all continue to be part of.
mr. president, if we're talking about medical devices, we have to talk about essure. essure is advertised as a permanent birth control system without surgery. the multinational bayer has sold this device to a million women. since its approval in 2002, negative effects have been reported in women worldwide: heavy bleeding, pelvic pain, immune system disorders, and, to top it off, a high rate of unwanted pregnancies. the procedure to remove the device ends, in many cases, in a hysterectomy. essure has had appalling consequences for thousands of women. such a contraceptive method should never have been allowed to be marketed and its sale should be prohibited immediately. i am therefore pleased that the spanish national court has allowed a claim by the association of persons affected by essure: finally, the authorities responsible for monitoring a device like this will be investigated. something like this cannot happen again, at least in europe. we failed the women and now we must regain their trust.

in writing. under the name of hate speech, article 510 of the spanish penal code incorporates a catalogue of all-encompassing conduct that is punishable by a prison sentence of one to four years. criminal types such as the one i have just cited are the result that the legislator achieves when he is thinking exclusively of punishing and does not strictly respect the terms and concepts set out in dm2008/913/jai. today, a public opinion is almost inevitable as a result of the social media revolution. but what speech is liable to criminal prosecution? the trend in international law and the echr is not to condemn hate speech unless it directly contributes to discrimination or violence. i mean, he's advocating the narrow interpretation. this shows that member states do not always meet european standards and create hate crimes which symbolize contempt for freedom of expression, belief and ideology, which must not be forgotten, are fundamental rights. it's okay to use the law as a tailor's drawer. the european union and the european parliament must ensure that hate speech is only prosecuted when it genuinely generates a potential danger of discriminatory or violent acts.
mr president, mr vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, on 15 june, when any citizen of the european union uses a telephone, accesses the internet or sends a message, he will not have to pay any additional charges for being in a roaming situation. this is a huge step forward which benefits all the citizens of the european union, those who go out more and those who go out less, because it is an instrument to enable our companies, our professionals, our students to have greater freedom of movement, to have more and more opportunities in the european union, in all the countries that make it up. this is what you really have to consider. it was this parliament that proposed it. it was this parliament which approved it and negotiated it with the council - in close collaboration with the commission, of course. and we in this parliament must be very pleased that we have succeeded in getting these additional burdens out of the way by 15 june and have therefore taken a step towards the development of a european digital market, towards the development of a more integrated europe with more opportunities. in addition, we must be careful - as some members have said - to see whether or not distortions occur and whether or not they have an impact on the national market, because perhaps there are other factors than roaming. all this can also be taken into account, but today is a moment of real satisfaction, because we have taken a step forward in european integration, in responding to the real demands and needs of the citizens of the european union.

the next item on the agenda is the debate on the commission statement on the decision adopted on the european pillar of social rights and the initiative on work-life balance [2016/3020 (rsp) ].
first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, the eu is not a market or a currency, those are instruments. it is not just about consumers who consume, it is about citizens, real people, who are trying to make a living, getting their kids through school, struggling for a better future. europe has a role in protecting and strengthening the rights of all our people, and we are not a day too late in doing so. in the wake of the white paper on the future of europe, the first reflection paper on the social dimension has now been published, setting out scenarios on what choices we could make together. we are also here today to speak about the pillar of social rights and the principles that we believe are important to help member states to reform and together converge upwards. valdis dombrovskis will give a detailed presentation on both the reflection paper and the pillar, and marianne thyssen will conclude the debate on behalf of the commission. for now, let me focus on one of the initiatives we are bringing forward to put the principles of the pillar into action. it is a joint proposal by marianne thyssen and věra jourová that i wish to attach great importance to and of which i am frankly very proud. the commission today adopted an ambitious new initiative to support the work-life balance of parents and carers. with this package of legislative and non-legislative action, we want to increase women’s participation and representation in the labour market and ensure they are not obliged anymore to choose between a family or a professional career. and this is not just about women, it is about men as well. existing policies have not brought equal opportunities that allow fathers and mothers to work in care together for the welfare of their children, elders and society at large. today, the employment gap between men and women is more than 11%, and in full-time equivalent it goes above 18%, because part-time workers are mainly women. when families have young children, the gap widens hugely. women also spend five times more time than men on care and household activities. this explains partly the pay gap of 16% and the pension gap of 40%, which increases women’s exposure to poverty and economic dependence. the main drivers of the problem relate to parenthood, the unequal share of care responsibilities, the shortage of childcare and long-term care facilities and financial disincentives in tax benefit systems for the second earner. the economic loss due to the gender employment gap is estimated to be around eur 370 billion per year. in the context of demographic aging, we cannot afford to leave this huge talent untapped. this is a social and an economic imperative and of course, above all, a moral imperative. our proposal, once adopted, will repeal the parental leave directive to replace it by a directive on work-life balance for parents and carers. we propose maintaining the existing four months’ parental leave entitlement for each parent, but paid at sick pay level and non-transferable. we introduce a paternity leave of 10 days and care leave of five days per year and per dependent relative, also paid at sick pay level, and we also extend and modernise the use of flexible work arrangements. at the same time, we will promote the provision of affordable and quality formal care services across the union, including by optimising the use of available eu financial support. we will ensure better implementation and effective enforcement of the protection against dismissal, provide guidance to member states and monitor the development of their work-life balance policies. honourable members, we must stop wasting all that female talent and give fathers a real chance to be with their children as well. we are in times when we see around us a so-called cultural counter-revolution emerging, throwing us back into the past, often to the detriment of women. i am more than convinced that we need this package now. i do not want my daughters to be in the same situation as my grandmothers were. europe is not telling anyone how to live. there is not one right balance, but i do not accept that our daughters have to fight again the battle that their grandmothers won. work-life balance is about a real choice for fathers and mothers on how to organise their lives. this is our message: it is great to be a mum, it is cool to be a dad, and it is fantastic to be able to combine both roles with a carer.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, today the commission adopted its first reflection paper as part of five contributions announced in the commission’s white paper on the broader debate on the future of europe. it is fitting that the first reflection paper covers the social dimension as that is something that is close to the heart of every citizen. since the adoption of the treaty of rome, the european social dimension has been the founding principle of european integration. it should bring social progress and real benefits for people and has been the cornerstone of the european union’s success. our aim today is no different. we have come a long way in 60 years. we should be proud that our social model is a success. europe is home to the most equal societies in the world. the reflection paper provides an overview of the social realities in europe and the challenges awaiting us. digitalisation, globalisation and demographic transformation are already making their impact felt and will only deepen with time. new working patterns, often based on freelance or self—employment, increasingly also in the collaborative economy and online platforms, all add to the need to revisit our social acquis. the rome declaration emphasises the need for a social europe, based on sustainable growth which promotes economic and social progress, as well as cohesion and convergence. it is time to look ahead at what kind of social europe we want, what kind of future we want for ourselves, for our children and, more importantly, how we want to achieve this. who will be taking what responsibility? we propose to look at three options: limiting the social dimension to free movement only, progress in the field of the coalition of the willing member states – which could be the euro area, but also another grouping of countries – and deepening the social dimension of europe together with all 27 member states. all these options are feasible within current treaties and of course mix-and-match is possible. the scope of the reflection paper is to present a wide approach to social issues. it does not reflect the commission’s preferred option at this point. we look forward to continuing this debate with you and other stakeholders in the coming months. but today’s package is not only about reflection. today we have presented a european pillar of social rights. this proves that social europe is not a purely theoretical principle, but an evolving reality on the ground. by delivering on the promise to reinforce the social dimension of the european union, we are making a difference in the lives of our citizens. the essence of our proposal is the following: investing in people is investing in their future as well as in our economy. the social dimension is needed to create a resilient economy and sustainable growth, and to strengthen our competitiveness. with our initial european pillar of social rights we set out to do just that. more than a year ago we presented the first outline of the european pillar of social rights and, in the course of far—reaching consultations, we listened and took on board the suggestions expressed by governments, national parliaments, stakeholders, social partners and citizens across europe. all in all, we had more than 16 000 replies. in particular, i would like to thank you for your far—reaching report last january. today these contributions are crystallised in our proposal with 20 principles and rights. the central objective remains that the pillar should be a reference framework to drive the process of reforms at national level. more specifically, it will serve as a compass for a new renewal process of both economic and social upward convergence. as was announced from the start, the pillar is primarily conceived for the euro area, but is open to all eu member states. indeed we are proposing to adopt it through a joint proclamation with the parliament and the council as eu institutions and we hope that all member states will be part of it. the pillar is essentially a joint endeavour. those of you with long memories will remember that the charter of fundamental rights of the eu was adopted in 2000 via an interinstitutional proclamation by the parliament, council and commission. we aim to reach a political endorsement at the highest level of this proclamation in the second half of this year. the first vice-president has already elaborated on one of the specific initiatives accompanying the social pillar, but we are bringing forward three other accompanying initiatives to put the principle into action. the commission is responding to your request for a framework directive on decent working conditions in all forms of employment by consulting social partners on two possible initiatives. firstly, on ways to better align our social security system with the new forms of work. we want to ensure that as many people as possible, including the self-employed and gig economy workers, are covered and can build up rights against their social contributions. secondly, by modernising eu rules on what needs to be spelt out in a job contract through the revision of the written statement directive. more specifically, we want to ensure clarity for workers and employers on their contractual relationship irrespective of the type of contract. for both initiatives we would like to give social partners the possibility to look for mutually acceptable solutions before considering any legislative steps. lastly, we are issuing guidelines to help provide national legislators and employers with a clearer picture on what counts as working time, what happens to untaken paid annual leave with the interpretative communication of the working time directive. we are also responding to your request to ensure better monitoring by issuing a social scoreboard. this will expand the existing scoreboard of key economic and social indicators used in the european semester to better take into account social considerations. it will also help us show progress towards a triple-a social europe. our proposals pave the way for a balanced project that allows all of us –citizens, politicians, entrepreneurs and businesses – to reap the benefits of today’s modern reality. let me be clear, however: our aim is not to legislate on every aspect of the pillar. the red thread running through the pillar is subsidiarity. eu institutions, social partners and all levels of government have joint competence and joint responsibility to make sure competitiveness and social progress go hand in hand. i count on your support to make the european pillar of social rights a reality.

mr president, there is no doubt that the social dimension must be on the same level as the economic or monetary dimension. the future of the union is at stake and that is why we must ethically strengthen citizenship. this community framework for social and employment policy is of the utmost importance in creating a strong european project targeting the vulnerable sectors. the principle of equality, the principle of non-discrimination, equality between men and women, the integration of disabled people into all sectors of society, active support for employment for disabled people and support for their families must be upheld. as i said, we must fight against discrimination against all groups that suffer exclusion, such as lgbt people and others. we must also negotiate fair working conditions, with social protection and fair pensions. there is no one-size-fits-all model, but there are principles that bind all member states together. the principle of the union is at stake and that is why i support the commissioner and the commissioners in their efforts to regulate this social and political framework, this european social pillar. it's a need, it's an opportunity.

i think it is good news, mr president, that the commission is committed to including the initiative on work-life balance in the social pillar. mr timmermans has spoken about the proposal for equal paternity and maternity leave, four months for each parent, and that could be great news. however, he did not mention what i consider to be the key point in this matter: are we talking about individual licences, that is, non-transferable, compulsory and remunerated licences? or are we talking about maintaining transferability and non-mandatory permits? because it is precisely the transferability between parents that causes more than 90% of leave to be taken by women with a double perverse effect: to perpetuate the burden of care falling on women. perpetuate discrimination in the labour market. the outdated maternity and parental leave directives need to be reformed and merged into one. but let's keep in mind the key here: permissions have to be individual so that we don't keep making the mistake that got us into this situation.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, i am pleased to be here today ahead of the vote on the structural reform support programme. it will allow for providing technical support to member states, upon their request, for the implementation of reforms. these reforms – to modernise economies, strengthen competitiveness, encourage investment, generate jobs and raise living standards – are crucial for cohesion and upward convergence. such reforms work. we have seen how the countries that embarked on an ambitious reform path, such as ireland, spain, the baltic countries and portugal, have been able to catch up remarkably ever since and return to growth and job creation. this means less poverty and less social exclusion. yet, in general, the implementation of structural reforms is not satisfactory. our assessment shows that member states have made only between ‘limited’ and ‘some’ progress on last year’s country-specific recommendations. the overall record since the inception of the european semester in 2011 points to differences in the pace and depth of reforms. we all know that reforms demand political courage. they may impinge on powerful vested interests. their technical complexity is often a barrier, while others may imply budgetary costs. some countries face challenges in terms of institutional and administrative capacity. it is not enough to legislate, the reforms need to be implemented in a timely and efficient manner. this is where the structural reform support programme can make a real difference. in 2016, technical support provided by the commission’s structural reform support service was requested by six member states: bulgaria, croatia, the czech republic, romania, slovakia and slovenia. we have been able to assist governments with their public finance management, implementation of administrative, judiciary and health-care reforms, development of capital markets and access to finance. in parallel, the structural reform support service has continued to coordinate comprehensive support for the greek administration. for example, with the help of technical assistance, in february greece started to roll out the guaranteed minimum income scheme nationally. this represents a fundamental change of the social welfare system to provide protection to those who have been left outside any safety net. based on feedback received and numerous expressions of interest, such support is clearly deemed useful, even necessary. but this support cannot and will not replace the role of the authorities, which remain responsible for the reforms, their design and successful implementation. i am happy that thanks to very constructive interinstitutional cooperation, we have succeeded rapidly in accommodating our concerns. i wish to thank the european parliament, in particular the committee on regional development (regi) and the committee on economic and monetary affairs, and all other committees involved for their valuable contributions. i would also like to thank the co-rapporteurs, mr van nistelrooij and ms krehl, for their dedicated work, and the regi chair, ms mihaylova, for her constructive and open approach during the trilogues. together with the outstanding work done by the dutch, the slovak and the maltese presidencies, we have an improved text that awaits your vote. the key features of the programme are as follows. it will have a budget of eur 142.8 million for years 2017-2020. the scope of its actions is broad in order to enable to support whatever needs are pertinent in member states. but at the same time, cohesion policy elements are clearly emphasised. the support is to be provided on the request of the member state. it is to be tailor-made and adapted to the country-specific needs and effected in full cooperation with the government involved. we support the involvement of the social partners and civil society in the preparation and implementation of reforms. their support is a key success factor. such involvement should take place in accordance with the legal set-up of each member state and in compliance with their institutional framework. while underlining the spirit of cooperation and partnership, the administrative procedures remain light, so as to enable delivery of support as swiftly as possible, but always in full respect of the financial regulation. we are fully committed to ensuring proper monitoring and evaluation. transparency is crucial to all of us. therefore, we will transmit to parliament without delay the cooperation and support plans agreed with the member states, and in line with the conditions set out in the regulation. we will also provide information on the annual work programme, annual monitoring report and independent interim and ex-post evaluation reports. i am confident that the programme will be a positive instrument to make our economies more resilient. i also believe that the support provided under the new programme would substantially contribute to the cohesion of the european regions, as strongly advocated by the european parliament. i count on your support – both now and throughout the implementation of the programme – to make it a success.

mr president, commissioner, the european cultural heritage is one of our greatest assets, ranging from museums to customs and traditions to natural landscapes. but cultural heritage is not just monuments and works of art; it is also intangible and intangible goods. among them is europe's gastronomic heritage. of a wealth without equal. a legacy that has been passed down through generations of families. sadly, the hustle and bustle of modern life can put it at risk; and it should be the school that takes over. our gastronomy is a source of cultural, artistic, tourist and economic wealth and represents more than 300 000 direct jobs and 7 million indirect jobs. i would not like to forget another essential element of our intangible heritage: traditional european sports. many of them do not belong to the federal sphere. they don't earn medals for their practice, but they are part of our cultural richness. we must know them and support them so that they are not lost in the next generations.
in writing. cultural heritage, in addition to being a symbol of identity and of the historical heritage of the different european peoples, is an element that contributes both directly and indirectly to the economic growth and social development of the various european localities and regions. the conservation and restoration of the material cultural heritage, especially in rural and sparsely populated areas, will help to promote sustainable tourism, create jobs and prevent the deterioration and neglect of not only these historic assets, but also the towns and regions in which they are located. to ensure the success of the process, attention must be paid to training and specialisation of workers and to the recognition at national and european level of the various restoration and conservation techniques, which must be adapted to the specific characteristics of the work in question, from the type of materials used to the reasons for its deterioration.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, this report on the regime for the fishing fleet in the outermost regions is one of those extraordinary occasions to go from words to deeds and to call for coherence, empathy and understanding from the organisations which traditionally and wrongly associate any fishing activity with the attack on marine ecosystems. i believe that the first to be concerned about the sustainability of fishing activities are the fishermen themselves. i have seen this in the canary islands, for example, when i listened to the leaders of the associations and the professionals who spoke with love and respect for the sea and its life. i therefore wholeheartedly support their right to receive intensive european aid to renew their fleets. we are talking about improving their safety and working conditions in an environment that needs more and better employment. we are talking about operating more energy-efficient, less polluting and more modern ships, which will certainly make it easier to control their activity. we do not therefore intend to increase fishing capacity. fleet upgrading is not done at the expense of the balance between extractive activity and conservation. finally, i would like to stress and encourage a serious study of the impact of recreational fishing in these areas, a persistent demand of the sector, especially where tourism is growing the most. the fishermen want and have a right to more information and control over these recreational activities which, because of their current size and growth, put pressure on fish stocks.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, the overseas fishing fleet is ageing; the average age of the boats is between 30 and 40 years. therefore, for safety reasons, these vessels fish near the coast, where the resource is decreasing, while offshore it is literally being plundered by illegal fishing, which is exploding, particularly in french overseas. it is therefore time for the european union to agree to finance, through the european maritime and fisheries fund and through the member states, the renewal of the small-scale fishing fleet, which it has not allowed since the 1990s in order not to increase fishing capacity. the report by mrs rodust acknowledges, but does not call into question, this prohibition. that is why i will support with my group the amendment allowing this funding. i would remind you that overseas, the unemployment rate for young people is sometimes above 50%, particularly in guyana, and fishing can create many jobs. it is therefore essential to take sensible measures to develop economic activity in these neglected areas, while promoting sustainable fishing.
mr president, commissioners, you can imagine that it is a pleasure for me as a canarian to be debating the report on the management of the fishing fleets in the ors. in it we call for a single instrument dedicated to supporting fisheries in these regions: a posei programme for fisheries. i would also like to see better exploitation of the potential of aquaculture in these regions and, of course, better incentives to encourage young people to work in the fisheries sector and, of course, always taking into account the specific characteristics of the ors. but we are missing something: the possibility of allowing, under very strict conditions, really strict conditions, and in line with the objective of sustainable fishing, financing for the renewal of the artisanal and traditional fishing vessels of the ors. it's not true what's being said. there is no longer any fishing. it is about fishermen from the outermost regions being able to go fishing where others go, who also fish the seas. it's not about protecting the hundred miles for the local fleet. how can the local fleet go 100 miles with obsolete ships over 20 years old, without safety conditions, without hygienic conditions, without insurance because the insurance companies themselves do not insure that fleet? it doesn't make any sense. we are not talking about opening the field to giving more money to renew fleets without any kind of limit. we are talking about renewing, with all the limitations, the artisanal fleets of the outermost regions, which will also land in those regions. i advise you to read the amendment, to stop making demagoguery, to stop using the organizations as you are using them to go against the fishermen of the outermost regions. please read the amendment and you will see that what you are saying is absolutely untrue.
mr president, i am speaking in support of the work of our rapporteur, ulrike rodust, but also as a canarian, born and resident in an outermost region. because the outermost regions are the only ones mentioned by name in the primary law of the european union, in article 349 tfeu, which allows arbitration of individual exceptions in both primary and secondary law. and this is exactly what needs to be done to protect traditional and artisanal fishing in the canary islands, to enable the commission to allocate special aid for the renewal of an obsolete fleet, to improve its conditions not only in terms of hygiene and safety but also in terms of environmental efficiency, to do without more polluting fuels and thus to give a future opportunity to a fishery which will not increase fishing capacity, much less the loss of species, but which will, on the contrary, give a future horizon to a fishery made with great dedication, made with great passion, by people of flesh and blood, making a better europe where it is needed most: in the less favoured regions, in the most remote regions, in the outermost regions.
the rapporteur. mr president, this week marks the fourth anniversary of one of the greatest industrial crimes in history: the collapse of the rana plaza building in bangladesh, where clothing for european firms was being produced in bulk. it claimed the lives of over 1,100 people and injured over 2,500. the difficulty of establishing legal liability for this crime has made it clear that production chains as complex as the textile industry require control rules to be in accordance with it. but it also raised awareness about the origin of the clothes we wear: people don't want to continue to wear clothes at the expense of enslaving others. and what is being done by the european union to ensure the dignity of women workers in the textile sector? it is true that initiatives have been launched by public and private actors to try to respond to public pressure; but they are all voluntary, many of them are simple image washings that have not prevented exploitation from continuing in the factories. in addition, many of these initiatives overlap and do not cover the entire supply chain. so the problem remains, and that is deregulation. in 2015, the european commission promised an initiative on the sustainability of the sector at global level, which it also called a 'flagship'. two years later, you can say that they have done practically nothing, because the working document, which they just happen to present this week, is not going to stop the abuses. seventy-five million people live their particular rana plaza every day around the world: it is urgent that we step up. this report seeks to put an end to this situation, which is invisible in the western world but which consumers unwittingly exploit every time they dress. the most important aspects of the uzbekistan, dyed in morocco, made in sri lanka and with buttons sewn by exploited women in honduras. this industrial model makes traceability of each garment especially complicated. clear and specific criteria are therefore needed to ensure effective transparency. we have a right to know what we're wearing. finally, there is the regulatory dimension. if we have learned anything in recent years, it
