mr president, it is clear that we must reduce food waste at european level. the figures are outrageous, and they have been repeated here during the debate. and that is why i am in agreement, as it could not be otherwise, to ask for reduction commitments between now and the years 2025 and 2030. but i would have liked it to have been mandatory, and not just a recommendation to the states, which we know what happens. i also think that there are very positive aspects to this report, but like the whole of the commission's proposal on the circular economy, it forgets the state of agricultural and livestock production. we are still in a runaway model which tends to overproduction and the absence of living wages in the european countryside. in the meantime, we are also continuing to feed free trade agreements with falling agricultural prices. the only valid alternative, therefore, is to defend food sovereignty, short distribution channels and organic farming within the european union.
in writing. reducing food waste is a moral obligation of a developed economy such as the european union. food waste occurs throughout the entire food production and supply chain, and all actors have a responsibility to prevent and reduce the problem, starting with agricultural production. short food marketing channels can be an effective way to reduce crop losses, because productions linked to nearby consumption centres are more in line with real demand and crop losses are lower. in addition, these marketing channels are the backbone of the territory, consolidate the population and are an opportunity for job creation in a sector lacking generational relevance. the relocation of large production centres contributes to increased co2 emissions due to over-mechanization, long distances from consumption centres and compulsory packaging, which increases losses when they are discarded. local production at or near zero kilometres is the complement to the food supply chain with the lowest generation of crop waste, and the cap financial mechanisms should widely promote its advantages.
on behalf of the s&d group. madam president, commissioner, i would like to start by congratulating the rapporteur on her excellent work and on incorporating most of my contributions. the customs union is certainly one of the first achievements of the union, but it is not finished: we are far from achieving adequate harmonization of customs controls. in some sectors, economic operators are looking for european ports with lower inspection and control requirements and penalties, allowing products that do not comply with european environmental and phytosanitary requirements to enter our markets and, of course, allowing counterfeit products and illicit goods to enter. and these divergences are allowing unfair competition not only with our industry but also between european ports, by penalizing those who demand higher requirements and controls, and are causing market distortions, trade diversions and, of course, a negative environmental impact. this situation, i think we can all agree, is unacceptable. it is avoidable and depends on the political will to defend our union. the european commission, the council and the member states must do everything necessary to achieve a genuine customs union with perfect harmonization. and so does the european parliament. that is why we are here, bringing this magnificent resolution, introducing concrete measures to help solve this problem. the european union needs to harmonize the criteria for inspection and the number of checks at customs; it needs to establish indicators for assessing customs practices. i would also like to say that we must have a european control body which really guarantees harmonized treatment at ports of entry into the union. it cannot be such a complicated process that we have to go on living in the present situation. it is also necessary to improve coordination between customs authorities, olaf and euipo, and to harmonise sanctions and strengthen cooperation to ensure the protection of intellectual property rights. illicit trade - as we have already said - also contributes to the financing of criminal organisations involved in terrorism, money laundering, drug trafficking and arms trafficking. in conclusion, the european union needs harmonized controls, inspections and sanctions.

in writing. i do not share the discourse of those who argue that the euro was badly designed - at least not from the perspective of those who created it. the independence of the ecb means that national financial systems and debt markets are at the mercy of international capital, which has complete freedom to decide which policies and investments are financed and which are not, giving it ultimate control over the economies and budgets of the member states. in this sense, adding new levels of governance or strengthening the powers of the central bank seems to me to be just an attempt to formalize and legitimize the functioning of the ecb during the crisis: that it blackmails greece and spain to implement labour reforms that it goes to private auctions of large multinationals to finance at zero cost. i don't think this is the way. the ecb must be subordinated to the public authorities, both national and european, and must resort to the public debt markets when financial capital loses its predatory appetite for them. only in this way will it generate the stability needed to finance the social policies and public investment that europe needs.

author. – mr president, ethiopia is a key partner and a hope for economic improvement and political stability in a troubled region, but the truth is also that the country’s regime is authoritarian, cracking down mercilessly on those who voice dissent. economic growth and enforced political stability are prioritised at the expense of human rights and civil liberties, and especially the fundamental rights of the country’s unrepresented groups are being violated on a daily basis. most of these groups are systematically marginalised by the central government. those living in the ogaden and oromia regions are most vulnerable to the persecution, as the case of dr gudina and others show. there is a need for greater ethnically-diverse democratic participation and more equal access to political, economic, social and cultural opportunities among the different groups. being aware of the importance of ethiopia for the economic and political stability of the region should not relieve us from the moral obligation of addressing and denouncing the severe human rights violations still taking place there.
author. – mr president, the situation in south sudan is a nightmare. civil war, appalling human rights violations and under-development have caused huge suffering to the population and have forced millions of its citizens to flee. famine has been declared in some regions, and particularly worrying is the situation for the children. they make up 62% of the refugees and 17 000 have been used as child soldiers. arms trafficking is fuelling the tragedy, and the un report gives details about arms trafficking networks within the european union. this is a clear violation of the eu common position on exports of arms and dual use goods. this is outrageous, and i appeal to the member states concerned to fully take their responsibilities. the eu is a major humanitarian and aid contribution to south sudan, but the laxness of at least one of our member states when it comes to arms exports counteracts all these efforts.
mr president, since 2013 south sudan has plunged into an ethnic civil war, and according to the un, the conflict has generated three and a half million displaced people, of whom two million are children. in addition, the worst drought in the country's history has left two out of every three sudanese in grave danger of starvation. but the terrible scenario of repression, ethnic violence and curtailed freedoms, as well as the effects of climate change, is man-made. it is unacceptable that our external action is only contributing to the problem. it is shameful that our aid policy is only responding to our misguided geostrategic interests, completely ignoring the needs of the sudanese and reinforcing the legitimacy of a criminal government. the khartoum process is an example of this, because it allocates development aid to outsource border control, embellishing it with a nice human rights rhetoric. the role of the european union should therefore be to establish channels of aid guided by criteria of effectiveness and not by conditionality linked to collaboration on migration policy, such as the control of border flows.
author. mr president, one is bored enough with the condemnation rhetoric that we all agree on to come to nothing but to appease our own conscience, sometimes our own hypocrisy. sudan is a tragedy that is made by men. it is an ethnocide created by the human race, specifically by the two leaders (the nuer and the dinka) who are salva kiir and riek machar. we have to establish a ceasefire first. secondly, the presence of real troops to intervene. active troops, not the monusco scandal in the congo, that is, "tourist soldiers". we are truly forces of intervention in the face of the tragedy of the congolese people. thirdly, it will allow humanitarian aid to arrive. and finally, to establish a criminal court that brings to that court the criminals, the ethnocides, who are the leaders of south sudan. the ruling leader and the opposition. and, of course, freeze their assets abroad - in european banks! - which are the result of corruption.
madam president, mr vice-president, madam commissioner, a strong transport sector is necessary to support the economy of the european union as a whole, to increase the competitiveness of our industry and our global presence. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the transport of goods by road is an economic activity. the road initiative for the transport sector is fundamental to its good functioning, competitiveness, fairness, cleanliness and innovation. in the european union, efficient transport links have facilitated the creation and deepening of the internal market. investments in transport infrastructure drive economic growth, create wealth, improve trade, geographical accessibility and people's mobility. demand for road transport has been increasing because of its competitiveness, its ability to improve accessibility and to adjust to customer demand. it is therefore our job and duty to achieve goals that are in line with the new times. parliament is committed to working on all these reports, whether they are regulations or directives. it will be a long road, ladies and gentlemen, and sometimes even arduous, because this package is loaded with sensitive issues, whether social, environmental or innovation. but we must ensure that the result reflects a land transport policy that promotes fair, efficient, safe and environmentally friendly mobility, and that is also sustainable. america has one path; we will follow another that we believe is fairer.
madam president, the message of this package cannot be perceived as being against the european road transport sector in the face of other sectors that are less clean, less competitive and even less connected. and even less can it be a message against professional road users. i therefore thank the commission and the commissioners present for their offer of full cooperation. the eurovignette is coming up. firstly, we hope that the dispute with germany over the non-discriminatory application of the toll will be settled as soon as possible. we also call for clear and sufficient attention to be paid to compensation for peripheral countries, whose products have less added value, since they are poorer, and hence the added burden is unbearable. we are also concerned about opening pandora's box in terms of driving and resting hours, because the agreement has cost us a lot and we hope that we will not make it worse. as for mobile workers, we hope to improve their situation too, but above all to preserve their jobs and return home. and fighting as we do against social dumping, we would prefer to attack the guilty companies via blacklisting, but without putting the burden of proof on the workers, on the truck drivers. finally, one thing i regret missing: road safety. commissioner, how long will the infrastructure and the fines be in place?
madam president, i would like to thank the commissioner for her initiative and the effort she is making, and i thank her for the clarity of her intervention in order to be able to deal with a problem which is fragmenting the internal market. they can count on our cooperation to put an end to social dumping, to ensure that working conditions for professionals are dignified, that home-based rest is encouraged for professionals and that uncertainties affecting cabotage are resolved. we are simplifying procedures, reducing administrative burdens, supporting the decarbonisation of the sector with concrete programmes and helping it to take advantage of all the opportunities offered by digitalisation. and of course we are all going to work together on this regulation with the sector concerned, which provides a lot of jobs and is fundamental to european competitiveness. i call on the member states to stop their unilateral initiatives and to think, for once, that a good union is good for all its members.
madam president, we would have liked more time to study the commission's proposal on road transport. in any case, the transport unions were asking for something very simple for drivers: their right to a minimum wage, their right to rest, and to fight against fraud on the road. and yet, none of this has been picked up. the new regulation expressly allows short breaks to be taken in the cabins and long breaks to take place only every four weeks. travel for up to three days and cabotage for up to five days will also be allowed without receiving even the minimum wage. but above all, we fear that the rules will still not be applied properly to the workers. simplifying the rules, facilitating digitisation, etc. is good. but what we must do is to oblige the states and the companies to comply with the law and to guarantee labour rights. we expected a more decisive action and we are sincerely disappointed.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the new consensus opens the door to using official development aid to control migration flows or, what is the same thing, to outsourcing control of european borders to third countries, to countries in need. in other words, aid is made conditional on countries acting as a buffer state to prevent forced migrants from reaching europe, rather than using it to tackle the root causes that force people to migrate. this is just one example of parliament's position being ignored during the negotiations. other issues include the 0.7% target, the securitisation of aid and the gender issue. in short, we consider that parliament's position has been ignored; we consider that the text represents a huge step backwards from the previous consensus and, for all that, we will table an alternative resolution which underlines all these positions.
madam president, i think we should welcome this tripartite declaration on this new consensus on development in the world, and i think the title of the communication is a very suggestive one: 'our world, our dignity, our future'. i think that in view of the figures - the european union is the main donor of development aid, the main donor of humanitarian aid - no one can say that we are a selfish europe, although it is also true, commissioner, that every euro invested outside our borders is a euro also invested in europe. i think that this framework is certainly a suitable framework which must be developed later on and which places the problem, both in the internal dimension of the european union and the member states and in the external dimension, within the scope of the united nations' sustainable development objectives. he's very good at distinguishing between the short and the long term. and in this context, commissioner, i would like to express my concern about the situation in the middle-income countries. i hope, commissioner, that, as you announced in your communication, other criteria can be found besides the per capita income criterion, because there are also large pockets of poverty in these countries.
mr president, development policy may disappear from the international agenda. it would not be impossible, given what has just happened with president trump's decision and his commitment to break the climate change agreements. it could disappear, and the truth is, it's probably still more necessary than ever. it is perhaps the last chance to really change the order of things, which is causing half of humanity to live in extreme poverty. this is a consensus. it is certainly not the consensus that the socialist group would have made. it is far from what we would have liked, but this is the consensus that has been built up, taking into account, moreover, the council we have at the moment, which is not an easy council for this policy. so, turning necessity into virtue, our group will support this consensus. we believe that we are at the key defining moment between those who want to end development policy and those who want to turn development policy into anything but development policy. and that is why my group will support this consensus, even if it is not the consensus i would have wished for.
mr president, a lot has happened in the world since we adopted the current european consensus on development more than a decade ago. we have changed the development goals: we have made them more global and more ambitious. we have seen long-running humanitarian crises and conflicts associated with climate change. we have seen that we lack the resources to finance development cooperation. it is therefore time to review that consensus and to make a leap forward with a new consensus. in this new consensus we must apply daily policies that go beyond the consensus to preserve that development policy is directed at fighting poverty, to ensure that we reach 0.7%, and to continue working so that no security conditionality can put at risk the aid to those countries that need it, to those populations that are in a situation of dependence.
author. mr president, commissioner, mr representative of the council, the european union already has on its balance sheet a wide catalogue of initiatives in favour of providing resilience in various parts of the world: at the beginning of this decade reacting to food crises and, shortly afterwards, adopting a resilience action plan, targeting those countries with recurrent crises for the period 2013-2020. the council, parliament and the commission have worked together in preparing meetings, resolutions and decisions and in making commitments at various world summits: starting with the sendai summit on the prevention of risks in natural disasters; followed by the new york summit, changing the dimension and ambition of development objectives; drawing attention at the addis ababa summit to the lack of development funding; supporting at the istanbul summit a greater commitment to responding to the humanitarian crises that are plaguing the world, and finally in paris, where a great responsible president took a leap forward for the prevention of risks to humanity - because with climate change we are not only risking our world, but even whether our world will exist. and now, a small president has taken a leap backwards that puts the resilience of the entire world at risk. in this resolution, we welcome the recognition of the importance of resilience in the framework of the global strategy as a priority element for the union's external action. we reaffirm the need for the member states of the union to meet their commitments in the field of development aid, in particular by reaching 0.7% of that gross domestic product. we emphasise the multisectoral nature of resilience, which of course affects the economic dimension, the environmental dimension, the social dimension, the political dimension and the security dimension, but whose centre and focus is the human being in the midst of all these very multidimensional characters. we urge the commission to incorporate resilience into its policy dialogue with other global actors and underline the special position of humanitarian aid, which must be delivered with the utmost respect for the principles of humanity, neutrality, impartiality, independence and protection of human rights. respect for these principles is an essential condition for subsequently demanding access to populations in need and for guaranteeing the protection of humanitarian workers. we stress the importance of disaster risk reduction and call on the union to ensure that the new communication, which will be published in the coming days, is in line with the commitments made in the sendai framework and the action plan for developing the sendai framework. we also call for the formulation of inclusive local and national disaster risk reduction strategies. we ask that special emphasis be placed on the protection of the most vulnerable groups, the poorest populations, minorities, families, women, children, migrants, people affected by aids, lgbt people, people with disabilities. we call for gender-sensitive programming, and we also stress the need to extend the convention on the status of refugees and the kampala convention to protect displaced persons. we underline that resilience is based on respect for human rights, the strength of democracy, the rule of law, good governance and trust in institutions. all these are objectives which must be promoted in the implementation of the european union's global strategy, and we ask that it cover not only the territorial framework closest to us, where the crises are developing and whose effects are closest to us, but also the global geographical framework. we want to serve all parts of the world, with a special focus on the most fragile countries. and finally, we understand that providing education to children in humanitarian crisis is not just about giving them a right that belongs to them, but preventing further conflict and restoring peace where it has been definitively broken.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, we have heard our fill of how uncertainty reinforces the need to promote new governance models that strengthen resilience. numerous studies have shown that resilient democracies enjoy lower levels of social violence and higher well-being rates. we are therefore deeply concerned about how the union will promote the alignment of this new initiative with many of our international commitments such as the 2030 agenda, the paris agreement or the world humanitarian summit. building resilience must go beyond narrow visions based on, for example, security. this is a question that is closely linked to the whole of a political and social system. so, beyond the cheeses, we care about the commos. decentralisation of the energy model, food production, the promotion of open knowledge or the advancement of democratic participation processes are crucial issues for the fulfillment of our international commitments and also indispensable elements for the construction of truly resilient societies.
on behalf of the s&d group, madam president, commissioner jourová, as a constitutionalist, professor of constitutional law and academic, as a socialist and as a representative of the people, i have always worked for fundamental rights and against any form of discrimination against persons or minorities on the grounds of their sexual orientation, their membership of an ethnic community, the roma population, and their membership of a cultural and religious identity, such as the jewish population in europe, in the member states of the european union. that is why i am promoting this resolution and i have signed it in the full conviction that it sends a signal of solidarity with the victims of the wave of attacks and the growing aggression and offensiveness against jews in europe, as witnessed by the events in toulouse, brussels, paris, copenhagen, which resulted in a large number of deaths and, above all, the spectacular increase reported by the european union agency for fundamental rights in its annual reports - from 40% to 48% in recent years in france, belgium, hungary, the united kingdom and austria. this deserves a message of solidarity, and this is what this resolution is doing, by committing itself to a working definition, a working definition, which is not legally binding, but which is endorsed by the international holocaust remembrance alliance, which is an intergovernmental organisation with diplomatic representatives from the vast majority of the member states of the european union, on what anti-semitism is as inciting hatred of jews for being jews and violence, and therefore to attack jews for being jews in europe. it also advocated the strengthening of the security of jewish communities in europe and the establishment of parliamentary action mechanisms, special envoys and specific commitments by parliamentary groups against anti-semitism. this definition of work does not come from any jewish lobby: it comes from cooperation between the member states of the european union and has been endorsed by the commission, by the commissioner for fundamental rights and justice, commissioner jourová herself, and by the action of the commission's coordinator against anti-semitic actions in europe, mrs schnurbein. and my final message is that this has nothing to do, of course, with the sensitivity that legitimate criticism and the right to criticise the settlements and the violations of the fundamental rights of the palestinian population arouses. because it is not fair to link the settlement of the conflict in the middle east, which has lasted for 70 years, and the occupation of the occupied territories, which has lasted for 50 years, with the condemnation that every attack on jews in europe deserves and the message of solidarity and commitment to their fundamental rights that this parliament deserves. that is why i call for a vote in favour of this resolution.
mr president, anti-semitism is no longer the heritage of the right. in spain, 70 municipalities governed by the left have joined the boycott, divestment and sanctions operation, and some have declared themselves "zones free of israeli apartheid". apartheid in israel? israelis and palestinians even live in the same neighborhoods. hamas and the pa, on the other hand, proclaim their intention to expel all israelis. anti-semitism is today disguised as a demand for the rights of the palestinians. i too want rights for the palestinians, which is why i call on hamas and the palestinian authority to hold democratic elections and to guarantee the rights of women and all minorities. i would like to ask my podemos colleagues, if they were here, to explain to me whether it is okay to accept money from the iranian and venezuelan tyrannies, but not to trade with the only democracy in the middle east.
member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, thank you all for this very important debate. the eu is already today sri lanka’s biggest trading partner, taking 30% of the country’s exports. therefore, the potential to boost exports in clothing, fisheries, tea, spices, machinery and other products, as well as to attract investment, is of course considerable. this would bring clear benefits to the people and the local communities in sri lanka. granting gsp+ to the country gives a clear political signal to sri lanka that we, the european union, want to engage, to invest in its sustainable development, to support a government which has as its prime priority to re-engage with the eu and the united nations system, and to rebuild and reconcile the country after so many years of terrible civil war. nobody denies that there are still problems in sri lanka. it takes time to reform a country like this. we will engage with the government as we have done and we will deepen that engagement. we will be watching to ensure that they respect the 27 international conventions that they have signed up to. we will be watching the anti-torture legislation and the terrorist legislation. we will be watching the labour laws. we will be watching the situation for lgtbi persons. we are concerned about the criminalisation of homosexuality, for instance. experience shows that a positive engagement with a gsp+ country contributes to economic development and creates platforms and possibilities for dialogue on all these issues with the government, of course, as well as with business, trade unions and civil society organisations. this in turn builds the building blocks for improvement. we will be dedicated to the monitoring and we will be looking forward to informing you on this process. as i said, we are already sending a mission in september this year, and i will be happy to report back when that mission has written its report. so thank you very much for your support on this. thank you for this debate, and i am looking forward to working with you on sri lanka in the future as well.
in writing. in recent years, sri lanka has taken important steps to improve governance and respect for human rights, especially with regard to the investigation of missing persons cases, to provide better protection for witnesses and victims, to combat child labour, and to re-establish the independence of key institutions such as the national human rights commission. however, much progress still needs to be made. in particular, sri lanka should ensure that its anti-terrorism legislation is fully in line with international human rights conventions, end the use of torture by security forces and related impunity, and adopt policies and legislative processes to improve the rights of women, children and the tamil population. the granting of the special eu generalised system of preferences (gsp+) regime to sri lanka provides an incentive to improve trade access to the eu market, subject to ratification and progress in the implementation of 27 international conventions on human rights, labour conditions, environmental protection and good governance, by establishing mechanisms to monitor the effective implementation of these conventions.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, the european institutions are not the closest to the citizens, and that is why there is a great deal of ignorance about how they work. on the one hand we have legislative reports, which then become directives, regulations, which are binding, and on the other hand we have non-legislative reports, declarations, recommendations, which are not useless, but rather useless. in fact, they are often used to whitewash the european union or to make certain political groups in this house appear to be progressive. today, for example, we have here the recommendation on the multiannual framework for the eu agency for fundamental rights. of course, he is of the second type, 'second class', and that is why he speaks of promoting equality, non-discrimination, integration for migrants, fighting xenophobia and fighting gypsyophobia. and these are the same people who a few weeks ago voted in favour of a report - yes, legislative - to deport migrants. the multiannual framework for the fundamental rights agency will be great. and i'm glad to hear it. but what's the use? what good is it if they continue to build fences on the borders, if they continue to force trans people to be sterilized or if they continue to segregate roma boys and girls in schools? it's really not going to do any good. it will, in any case, serve to make it appear that some people in this house are concerned about human rights.
in writing. i am pleased to see the broad parliamentary consensus to support the work of the european union agency for fundamental rights (fra). like the rapporteur, i regret that the eu council has left out of the new multiannual framework issues such as police and judicial cooperation, which had been recommended by the fra management board, but i have no doubt that the agency will be able to orient its activity within the broader framework of the eu charter of fundamental rights. i'll take the example of the work done by the fra in their 2015 study on severe labour exploitation. focusing on the situation of migrant workers who suffer disproportionately from the most serious forms of exploitation (slavery, prostitution, etc.) , the work broadened the focus to realities such as those in the domestic, agricultural, hotel or construction sectors, where many forms of severe labour exploitation are generally unnoticed. the conclusions, such as the use of article 83 (2) tfeu to establish european minimum standards for criminal sanctions for breaches of social policy, represent a concrete example of an innovative proposal that recognises labour rights as an integral part of the fundamental rights that the eu must protect.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group, madam president, un ocean goal 14 sets out to prevent and reduce marine pollution, of which fishermen are the main victims and on whom the entire responsibility for the conservation of fishery resources should not be placed. in this context, we want to emphasize once again the need for regenerating elements in the lagoons and the halting of works which cause changes in currents and impacts on the environment. in the field of prevention, we want to draw attention to the impacts of blue growth and encourage this parliament and the commission to take on the need to prevent any activity that endangers fisheries. we are expressly calling for a ban on seabed mining, for the seabed mining concession in papua new guinea to be cancelled and for oil exploration to be stopped. i would like the eu to defend this issue too, commissioner.
on behalf of the enf group. madam president, the question i have put focuses on helping third countries to combat illegal fishing, highlighting the role of the regulation on illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. but above all it calls for better coordination between the fight against illegal fishing and trade policies. we are the world's largest importer of seafood and it is imperative that we close our market to products from illegal fishing. this is far from the case today. the commission does not prohibit imports from countries which do not fight illegal fishing sufficiently. it issues red cards, yellow cards, sparingly, to these countries, while it is much tougher on european fishermen who do not respect the rules. finally, ngos published a report last march highlighting the weakness of border controls and checks on catch certificates. i am pleased that there is a renewed interest in border controls and i also expect that these controls will be improved.

in writing. when we talk about the planet, we forget that three quarters of it is seas and that global warming is extremely affecting the oceans. sea currents are the planet's thermal regulator and can change the climate abruptly. the increase in temperature, acidification, sea level rise and the accumulation of waste and pollutants on the seabed and on the surface of the sea are irreversibly affecting our way of life, putting the livelihoods of millions of people at risk. the lack of jurisdiction aggravates the problem of over-exploitation of resources, illegal fishing and the dumping of all kinds of waste and pollutants, and the international authorities do not have sufficient legal instruments to punish these actions. technological advances, which allow us to know the state of the seas at close range, are key to ocean governance and will need to be deployed as a means of monitoring and control. the urgent convening of the un high level conference, focusing on the need for action at the global level to mitigate the impact of human activities on the oceans, should be a clear signal for policy makers to become aware of the serious state of the marine environment.

mr president, we are dealing here with the protection of vulnerable adults, that is to say, all adults over the age of eighteen who, temporarily or permanently, are unable to manage themselves because of disability or are unable to manage their assets. there is no doubt that the member states, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, already have their own set of rules, their own rules, their own legal framework to ensure this protection. but there is a legal vacuum - and that is why we are here today debating this issue - when a vulnerable adult goes from one member state to another, moves from one member state to another or has assets distributed in different member states. a legal vacuum is created to guarantee the freedom of movement of this vulnerable adult and also to guarantee his assets. we therefore propose to use, create a european mechanism which can protect these disabled people, these people in difficulty, these vulnerable adults, so that they can move around and so that the protection which a member state has provided to that person, to that vulnerable adult, can be recognised and enforced in another member state, so that that recognition can be guaranteed. we also propose to strengthen coordination, cooperation and communication between member states in order to ensure this protection. there is a need, therefore, to protect and to fill that gap, even if there is only one vulnerable person. the european parliament and all the european institutions do not create rights, but they do have to guarantee them, and that is why it is necessary to ensure that not a single vulnerable person is left without the protection of his or her rights. the hague convention is undoubtedly the 'flag' instrument of private international law, but it has only been signed by nine member states and ratified by seven. the united nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities should also serve us. i have seen that the commissioner has a lot of goodwill. i ask you, commissioner, to fill all the legal gaps to guarantee the rights of all people, and especially vulnerable adults.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, dear rapporteur sofia sakorafa, i am delighted to be in the european parliament today on the eve of the vote on prima. our modern concept of northern and southern mediterranean is an artificial distinction. proximity to this sea creates a shared heritage, and with that comes shared challenges; and science and innovation must be the tools to tackle those challenges. prima is recognisably the greatest achievement to date in euro-med collaboration in research and innovation. it is also an excellent example of successful cooperation between the european institutions. this cooperation would not have been possible without the personal commitment of ms sakorafa, and the tireless efforts of the maltese presidency and the hard work of the negotiation teams are a testament of this cooperation. so i want to seize this opportunity, as ms sakorafa just did, to thank the european parliament, and in particular the rapporteur, ms sofia sakorafa, but also everyone involved in this work and this amazing team that put all the institutions working together. today, during this debate, we need to keep in mind three things about prima: the what, the why and the how. first, the what. prima will seek to ensure two of people’s most basic needs today: food and water. why is this an issue for us? it is an issue because it is the biggest issue that we have in front of us as people, as human beings. without food and water we cannot make it. but if you look at the mediterranean region, with 180 million people that are considered ‘water-stressed’, this water stress was brought on by changing climate patterns, but also by unsustainable resource management and demographic changes. water availability, and thus agricultural production, is of strategic importance for the whole mediterranean sea. it means the livelihoods of rural and urban populations, and it means territorial development. water shortages have a negative impact on crop yields, so access also means the health and well-being of the population. we have to acknowledge that these issues are the root causes of migration, both within and beyond borders. how do we solve these issues? i think that part of that answer is exactly prima. these challenges are border blind and are often too big to be addressed by a single country. so no effort can be spared to identify novel approaches to ensure water availability. right now there is an insufficient level of research and innovation and investment in the region. this means a lack of innovative solutions that are adapted to the mediterranean region’s geographical needs and that are easily transferable. but we have to put in the means, we have to put in the resources. so prima will fill this critical gap. it will bundle know-how and resources to encourage long-term research and innovation cooperation between the mediterranean countries, from the north to the south. ladies and gentlemen, i am personally invested in seeing this unique initiative succeed. i count on you, honourable members of parliament, to seize this historic opportunity, and to help shape the future of the mediterranean basin by adopting the prima initiative in tomorrow’s vote. the mediterranean region has a shared history. as the great croatian writer predrag matvejević once said, and i quote: ‘being mediterranean entails more than history or geography, tradition or memory, birth right or belief. the mediterranean is a destiny’. let us then help the mediterranean countries to take charge of their shared destiny by embracing cooperation and by uniting against their common challenges.

the rapporteur. mr president, first of all i would like to thank the commission, commissioner moedas and, in particular, the rapporteurs for the report. i would like to thank the atmosphere of collaboration between all the political groups, because the importance of this report requires consensus, especially with a view to the next ninth framework programme. first of all, you must know - as you know - that horizon 2020 is the largest publicly funded research programme in the world, whose challenge is to respond to the social and economic challenges of society, so its evaluation can only begin by recognising its success and its opportunity. a programme that was born under the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy, especially conditioned by the situation of economic crisis and deindustrialization in europe, which gave an important role to innovation, improving competitiveness, strengthening smes. all this from the excellence as a priority, which has allowed a leverage effect of one euro over eleven. however, the rapid and profound changes facing european society - such as populism, xenophobia, terrorism, migration flows, socio-health, technological challenges, etc. - provide a new paradigm to respond to and which we must include. science should serve to achieve a knowledge society serving the interest of citizens, a sustainable and inclusive society in which the scientific community and industry are means to achieve the ultimate goal of a science for and by society. in short, to respond to these social challenges. however - and this is the first point to be made - it is necessary to strengthen the commitment of all actors in the european union to research and innovation. the european union invested an average of 2.03% of its gdp in r&d in 2015, ranging from 0.48% to 3.26%, far from the 3% target set in the europe 2020 strategy and far from the 4% target already surpassed by some of the most competitive countries in the world in research and technology. these data highlight this disparity and the need - and this is the first call - for member states and regions to make a greater effort in r & d. secondly, there must be an adequate budget for the programme. we need at least €120 billion to respond to and accommodate all the excellence that has not been accommodated in just 14% of projects that have received funding from the programme. excellence, of course, must remain the focus of evaluation. but we need more excellent centres. a more excellent europe also needs excellent centres, and therefore the under-represented regions must be given a greater say. the social sciences and the humanities also have to be taken into account and, of course, the impact criterion needs to be better defined. to address the gaps between regions, in addition to budget, we have, among other measures, to improve and make synergies a reality. this requires strengthening the role of r & d, but also reviewing the rules on state aid, harmonising the rules of the structural funds with horizon 2020 itself and ensuring that member states comply with the principle of additionality between funds. social challenges: we continue to argue that parliament must have a special voice in defining and guiding them in the next framework programme. we need the social sciences and the humanities to be better integrated and to have adequate financial resources. we need the recognition and introduction of research and entrepreneurial capacities from the earliest stages, with a reinforced role for young researchers, a fair return from the public, as well as greater effort in open science, the separation of defence from the research programme and a greater effort from industry... - i conclude, mr president - greater investment from industry, involvement in open access and, above all, added value from their projects. and finally, greater participation in gender issues to achieve the objectives we have set ourselves in horizon 2020 itself.

on behalf of the ppe group mr president, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur for his work and his understanding, which has enabled us to reach many agreements. i would also like to recall, first of all, the particular situation in the mediterranean. its waters are home to more than 17 000 marine species and its coastline is shared by 19 countries, which means that it must continue to receive differentiated treatment from the other sea basins under the common fisheries policy, as third countries play a key role in the state of its resources. but it must be admitted that the situation of the populations is far from the best. this is due to a number of factors, including overfishing, pollution and climate change. this situation requires action, but it must be backed up by tangible and reliable scientific data, which unfortunately does not exist at the moment. as for quotas, they must remain exceptional measures and be respected by all countries. socio-economic aspects are other factors to be considered, including those relating to recreational fishing. small-scale fishing accounts for 80% of the fishing fleet and 60% of jobs, so any measure that is assessed must take into account its impact, as well as the possible repercussions on many coastal stocks dependent on small-scale fishing, as a bad decision can have reversible effects. therefore, in order to strike a balance between the sustainability of resources and socioeconomic aspects, the views and experience of fishermen must be taken into account. finally, i would like to conclude by stressing the need to strengthen cooperation with third countries in the mediterranean basin. no measure we propose, whether it be spatial and temporal restrictions on fishing, the fight against illegal fishing or the inclusion of protected areas, can succeed if third countries are excluded.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, i would first of all like to congratulate mr affronte on his report. the prerequisite for any action is awareness, and in the mediterranean there is an urgent need to become aware of the state of a sea which is in poor health and suffering from the effects of great human pressure. but the mediterranean is also a sea of diversity with very varied types of fisheries, dominated by small family businesses and artisanal fishing, and where third countries also play a major role in the state of resources. any initiative to end overfishing must take account of the uniqueness and diversity of the fishing activity in this sea, as well as the fact that the sector has accumulated years of difficulties, due to rising production costs, deterioration of stocks, reduction of catches and a steady decline in revenues. innovative co-management models adapted to the specific characteristics of fisheries in each area and involving administrations, fishermen, the scientific community and other actors in the sustainable management of resources are certainly a good way to restore balance in the mediterranean.
the commission's proposal for a regulation on the conservation of fishery resources in the mediterranean is a good one, but it is not enough to ensure that the resources are used in a way that is compatible with the objectives of the common fisheries policy. we also think it is very appropriate to stress that the protection and safeguarding of fisheries and marine resources should not be the exclusive responsibility of fishermen, and we consider it essential that measures be taken, including the prohibition of those activities in the blue economy which endanger the future of the oceans and fisheries, such as oil and gas extraction, mining, industrial aquaculture, etc. it is urgent and essential to tackle the cleaning and regeneration of rivers and prevent tons of garbage and plastics from ending up in the sea every year. it is also urgent to establish the necessary preventive measures to detect, eradicate and prevent invasive species. another positive aspect of this report is the support for the need for fishing opportunities to be allocated on the basis of objective and transparent criteria, taking into account social, economic and environmental aspects, and for the allocation to be made in a way that does not discriminate against small-scale fishing and small-scale fishing, both because of the level of jobs they generate and because of their lower impact on the environment.
mr. president, i want to thank mr. affronte. the mediterranean has for many years been the great forgotten part of the common fisheries policy and i am therefore particularly pleased today that in recent times many encouraging initiatives have been taken to address the problems and challenges of this basin. as veronica lope said earlier, the mediterranean is an extraordinary resource which the coastal countries have the opportunity to share, but those same countries have the obligation to preserve this resource. any measure taken on one side of the mediterranean is doomed to failure if there are no similar measures on the other side. on the contrary, measures will be doubly effective if fishermen feel that they are not discriminated against, if they feel that there is a level playing field for everyone. a multiannual approach with adapted technical measures and adopted with the full participation of the sector is the right approach. in my report on technical measures which is now being drawn up, i am advocating real regionalisation. the socioeconomic fabric of the mediterranean is very fragile, composed mainly of artisanal and traditional fishermen who are also very respectful of the marine environment. these arts and techniques must be preserved as part of the region's cultural integrity and heritage and deserve special consideration and incentives. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing industry is not affected by the current crisis. the mediterranean deserves our full attention. let's not ignore our responsibility.
mr president, we are in the middle of an important debate. it is an own-initiative report on the mediterranean sea, and that has led us to an important reflection. i am from spain, and one of the seas we have for our fishing industry is the mediterranean. but i would like to mention here - a colleague has already mentioned this - that the situation in the mediterranean is not only affected by overfishing or the fishing sector. the increase in maritime transport also interferes; the urban situation of the coastline and the over-exploitation of mining also interfere. i am referring to the fact that there are many activities, not just fishing, involved in the mediterranean and in the serious situation. i agree that action must be taken in the mediterranean, but we must take everything into account. we've talked about small-scale fishing, but you know, mr. moedas, what's the problem? the problem is that when it comes to applying a differential to small-scale fishing, the member states do not do so. and when it comes to applying a quota system, they make a standard system and give more to industrial fishing than to artisanal fishing, hence the concern about the quota system. if they have to be applied in the mediterranean, then let them be applied. but we have to take into account the sectors that have the greatest sustainability and of course talk to this sector.

mr president, commissioner, since the beginning of this parliamentary term, the commission has led the transition of the european economy towards a low-emission, more sustainable economy. the multiannual financial framework 2014-2020 is proof of this, with 20% of the total union budget allocated to actions to combat climate change. it was with the summer 2015 package that the commission proposed a revision of labelling, mainly because with the development of new technologies it was necessary to update the legislation on labelling to make it comprehensible. mr eickhout said it: can anyone tell me the difference between an appliance with an a++ efficiency and one with an a+++ efficiency? that's what we're talking about. we must clarify the standard so that consumers can, according to their own criteria, purchase the products they are most interested in and point out that, thanks to this clarification on the labelling, together with the development of the ecodesign package, we can achieve a saving of 500 euros in each european household. and not only that, we can also make our industry more competitive, bringing it profits of 65 billion euros, according to the commission's own figures, and saving energy consumption equivalent to the annual energy consumption of italy and all the baltic countries combined. we have therefore returned to a clarification of labelling a to g, from dark green to deep red, introduced a product registration database to ensure that the competent authorities can exercise their supervisory role and empowered citizens, through a public database containing all energy labels, to compare the differences in efficiency between household appliances. i therefore believe that we must approve the agreement reached in the tripartite dialogue, and i take this opportunity to congratulate the rapporteur and all the shadow rapporteurs once again on the great work they have done.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, the reflection paper on the deepening of the emu contributes to the broader political debate on the future of europe started with the march white paper. the five presidents’ reports and the rome declaration underline that the union should promote convergence and that we need to work towards completing the economic and monetary union. i would like to thank parliament for its valuable input in several own initiative reports, namely brok, bresso, verhofstadt and berès. the euro is one of europe’s most significant achievements. it is the currency of 340 million people in 19 countries and the second most used currency in the world. it has brought price stability and has made it easier to do business and to travel. the euro quickly became the symbol of prosperity for our citizens and it should remain so. the financial and economic crisis underlines the weaknesses in the way the euro is set up. the determined policy response has made emu stronger but not filled all the gaps. there is still a lack of convergence and questions remain about the long—term resilience of the euro area. we cannot wait for another crisis to act. the reflection paper presents a toolbox on the way forward. it is more targeted at what can be done over the next two years to 2019 and more open about what might come afterwards up to 2025. key guiding principles for any advances are: a balanced approach in which responsibility and solidarity, risk reduction and risk sharing go hand in hand; the openness of the euro deepening process for all eu countries; and keeping the unity of the single market, transparency and democratic accountability. our ideas on the way forward are structured in three building blocks: financial union, economic and fiscal union, and governance and accountability. on financial union, we are aiming at renewed financial integration, safer financial institutions that can finance the real economy and more risk sharing via private channels. the capital markets union is key to broadening financial options, so i am glad of the recent agreements reached by the co—legislators on venture capital and securitisation and look forward to working with you on the initiatives on the mid—term review. we should further reduce risks in our banking sector based on the package of november 2016. we are also working on member states with a european strategy to reduce the stocks of non-performing loans. the eu framework for bank resolution will not be fully effective without a fiscal backstop to the single resolution fund, and without a european deposit insurance scheme depositors will not be protected to the same extent across the euro area. we need to further weaken the link between banks and sovereigns. in this context we are following the ongoing work in the european systemic risk board on so-called sovereign bond backed securities. they can deliver tangible benefits by increasing the diversification of banks’ balance sheets and by fostering private risk sharing. they do not involve debt neutralisation among member states or changes in the regulatory treatment of government bonds. for the longer term, we need a debate about the zero risk rates of certain banks under current banking rules and a possible new european safe asset. so there are both complex and sensitive issues. our reflection paper frames them with strong caveats, notably in terms of preventing unwarranted consequences for financial stability and for moral hazard. in the area of economic and fiscal union, the aim is to see convergence between member states towards more resilient economic structures. with the bulk of economic and social policies under national responsibilities, there is no doubt that we need to have a continued commitment to structural reforms. the european semester will continue to be the main platform for policy coordination and we will continue to seek improvements. the capacity of macroeconomic stabilisation in the euro area could also be reinforced. we are presenting three options for such functions to assist countries hit by economic shocks too large to cope with on their own. one option is the european investment protection scheme. in times of strain, public investment is the first item to be cut from the national budget and this can harm future growth. the investment protection scheme could take the form of a financial instrument and i believe could be set within the existing legal framework. other options include the european unemployment reinsurance scheme and a rainy day fund. in any case, it should not lead to permanent transfers among countries nor undermine incentives for sound fiscal policy—making at national level. finally, we need greater democratic accountability and higher transparency, integrating intergovernmental agreements into eu law and ensuring proper democratic oversight. pierre moscovici will be elaborating on this in more detail. i would like to underline that the white paper and reflection paper process is not an intellectual exercise for the commission. we hope to reach a constructive debate across europe in the coming months and to see a broad agreement emerging on the way forward.
member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, before i present some of the key ideas in addition to what valdis dombrovskis has just said, i would perhaps like to make a political comment. it was clear from the beginning of this process of reflection that, as far as our economic and monetary union was concerned, there was no question of whether we really needed to move forward. this time there could be no question of having several scenarios, one of which would have been the status quo, because we in the commission are convinced, and i welcome this, that we must move forward to complete economic and monetary union. why would you do that? for three reasons: first, because we have economic recovery in the euro area which is there, but which remains too fragile and too unequal. it must be revived and convergence promoted. secondly, because there is a real risk of a two-speed euro area. these consequences would be serious because, yes, it is true that populism has lost some political battles in europe - i am happy about it as a european, as a commissioner and as a frenchman - but it has not lost the war. it always feeds on economic dissatisfaction and inequality. finally, because it seems to me that there is a 'window of political opportunity' that is opening up in europe. there is now a pro-european wind blowing and i think it is time we took advantage of it. i want to stress that what we are proposing today is necessary and desirable for the member states. when i say 'for the member states', i mean all the current member states and i also mean the possible future accession of the others. it is not a question of forcing anyone to join, of course, but it is true that after brexit the only country with a formal opt-out clause will be denmark. all the others are expected to join the euro once the conditions are met. our aim is not to make the accession process compulsory, but to make it attractive, to make everyone want to join the euro. what are our concrete ideas? i am sure that you will agree with me that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. this is where we must articulate the principles of solidarity and responsibility most precisely. there are several concrete proposals on the table which should make it possible to combine risk reduction and risk sharing, particularly for non-performing loans. there are also other projects on which work is less advanced but which are no less important. this is the case, for example, with the idea of creating a new risk-free asset for the euro area, which could take many forms, but should not be confused with what were called 'euro-bonds'. what i would like to stress above all is the creation of a genuine economic and fiscal union, which we must pursue if we want a lasting and upward convergence of our economies. what does that entail? first, in the short term, we will explore the possibilities for strengthening the 'euro area' dimension of the european semester and creating convergence criteria with financial incentives to achieve them. there are also other possible ways to build up existing capacities in the european budget to help stabilise our economies. but we are convinced that in the medium term we will have to be more ambitious in creating a macroeconomic stabilisation function for the euro area. we believe that such an instrument would have many advantages: it would support the action of national fiscal stabilisers in the event of a crisis and it would allow for a better aggregated fiscal policy at the level of the euro area as a whole, especially when monetary policy reaches its limits. we know that this instrument should not be a permanent transfer mechanism, that it should not encourage moral hazard, but we believe that it should be put in place. of course, we must discuss its form, its use, its financing and its possible links with the european budget or with a reformed european stability mechanism. again, as i said, there are not many scenarios, but there are very clearly many options on our ambitious scheme. we also need to discuss the precise form it will take. this could be a system to protect public investment in the event of a recession, a european unemployment reinsurance mechanism or a rainy day fund - a reserve fund for hard times. the most ambitious interpretation of this idea would be a genuine euro area budget. this has been discussed several times in your assembly. each idea has its own merits. the only one we're excluding, if i may say so, is doing nothing. so let's get this debate started. last but not least, we want to launch a thorough debate today on strengthening the governance of the euro area and its democratic capacity. we believe that a stronger economic and monetary union depends on our member states agreeing to share more responsibilities, to take more decisions together on matters of common interest with a legal framework that is also common. the political integration of the euro area must therefore be further developed. this should be done gradually, and then, in parallel, perhaps new projects should be started. a first step could be - and should be, in our view - the formalisation, by the end of next year, of the already very regular dialogue between the commission and the european parliament on economic policy. we have an arrangement. i think they could be extended to other institutions, starting with the eurogroup, whose members - the finance ministers - will of course remain primarily accountable to their national parliaments. this could lead to an agreement on democratic accountability in the euro area, signed by all actors, in view of the next european parliament election in june 2019. in the longer term, i believe that such an agreement, if it were to be concluded, could be incorporated into the european treaties. it should be added that the integration of the 'budgetary pact' into european law was already decided by the participating member states when they signed the treaty. it should therefore be implemented without delay. another way could be explored, namely the integration of the european stability mechanism into the european system. this would of course be linked to the evolution of the european stability mechanism: some speak of a european monetary fund. what i think is decisive in ensuring that our decisions are taken more in the general interest is democracy. this is why, in my view and in our view, a new balance needs to be created between the commission and the eurogroup with the merger of the roles of commissioner for the euro and president of the eurogroup. we can and must also move forward. we have already made proposals in this respect for a unified external representation of the euro area. this is a continuation of what we said at the time of the phase 1 of the emu debate. we can go even further with the creation of a euro area treasury, which could take on the tasks of budgetary surveillance, coordination and management of the stabilisation function i mentioned earlier. this treasury could in a way bring together existing responsibilities and services, including the european stability mechanism, once it becomes an integral part of the euro area institutional scheme. this treasury could ultimately be placed under the responsibility of a euro-area finance minister. it is not a question of attaching to the appointment or the denomination. mrs mogherini, who chairs the relex working group and is vice-president of the commission, is not the union's foreign minister, it is not a question of supervising the ministers, but it could be a person who could just as well be president of the ad hoc council, of the eurogroup and a commissioner at the same time. finally, the idea of a european monetary fund, which would naturally be built on the european stability mechanism, deserves more debate. that's a quick roundup of the ideas we can come up with. they have varying degrees of ambition and precision. there are many options, but we wanted to build a set that is balanced. the euro is already perceived as a symbol and a guarantee of stability by europeans. our ambition is to make it, beyond that, a vehicle for prosperity. as jacques delors said, 'the euro protects but does not give impetus'. we must complete it in this direction and we believe that only by reducing economic and social disparities in the euro area can we permanently defeat populism, which is still dangerous in our countries. our ambition and intention is basically to say that now is the time to complete the path we started building at the time of the maastricht treaty towards a genuine and complete economic and monetary union with real institutions and with a dimension that is missing: when we are in the eurogroup, our fellow citizens are shocked and frustrated that they do not know what is happening there, behind four walls. the fate of peoples is sometimes decided without anyone, starting with you, ladies and gentlemen of the house, being informed. we need democracy, because there is no political union without democracy. i think we have done a serious job here, which is subject to your debate, and that is the debate we are of course quite willing to conduct with you and even more eager to do so.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, i would like to thank you for the opportunity to speak today in this timely topical debate. this is indeed a time of deep reflection for all of us on the future of the eu. i am happy to be here today to listen to your views. the title of this debate paints the picture of an eu which appeals to us all, one in which our values are placed at centre stage. one with effective and democratic institutions, one in which we pursue our genuine goal of improving the life and prosperity of our citizens, not just for the lucky few but across all of our society. this description is not such a far cry from the eu we have today and it certainly is in line with the eu’s clear ambitions. however, until only a few months ago, the eu’s efforts in this regard were largely ignored or discredited, either because the eu was perceived as doing too little or because it was seen as doing too much. but in recent months there seems to have been a shift in perception of the eu: rather than being considered as the source of many of our woes, the eu is seen as part of the solution. we are seeing some positive signs of renewed trust and more support for the eu. this may be because as the world around us changes, the alternative options to the eu are slowly losing their shine. we may start realising that populist rhetoric oversimplifies very complex issues and is beginning to show its limitations. we may also be recognising that working together on global challenges like trade, climate and terrorism is preferable to going it alone. perhaps most importantly, the more we feel our values come under attack, the stronger our wish to uphold them. this should serve to fuel our prospects and indeed give us an impetus to work even more eagerly towards our goals. however, only with a common vision of the eu’s future can we collectively pursue these common goals. in examining what future path to take, the eu cannot impose its vision on its citizens. it cannot come up with revolutionary designs if it does not have their support and backing. the eu needs to involve them in this debate. they need to feel that they are being heard and that their views matter. that is why the council very much welcomes the commission’s white paper process. it is a remarkable effort to steer an honest reflection and prompt a broad debate. i also commend you, the european parliament, for your constant efforts to ensure that the views of citizens are safeguarded and upheld. i understand that, along with the commission, you will be hosting a series of future of europe debates across europe. as for the council and the european council, as you know, leaders already began an honest reflection exercise after the uk referendum vote to leave the eu. at their informal meeting in bratislava last september, leaders set out a concrete roadmap with specific measures to address the most pressing concerns for citizens. this included tackling as a matter of urgency issues relating to migration, terrorism and economic and social insecurity. as work progressed on that front, the 60th anniversary of the rome treaties in march this year was another occasion to reflect on our common future. the rome agenda that resulted from this is a clear pledge to pursue our most important objectives over the next ten years. the european council has since then framed its work across these main priorities. it has focused largely on delivering tangible results and delivering on its promises. looking forward in relation to the white paper process, the council is taking careful note of the commission’s follow-up papers and is ensuring that they provide a valuable contribution to our discussions. so for instance the white paper on globalisation provides perspectives for a debate on trade or on globalisation at the next european council. i would just like to say one word on the concrete result of this process. reflecting on the future of europe is a drawn-out process. it requires time and building trust, neither of which can be rapidly glossed over. we do not want to run the risk of having to offer results prematurely and thus falling short of expectations. the council and the european council will continue to focus on achieving concrete results, demonstrating that added value of the eu in very practical terms. in that spirit, the future of europe debates will provide further impetus for the council to deliver on various key policies, rather than develop a new theoretical frame.
first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i would like to use the three minutes allotted to me to reflect on what mrs in 't veld said in her introduction because i believe she touched upon the issue of fundamental values in a very concise and precise way. she also dismissed the solutions offered by nationalists, extremists and xenophobes, but then the question remains: why do so many europeans still feel attracted to these political movements? i maintain that these political movements have assured quite strong support in the european union and will probably continue to get quite strong support unless we address the reasons why they feel attracted to these movements. i believe many of our citizens are worried because they fear a loss of position. this is the first generation that fears that their children might be in a worse position than they are. they are worried because of the threat of jihadist terrorism and see that some people want to attack our freedoms and take away our identities. they are worried because they see global developments in terms of peace and security, where they do not feel empowered enough to stand up for their values and their way of life. so i think that, if we want to rekindle the feeling for our fundamental values, we need to do something about these fears, and the commission’s starting point is that we can only do something about these fears if we stand together as europeans. so rekindling our values starts with advocating european approaches to european problems, european approaches to global problems, and with making clear to our citizens that we can only do this if we stick together. this is difficult at a time where identity politics roam across europe. this is difficult at a time when the other is presented as an adversary, and as somebody who is out there to take away what you have. if we redefine the european union only in terms of an internal market or a common currency and present these, or the cutting of red tape or whatever you want, as the goals of our cooperation – these are important instruments, but they only have meaning if they are based on our common values, and we do not talk enough about these values. the interesting thing is that the people who mrs in 't veld was, rightly, attacking because of their lack of solutions and the, to say the least, wobbly morality of their propositions, do have a moral approach to it. they start from their values. we should mirror that by starting from our values, the values that have made europe great: democracy, the rule of law and full respect for human rights. this is the tripod upon which our european cooperation is built, and modernising that in the fourth industrial revolution to show that we can create a society where diversity creates more ambition with people, creates more opportunity for people, and recreates the economy in the fourth industrial revolution, is the way forward for europe. but it will only happen if it is done on the basis of our values. that is the basis for the white paper the commission has written. that is the basis for all the analyses we have written, and we put them on the table as a starting point for debate with parliament, but also with the member states in the hope that the members of the council will use the paper to have a debate in their member states about where europe needs to go in the future. let me end on this. we have seen a sort of moment of awakening of a new generation in europe. we saw it in the british election the other day, we have seen it in the french election in many ways, and we see it in the women’s marches in the united states and across europe. why? because we understand now that, although our values are clear and eternal and cannot be questioned, they can be destroyed. the fact that we have now discovered is that, although our values are clear and are the basis of our cooperation, we now see that across the world these values are not unbreakable but need maintenance and that, if you want these values to survive, you need to stand up for them. you need to speak out for them. that is what i saw in recent elections. this is no longer about left or right. this is about whether you choose an open society with room for everyone, where no one is left behind, or you fall into the trap of thinking that your brother is your enemy. europe should be for an open society where everybody counts and no one is left behind.
