member of the commission. mr president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for inviting me and the commission to this debate, which has given me the opportunity to recall all that the commission and the union have done to make taxation more transparent, more efficient and fairer in the european union. the commission is, of course, aware of the links between the 'panama papers' and malta, which are the subject of judicial investigations in malta. the reason why we did not take a position is very simple, because the commission cannot comment on ongoing investigations. there is a principle that exists in all our democracies: that of the separation of powers and the independence of the judiciary, which we obviously cannot call into question. mr giegold said that a letter was sent to the commission today. the commission will examine and respond to the request. i just want to emphasize three points. the first is that several of you have explained to us that we have a restrictive view of tax havens when we consider that there are no tax havens in the european union. this does not mean that we are unaware of the fact that there may be problems and harmful practices in the european union which are being investigated, but a tax haven is another matter if we are to reason properly. why would you do that? a tax haven is a country that does not respect international standards and, moreover, the rules on transparency and the fight against tax evasion that are now enshrined in european law. i spoke of european leadership because, thanks to the determined action we are taking, european law goes far beyond international standards. all european countries have adopted these rules of law. they are all implementing them and showing that they have the need and the will to meet these commitments. there have also been several mechanisms, which i will call soft law, such as the introduction of a code of conduct on harmful tax practices. strong action is therefore absolutely necessary to combat unfair tax practices in the union. but to call a particular member state a tax haven is not, in my view, an intellectually satisfactory or rigorous approach. the commission will therefore not propose it. as regards the fight against money laundering, the commission considers that transparency and access to information on beneciaries are very important in the fight against money laundering and tax evasion and fraud. the commission defends its proposal because we consider it to be proportionate and balanced between, on the one hand, the need to equip the authorities with the necessary instruments to combat tax fraud and money laundering and, on the other hand, efficiency, which is also indispensable. finally, i am replying to mr ferber, who is displaying the letters we can send him. i hope to send others who will be equally visible and equally effective. on requests for access to documents, the commission, through its different directorates-general, in particular dg taxud, dg just and dg fisma, is working hard - i also tell president langen - to respond to the legitimate requests of the pana committee (the committee of inquiry into allegations of breaches and maladministration in the application of union law in relation to money laundering, tax evasion and tax fraud) for access to documents. mr president, you can testify that we have already handed over hundreds of documents to this committee, with which i am happy to be able to work under the best conditions. i would like to mention two things in particular. at this stage, more than 850 documents have been uploaded to the open internet platform under the pana commission. in addition, no less than 697 other confidential documents (including 375 for dg taxud, for which i am responsible) were provided to the pana committee in a secure reading room. it will be understood that a number of personal information about taxpayers must also be respected. in any case, it is not for us to make them public. but i want this transparency action to be carried out to the end, and you know very well - i am speaking to members of the european parliament here - that if there are shortcomings here or there, it is not the commission's fault, but rather that of the member states, which must also cooperate. that is what i wanted to say in the context of this debate, which i consider important. this debate must not avoid any situation. at the same time it must respect the separation of powers and must do justice to the member states and their action to incorporate new european regulations into their own national law. it must also continue its vigorous and unwavering fight against tax fraud and evasion. we have achieved extremely important results in recent years. in fact, many of the cases we are talking about are cases arising from shortcomings or gaps in previous legislation. they could not reproduce in the future. this is not a reason not to consider that we must go all the way with the investigations, but it is a reason for the commission to continue its legislative action in this matter all the way and to ask the member states not to weaken, not to fail and to stand by us in these advances which your parliament, i know, supports and promotes with us, and even more ardently than us.

in writing. the so-called panama papers have highlighted, on the one hand, that european standards, however stringent, are not sufficient without the cooperation of third countries, in particular by the full adoption of stronger standards within the framework of the oecd, and, on the other hand, the existence of complex schemes of aggressive tax planning and evasion involving third jurisdictions, such as panama, and certain member states, such as the netherlands, luxembourg and malta. it is thus typical to set up a company with no real economic activity in panama, gibraltar or a similar country, and then open the bank account where the assets of that company are held in luxembourg. the automatic exchange of information and company registers identifying the final beneficiaries are fundamental instruments in the fight against tax avoidance, but we also need rules to control intermediaries, which is something the commission is working on, and to put an end to aggressive tax planning on the demand side, i.e. the so-called specialisation of certain jurisdictions, including member states, in the creation and registration of companies and in the management of large fortunes.
in writing. today's debate could be titled: panama papers and the rule of law in spain, as panama is one of the favourite tax havens of the spanish right. ministers and former pp ministers, such as mr rato and mr soria, appear in the papers. even the chief prosecutor of the anti-corruption, a favorite of the current justice minister, had to resign when the press revealed his panamanian companies. according to gestha, the laxness of the treasury allows three out of four tax crimes to go uninvestigated. and given the current pp government's ties to corrupt and corrupt, nothing will change if the eu does not take action on the matter. the eu loses up to 237 billion a year to tax evasion in panama, 3.4 percent of its public spending, money for hospitals, schools and housing that the rich skim off to the working class. that is why i ask you not to be an accomplice and to act by immediately classifying panama as a tax haven.

madam president, we are adopting today a commitment to transparency and it is one of the rules on which the commission has made a report which we fully support. all companies with an overall level of revenue exceeding eur 750 million per year will be required to prepare and publish annual country-by-country reports in the interests of transparency. it is true that, as the directive says, this threshold, which must be lowered to bring it into line with the oecd, can be revised after four years. the safeguard clause is a good clause, because it strikes an essential balance between competitiveness and the necessary transparency, and it has been the result of many commitments until a balanced point has been reached. public information on those company data which are considered relevant, in particular for tax purposes, is very important in order to prevent tax evasion. but that's not the only reason transparency is important. it is important because it will undoubtedly strengthen corporate social responsibility and also corporate governance. it is certainly a benefit for everyone: for citizens, for workers, for shareholders, for the administrations themselves, for investors. it is true that confidence and the rights of workers are strengthened, because it strengthens dialogue and fosters mutual trust, since it provides objective and reliable data on the real situation of the company. it is important, therefore, to work on trust. one of the objectives of this initiative is to work on trust, social commitment and good governance. transparency is always a competitive value, without any doubt. it is a strategic investment, with benefits in the medium and long term, but it must also be sensible, and that is why the safeguard clause is necessary. mr president, saudi arabia is a misogynist country, where women suffer systematic discrimination, where crimes against women go unpunished. society is governed by a male guardianship system: parents, siblings or partners decide whether a woman can study, get a job, or even get a driving licence. the country has been elected to the un commission on the status of women. it might sound like a joke if we weren't talking about a very serious subject, but it's not a joke, it's a joke we can't shut up about. the socialist and democratic group strongly condemns this appointment. and we also find it intolerable that this has been possible with the support of at least three countries of the european union, according to the information we have. we must ensure that the european commitment to upholding gender equality as a fundamental right is reflected in a coherent position of the european union and its member states. it is up to us not to allow these international bodies to lose their credibility. let us stand firm in defence of women's rights.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to begin by thanking the council for the decision in 2014 to instruct the european external action service to start negotiations leading to an agreement with cuba. europe had limited itself in its relations with the island in december 1996 with the so-called common position. the european union actually self-imposed a blockade on that relationship, but really isolating cuba was not a good decision. a model negotiation has been worked on and concluded over a two-year period and the political dialogue and cooperation agreement between the european union and its member states and cuba was signed in december 2016. the high representative deserves the credit of this parliament for having promoted the change of decision, for having pushed this agreement forward and for having politically led the negotiation. we are going to be able to close, in part, the map of political relations between the european union and latin america and the caribbean. cuba is no longer the exception with this agreement, and i think that is good news. the european union is thus joining the ranks of the other latin american and caribbean countries with which the european union will cooperate. i also want to congratulate cuba on this step. the result of the effective negotiation was an international political agreement that is both appropriate and sophisticated and meets the needs of a relationship that will be complex, certainly, and very sensitive. it is a model agreement from which there is much to be noted. i ask parliament to give its approval tomorrow to this political dialogue agreement with cuba, as our committee on development has done, unanimously; as our committee on foreign trade has done, practically unanimously; as our committee on foreign affairs has done by a very large majority. the three committees have worked hard and i have also worked hard, but i think the result is good. the groups also decided to draw up a resolution; i presented a text, which i think was balanced, and the difficult part came later. commitment after commitment, we have distilled the majority positions of this parliament and i accept that i have to thank all my colleagues who have accepted my limits. we have decided not to make demands but to set political objectives for the dialogue. we do not put conditions, but we set challenges to the political cooperation which is now beginning, and always with respect for the sovereignty and independence of cuba. i would like to ask you to look at the agreement rather than the resolution. i would like all the agreements that the european union will sign from now on to be as clear and well structured as this one, and also to make it as clear how the european union and its counterpart will work on human rights. with the agreement, we all win: cuba and us. i have no doubt that the union has an interest in cooperating with the island. the central countries of the union have shown this in the last two years: the president of the french republic, the vice-chancellor of germany, etc. have all travelled to cuba with the same objective and, shortly, the president of the spanish government and the king of spain will do so, who are preparing official visits for the coming months. we've always been interested in the relationship with cuba. virtually all the member states had bilateral agreements signed with the island, despite the common position, and in recent years the european union has become the island's first customer and first supplier. it has been a great responsibility for me to be the rapporteur on this very important step that cuba and the european union are taking. europe has a great opportunity to show the united states, which is trying to back down, that it is possible to maintain the highest level of demand with the highest level of compliance as well.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the alde group takes a firm stand on the human rights situation in cuba and therefore wanted to accompany this vote of assent with a resolution expressing our concerns. we must not forget that the defence and promotion of human rights is one of our foreign policy priorities. under this agreement, human rights dialogues have been held with cuba and no progress has been made. to this day, the cuban government continues to repress dissent and political criticism; it continues to hold political and prisoners of conscience such as mr. cardet, leader of the christian liberation movement in its prisons, where they receive deplorable treatment, or the case of daniel llorente, an opponent accused of public disorder and resistance, who has been locked up in a psychiatric hospital. freedom of movement is still restricted: just last month, saily navarro, the lady in white, whom we had officially invited to an event in this parliament, was prevented from travelling. the agreement contains a suspension clause in the event of human rights violations. this parliament and the european union cannot ignore the involution of basic freedoms in cuba and it is therefore their duty to monitor the situation and respect for human rights on the island. in conclusion, i would like to borrow a few words from the cuban artist and activist tania bruguera, who in this parliament, on the occasion of the same event, said: 'i hope that we can see cuba not only as a place of investment, but also as a country where citizens can be free'. i share the same wish and i also hope that the european union will not turn its back on cuban civil society.

on behalf of the alde group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, since 2011 our parliament has recognised the need to integrate culture into the union's external relations. i would like to thank mr silvia costa and mr elmar brok for their work and the high representative, mrs federica mogherini, for the joint communication on a european union strategy for international cultural relations. we stress in the text the importance of culture as a tool for diplomacy and call for it to be recognised as the fourth pillar of sustainable development and as a human right. among the concrete measures we recommend: an annual action plan with a separate budget line to support international cultural relations; a mechanism for the prevention, evaluation and reconstruction of endangered heritage, including an emergency instrument to safeguard heritage in countries in conflict; the inclusion of culture in all existing and future agreements of the european union with third countries. the political objective of this report is to foster cultural cooperation between the union and its partner countries and to promote a world order based on peace, the rule of law and respect for fundamental rights. in the long term, cultural cooperation within and outside europe which respects basic values of civilization and common principles is the only way to achieve this desired order. we need to promote international cultural cooperation, understood in the broadest possible sense, from policies to safeguard cultural heritage to scientific diplomacy capable of spreading more rationality and love of knowledge in a divided world. the development of prosperous and cooperative cultures also represents a 'vaccine' to prevent movements, for example, of migrants who are destabilizing for the receiving countries and who are also not the solution for the countries of origin, as we are sadly seeing these days.

the rapporteur. madam president, thank you, commissioner jourová and commissioner oettinger, for being here at this late hour of the night, on the verge of midnight. after hours of debating strategic guidelines, recommendations and the situation in countries over which the european union cannot legislate because it has no jurisdiction over them... finally a legislative initiative! finally, a piece of legislation under discussion in this house; nothing less than the one that best expresses the political dimension, including the constitutional ambition of the european union, because it is european criminal legislation, finally, in the protection of the financial interests of the union, in the protection of the european budget against fraud on a european scale. it has been years of debate in which i am very grateful for the cooperation of the rapporteur for the cont committee, mrs gräßle. we have worked for more than four years to achieve this objective of the area of freedom, justice and security, this directive which harmonises european legislation, making fraud against the european budget an objective of european criminal law which will be necessary to set up the european public prosecutor's office, provided for in article 86, with the protection of financial interests as its first competence, but it is to be hoped that it will be possible to extend it to other serious crimes of a transnational scale in implementation of article 83 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are not used to the detriment of the member states. and that is exactly what this directive does with regard to fraud, corruption, misappropriation and embezzlement, by finally establishing minimum penalties, minimum penalties and a penalty of up to four years' imprisonment for these offences - of course, optional for the judge, to be decided by the judge. but the really important objective is that parliament has entered into a dialogue with the council, and this dialogue has lasted no less than two and a half years, because we adopted the first reading in april 2014 and we have been discussing with the council four main issues... the commission is also proposing to include vat fraud as an objective of european criminal law, which the council has opposed. we have finally succeeded in ensuring that this financial resource of the union - because it is indeed a budgetary resource of the union - is covered by this directive. the final commitment states that vat fraud will have to be of a significant amount over eur 10 million and that it will have to be cross-border in nature, i.e. involving at least two member states of the union. secondly, the discussion on fraud in public procurement is at european level, and the council is committed to considering the matter in the future implementation of the directive. minimum and maximum sanctions: a minimum sanction, applicable throughout the union, for fraud and related offences, with a commitment of at least up to four years' imprisonment, provided that the fraud amounts to at least eur 100 million. it is a necessary objective to protect the financial interests of the union. and the discussion on the limitation period, which is what is becoming ever more heterogeneous and divergent in the national legislation of the member states: we have established a standard term of at least five years from the date of the alleged offence, but it can be reduced to three years in the event that there has been an interruption of the limitation period by national legislation, in accordance with the relevant considerations in the process when the suspect has fled the country or had to be extradited before the process can continue. we are therefore dealing with a piece of european criminal law. finally, european criminal legislation that meets the objective set by the lisbon treaty, the area of freedom, justice and security, which is necessary for the council to finally be able to adopt its enhanced cooperation, to launch the european public prosecutor's office, which will undoubtedly be a result of this legislature's rapid legislative achievements in developing the area of freedom, justice and security. this legislature, which has been slow to meet the objectives of the lisbon treaty, is today finally striking a goal at the real door.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud in the area of vat. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. i would therefore like to extend my warmest congratulations to the co-pilots, mrs gräßle and mr lópez aguilar, for having managed to bring this ship to a safe harbour and, of course, to the stewards, mrs jourová and mr oettinger. i congratulate you very much, not only for making history in terms of criminal law and for having succeeded in fighting fraud against the resources of the european budget and in giving the tax authorities that legal basis, but also because, in a way, today we have rescued vat, we have defended it against those who at one time and in some state secretariat, in berlin in particular, wanted to end vat as a resource of the european budget. in that sense, i congratulate myself tonight as well.
the rapporteur. - madam president, this morning, more than 12 hours ago, in this very chamber, we paid tribute to simone veil, the symbol of the first parliament directly elected by the european people 38 years ago. since then this parliament has grown, it has matured. finally, it is a legislative parliament; it legislates on fundamental rights and nothing less than on criminal law, a competence traditionally attributed exclusively to the sovereignty of the member states. it is time to say very clearly that this parliament matters, that it is not a second-rate parliament; to say it to the 500 million citizens whom this parliament represents and to say it with particular courage, at a time when we are adopting criminal legislation which also provides additional resources in the protection of the financial interests of the union, when they are so necessary to supply the wreckage of austerity policy, to provide the necessary resources to restore the damaged european social model, so that the whole policy of the european social model that made europe the best can once again make sense. i think it is time for this parliament to assert its legislative, regulatory and binding character, because it frames criminal law and legislation on matters as important as fundamental rights in the data protection of the national parliaments of the, still today, twenty-eight member states; mentioned it here - it is part of the external investment plan which has a technical assistance component to help partner countries attract that investment, private capital, and help prepare and member of the commission. – madam president, on behalf of my dear colleague pierre moscovici, i would like to thank the rapporteur, the shadow rapporteurs and the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ) for their high-quality report and their very constructive and comprehensive work on the directive on tax dispute resolution mechanisms. this directive is yet another building block in the commission’s action towards a fairer, more efficient, more competitive and at the same time, more transparent corporate tax system in the eu. whilst proposing stricter rules against tax avoidance and ensuring that taxes are paid where profits are generated, the commission is also very much concerned about providing legal certainty for taxpayers and ensuring that when they operate cross-border they pay taxes on their income and capital only once, not twice. double taxation occurs when two or more countries claim the right to tax the same income or profits of a company. there are estimated to be around 900 double taxation disputes ongoing in the eu today between member states, under the current dispute resolution mechanisms, mainly dealing with transfer pricing issues. double taxation is a serious obstacle to cross-border investment in our single market, leading to uncertainty and discouraging cross-border trade. under the existing procedures, unresolved double taxation disputes between member states represents eur 10 billion in the eu. from an investor’s perspective, robust, reliable and stable procedures and predictable behaviour on the part of tax administrations as regards eliminating double taxation are important factors for doing business in a country. to remedy the current situation, the directive provides for mandatory and binding dispute resolution mechanisms with clear timelines and an obligation to reach results. it significantly improves the existing mechanisms for resolving disputes between member states. the text allows for a ‘mutual agreement procedure’ to be initiated by the taxpayer, under which member states must reach an agreement within a set deadline. if the procedure fails, an arbitration procedure is launched to resolve the dispute within specified timelines. the directive is also a direct response to the calls of this house included, for example, in the econ resolution from december 2015, known as taxe, and its taxe ii resolution of july 2016. econ’s report highlights some key elements of efficiency and effectiveness, such as setting ambitious timelines, ensuring independence of the members of the arbitration commission, deciding on disputed cases and enhancing transparency. as regards timelines, setting up ambitious time limits had to be balanced against the international environment and the procedures set out in tax treaties. other elements, such as the increased number of cases, fostering the capacities of tax administration, as well as business realities and the global tax environment, involving more complicated and sophisticated cases, were also considered. as far as independence of the members of the arbitration commission is concerned, the commission recognises the high importance of the issue. that is why we are fully committed to ensuring the right balance between the criteria of independence and integrity towards competence of the independent person, given the increased complexity and sophistication of the cases involved. with regard to increasing transparency, the publication of a summary of each decision on disputed cases, is regarded as highly beneficial. furthermore, the commission has also ensured that taxpayers’ rights and obligations throughout the procedure are significantly improved. finally, the directive ensures that the mechanisms do not result in double non-taxation situations. if the affected taxpayer cannot prove that there is double taxation, member states can decide to deny access to the procedure. i count on parliament’s full support for this important file, so that we can continue delivering our ambitious agenda for a competitive and growth-driven tax environment; full speed ahead! the most crucial imminent steps in this regard are: the introduction of a common consolidated corporate tax base (ccctb). the ccctb is exactly the fair, efficient and competitive corporate tax system that the eu desperately needs – now and for the future. first, because the ccctb will create a simpler, more stable and more attractive environment for businesses and investors inside europe. second, it will encourage growth-friendly business activities and will boost the competitiveness of the eu as a whole. and finally, the ccctb will make corporate taxation fairer and more efficient. it is the ultimate tool for combating tax avoidance.

member of the commission. – mr president, it is a pleasure to be here today in the plenary on the lulucf proposal. this is an important initiative to implement the european union commitments under the paris agreement and to contribute to the domestic european union 2030 greenhouse gas emissions reduction target. the european council’s guidance from october 2014 states that the eu target is ‘an economy-wide absolute reduction from base—year emissions’, reaching ‘at least 40% domestic reduction’ and covering all of the eu’s emissions. contribution from land use and forests in reaching the long—term climate mitigation objectives is critical because of their potential for anthropogenic removal of carbon from the atmosphere. forests alone currently cover more than 42% of the european union land surface and have a huge potential for climate change mitigation through additional sequestration and storage of co2 and through the potential to substitute fossil-based energy and materials. this debate and the vote this week show that the european union is serious about its international climate commitment under the paris agreement. by doing so, parliament is also making swift progress on one of the key legislative priorities of the union: under the joint declaration of the european union’s legislative priorities for 2017, the three institutions have agreed that the 2030 climate action proposals are given priority treatment in 2017. i appreciate the hard work of the rapporteur, mr lins, on this proposal and would thank him for the excellent cooperation. many of the key elements of what you are proposing for vote in this house are in line with the commission proposals, notably on the need to ensure the robustness of the accounting rules, in particular for forestry, and the sustainable management of forests. this is encouraging, as – like in the commission proposals – this maintains a careful balance between the need to respond to an increasing demand of biomass availability and climate mitigation objectives. i also note your efforts to further strengthen the environmental integrity of the framework by introducing additional safeguards. let me offer a few comments on the key aspects of the rapporteur’s final proposal. first, the report adopted by the environment committee retains the main principles of the commission proposal on the construction of forest reference levels. however, it modifies the reference period to a more recent one – 2000 to 2012. this period would include policies promoting increased harvesting in the benchmark and risk hiding real emissions of forest biomass. we should instead be incentivising sustainable forest management and we are open on how to address this challenge. however, the use of a more recent reference period risks compromising the environmental integrity of the lulucf accounting framework. second, we understand the concerns of some over the proposal’s language on management intensity, especially that of harvests. the commission proposal is a way to acknowledge that the management intensity of forests must vary, in accordance with the national characteristics of the forest. if forests become older, more trees will reach maturity and increased harvest may be needed. the commission proposal acknowledges that the future forest dynamics need to be captured in a forward-looking, projected forest reference level and does not fix the harvest to that of the past. the commission has, for example, even shown that a harvest increase of up to two per cent may be justified in the projected forest reference level, averaged across the european union. third, we must also consider this treatment of biomass emissions vis-à-vis the other legislative proposals. emissions from combustion of biomass under the ets and the esr are zero rated. if instead the accounting of biomass emissions is done downstream in these sectors, the administrative and technical burden would be extreme. we need therefore to be pragmatic. a credible, robust approach compatible with the other pillars of the policy is required. fourth, i note with interest the proposal to give more visibility to harvested wood products. we see that this aspect of lulucf is positive, not only for the climate, but also for jobs and the economy. that is why it deserved a special place in our proposal, as the only carbon pool with specific rules and a specific article. fifth, i welcome the specific improvements enhancing environmental integrity, such as the progressive inclusion of wetlands in the accounting scope, as of 2026, and the safeguard discussed of ensuring that the union’s forest sink does not decrease, compared to the 1990 to 2009 average. lastly, i note that the report closely tracks the commission proposal in respect of agricultural land accounting. we are pleased to see that a proportioned and balanced approach seems to have been found in determining flexibility towards the effort sharing sectors. the commission fully supports the efforts of parliament and the council to agree on the ets and non-ets proposals before the end of the year. on the ets file we are in trilogue negotiations, and i welcome the renewed efforts to progress there. i look forward to continuing to work with you on the lulucf proposal and bringing it to a successful conclusion.

mr president, commissioner, forest environments and their needs differ between member states. we wanted to make that clear in this house's report on the new european forestry strategy. european forests are growing in the north but shrinking in the south, and mediterranean forests are in danger of disappearing into ashes as a result of climate change. however, there is something common across europe, and that is the belief that active forest management brings benefits, both for the economy and for the promotion of rural life and the fight against climate change. i would therefore like to thank the rapporteur, mr lins, who has made a great effort to strike the difficult balance between the uncompromising commitment to the paris agreement - of which the union must be a leader and an example - and the active management of forests, which are, in the end, two sides of the same coin.
in writing. european forests and good soil management are responsible for sequestering more than 300m tonnes of co2, almost 10% of the eu's emissions. land use will soon be a part of the climate policy of the union and its member states, which will have to comply with accounting rules to balance ghg emissions and removals. however, these standards do not account for emissions from energy generated from biomass. this reduces the absorption and sink capacity of forests and soils compared to their exploitation as biomass or wood, a factor that should not be excluded. the energy policies of some states include the use of biomass to achieve renewable targets thanks to forests, causing two negative consequences: a) extracting biomass with more permissive levels can lose the forest co2 fixing capacity, and b) all emissions from this burning are out of the count, that is, they contribute to warming without being accounted for. europe cannot and must not deceive itself with an energy policy which undermines the importance which its forests and its soils deserve as decisive actors in reducing carbon emissions.

member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to say that i am very happy about those broad debates. some of you made political statements. of course, i agree that the commission is responsible, as ms gosiewska said. i am responsible, i am personally responsible. it is a big test for me – and for you also, for all of us, because the situation is very delicate. on the one hand, we know very well that we need to have facts, arguments, scientifically-based criteria and, of course, reality and fact-finding checks, not just talking generally. because dissemination of mistrust, dissemination of fear, dissemination of misleading information also affects consumer perception. we need to understand balance and to see how to move forward together. this is not the time to name, blame and shame. it was a big test for me on 20 july because i faced for the first time such a big challenge and we decided, on the one hand, to be very active, very precise, to communicate with governments, to discuss with ministers, and on the other hand, to manage information, to provide information for consumers. you mentioned failures of the rapid alert system. no, this is not true. only the rapid alert system allows us to understand where we are, how many countries are affected. the european union produced 360 million eggs per day – please, calculate that per one week and then, can you imagine it, we withdrew 20, 40 million eggs from this big amount. it shows that our rapid alert system and tracking and tracing system is effective. that is true. another question is: how are we using information, how are we acting, especially in using two different systems with different tasks. a criminal investigation in one hand, the food safety issue in the other. how to build a coherent approach? it is our task to move forward and to enforce our situation. let me start with some concrete questions. ms dalli, mr agnew and ms rivasi raised questions on public health. as regards a possible risk to public health, eggs from only three farms exceeded the acute risk level. i would like to provide you with this real information. only three farms exceeded the acute risk level. this means that the consumer would need to consume several eggs from these farms in a short period of time to exceed the acute reference dose. as regards the chronic risk, long-term exposure to fipronil via eggs and egg products should not exceed the acceptable daily intake. from the analytical results available, the majority of the eggs are below that level. this is why we once again draw your attention to this. the risk to public health is really very low. this is not to minimise the incident, as it relates to the illegal use of unauthorised substances. so all in all, consumers are safe, as i mentioned. talking about action in the future: mr belet, ms dalli and mr demesmaeker raised those questions. after managing the consequences of the incident and having taken the necessary risk management measures, we now have to move on and understand what lessons can be learned from this situation. on 30 august, a meeting of the standing committee on plants, animals, food and feed discussed the situation at a technical level and i asked member states – france, the netherlands, germany and belgium – to provide a coherent approach and to present their views and, of course, a thorough assessment and also proposals on how to deal with those issues together. this means that i will organise a high-level ministerial meeting on 26 september because we need to address all the situation and we will present our conclusions to the agriculture and fisheries council in october, because this is a sequence of problems. speaking of delays by the member states, we have to look at mr president, commissioner, please convey to mrs mogherini what we are discussing today. today we are not talking about a political crisis between two parties in venezuela. dear colleagues, in venezuela there is an installed tyranny, there is a corrupt plot, with bosses linked to drug trafficking or to plots like odebrecht. and they will do whatever it takes to stay in power: lying, repressing, starving the population or murdering dissidents. we are talking about 130 people killed by armed groups in venezuela so far this year. we are talking about 603 political prisoners, according to the latest list compiled by the venezuelan criminal forum. in the face of the tyrant maduro, in the face of his corrupt henchmen, dialogue is not worth it. the dialogue we know has failed. what is needed is to give value and recognition to the democratic opposition and civil society that represent the dignity of venezuela. they expect us to act and we owe it to them. if we impose sanctions on other countries, why not venezuela? it is time for sanctions for them, for the rulers responsible for human rights violations. the un high commissioner has established clear examples of systematic institutional violence: a case of crimes against humanity. what are we here for, if not to ask for sanctions and to ask for accountability? it is time for us to act, and venezuela deserves this and much more from us.
mr president, the situation in venezuela - as has already been said - is very serious. the elections to the so-called constituent assembly on 30 july were a very important milestone in the process of the regime's involution into a dictatorship. it practically ends the division of powers, violates multiparty system, and democratically elected institutions are unknown, ignored. the european parliament, like other eu institutions, its member states and much of the international community, does not recognise these elections. they unite us with latin american countries, principles and values. that is why we cannot be indifferent to the political, economic and social crisis that venezuela is going through. many of its inhabitants are of european origin: spanish, portuguese and italian citizens; in short, many europeans emigrated there when the country was different: respectful of freedoms, democracy and very prosperous economically. recently vargas llosa wrote that venezuela was for decades an exemplary democracy, and that then its governments, literally, "fought a relentless battle against the dictatorships that thrived in the rest of latin america". today, unfortunately, the situation is very different. today there are many venezuelans trying to flee their country; there are many political prisoners and also many torture sufferers, recently denounced by the united nations high commissioner for human rights. the recent testimony of yon goicochea is shocking. on the other hand, until recently, the attorney general luisa ortega, now in exile, speaks openly of rampant corruption. these and other issues are the subject of a specific amendment on venezuela which many of us have tabled to mr lópez's report on european union-latin america relations. i hope that this amendment will be accepted tomorrow. and that's the end of it. venezuela needs the release of political prisoners and elections as soon as possible. i am sure that free and democratic elections will bring a decisive end to the lamentable maduro regime, which a country like venezuela does not deserve. and i repeat, mr president, what i have said to mrs mogherini on other occasions: you must get more involved. the european union's action in venezuela, in this very serious crisis, has no visibility whatsoever and i fear that it is also ineffective.
mr president, unfortunately, the situation in venezuela is continuing to worsen. a crisis, that of the country, which has multiple faces. a political, institutional crisis, aggravated this summer after the convocation of a constituent assembly, which the opposition did not recognize, and with a process without democratic guarantees, in a country that we already know has politicians in prison. but also a humanitarian and economic crisis, with a country economically broken, which has seen much of its prosperity laminated, with hyperinflation, needs for basic resources ... all of that combined with a security crisis: violence in the streets, deaths in political protests. we therefore want to send three messages. first, to support the non-recognition of the constituent assembly by the high representative and the member states. secondly, we must promote the path of national reconciliation, dialogue and free elections. and thirdly, the european union and its member states must use all the political and democratic tools to push in this direction.
on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, first of all let me thank all of you for your substantial interventions. as i have already said, we will continue to follow closely the developments in venezuela. regarding our efforts in the humanitarian field, i have already described all of our efforts and we will definitely keep in touch with countries in latin america, the caribbean and other partners in order to be on the same line. we remain committed to supporting efforts to foster a peaceful, negotiated solution, but we are also aware that the time for engaging seriously in such efforts is quickly running out. we are ready to consider all available instruments to help the country find a way out of the crisis. the european union and its member states, our member states, continue to monitor the evolution of the situation closely and will adjust the eu’s approach as dictated by circumstances, without ruling out any option, in case democratic principles are further undermined. i trust that we will continue to count on your support and the support of this political body, the european parliament. we have played a crucial role in calling for a peaceful and constitutional outcome to the crisis in venezuela. give me the chance to encourage you to continue doing so.
in writing. this debate on venezuela in the european parliament is a further example of the international concern about the situation in that country. in the context of economic crisis, shortage of basic products, citizen insecurity, political violence and acute institutional tension, the socialists agree on the following points: -the creation of a constituent assembly and the deprivation of its legislative powers to the national assembly violate the rule of law. the constituent assembly is not democratic and the eu does not recognise it. - we continue to demand from the government of venezuela: the release of political prisoners; the restitution of powers to the national assembly; respect for the separation of powers; that international aid be provided to the people of venezuela. -we continue to bet on dialogue and internal agreement between the government and the opposition to establish an electoral calendar, as the only peaceful and democratic way out of the current crisis. if this does not happen, we will ask the eu to study and adopt personalised sanctioning measures against the members of the venezuelan government and constituent assembly who are responsible for human rights violations.
in writing. the most painful thing about the situation in venezuela is the humanitarian problem. it's an economic catastrophe, it's the most indebted country in the world, which indicates that there is no option for foreign exchange, there is high inflation, deterioration of industrial production levels, collapse of agriculture... these events have led to a supply crisis. there is no food or medicine, poverty has increased by 82%, the mortality rate of inpatients has increased tenfold and the death of newborns in hospitals by a hundred percent. in conclusion: dead, starving, political prisoners and wounded. and in the meantime maduro invents an anti-democratic national constituent assembly; he dismisses the attorney general, luisa ortega díaz; he continues the persecution and continues to harass the venezuelan opposition and all citizens; he repeatedly rejects humanitarian assistance. i subscribe to the words of the united nations high commissioner for human rights, zeid raad al hussein, and i now reiterate my shared request for recourse and denunciation before the international criminal court for maduro and his accomplices. venezuela deserves democracy, freedom, justice, peace, security and human rights. long live the free venezuela!

in writing. this debate on venezuela in the european parliament is a further example of the international concern about the situation in that country. in the context of economic crisis, shortage of basic products, citizen insecurity, political violence and acute institutional tension, socialists agree on the following points: a) the creation of a constituent assembly and the deprivation of its legislative powers to the national assembly violate the rule of law. the constituent assembly is not democratic and the eu does not recognise it. b) we continue to demand from the government of venezuela: - the release of political prisoners - the restitution of powers to the national assembly - respect for the separation of powers - that international aid be provided to the people of venezuela c) we continue to bet on dialogue and internal agreement between government and opposition to establish an electoral calendar, as the only peaceful and democratic way out of the current crisis. if this does not happen, we will ask the eu to study and adopt personalised sanctioning measures against the members of the venezuelan government and constituent assembly who are responsible for human rights violations.
the rapporteur. mr president, as we all know, the world is undergoing a rapid and profound reordering of international relations, and europe is in danger of being caught between atlantic weakness, a neighbourhood full of conflicts with some aggressive actors and the rise of asia. but this should not only concern us as europeans; it also concerns us because it puts at risk the values and principles that europe represents in the world: the will to build international relations based on multilateralism, dialogue and rules. for all this, and faced with this new scenario, it also opens up for us, it gives us the opportunity to strengthen strategic ties with those who share this vision and who, moreover, share an agenda in the world. that is the purpose of this report presented here today: to explain and to tell all the european institutions that, as a result of the new international reality, relations between the european union and latin america are no longer just a matter of convictions. they're a matter of necessity. that we want to work together and we have to work together between both regions to promote inclusive governance, defend development goals, fight climate change and protect the paris agreement, fight for gender equality, impose governance, a globalization with rules and sharing its benefits. an agenda that we share with these actors - the latin american and caribbean - with both regions, and that we do not share with all the big players on the international stage. it is clear that we have many links - historical, cultural, human, economic - with both regions. but no relationship can be taken for granted, especially also because of the profound changes, the interactions that exist on this continent, in europe, but that have also been in latin america in recent years. since 1999, there has been a strategic partnership between the union and the subcontinent, but the relationship between the union and latin america has often been relegated. today is the time for it to become a reality. and we have the tools to do that. we have a long, long list of association agreements in negotiation: we have association agreements in progress with mexico, with chile, that can drive our relationship forward; an agreement in negotiation with mercosur; we also have a recent agreement for political dialogue and cooperation with cuba, which we understand has a regional impact. but we don't just have this list of agreements. we have an institutional agenda at the eu-celac summits which, unfortunately - and i will refer to it later - can be clouded by some of the problems of the region, such as venezuela. we must act with greater strength to coordinate our position at the g20, the united nations, the international monetary fund and the wto. we must and must continue to maintain development cooperation with the region. we must continue to work together to ensure greater mobility; to protect common security, especially that of some countries in central america - a threat that also exists in europe; to follow closely the hopeful developments in colombia, while at the same time addressing the very serious problems in venezuela. the time is now. it is now time to give our relations a boost, to continue working together, to set out a clear strategy for the region from the commission, to strengthen our ties and to speak out in defence of shared values and principles.
on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, since the beginning of this commission’s mandate we sought to further strengthen relations with latin america and the caribbean. our culture and economic ties date back centuries but we are also getting into a new era. our economies are more connected than ever. we are partners and allies on the great global issues of our times, from climate change to sustainable development. we share the vision of a more multilateral world, where all continents and all peoples have a say and contribute to global governance. as mentioned in your excellent report, the european union seeks to reinforce its partnership with latin america and the caribbean not only in terms of economic change, but as a partner in social progress and in the defence of common values. in order to do that, we have at our disposal powerful cooperation instruments such as eu-funded programmes and technical or high-level meetings that allow us to foster cooperation and strengthen the ties between both decision-makers and civil societies. latin america and the caribbean are now looking for their own way towards regional integration, both on a continental scale and within its sub-regions. for instance, we are deepening our engagement with the pacific alliance, in particular on academic exchanges, consular assistance, free movement of citizens or investment policies. in your report you urge the high representative to ‘look into the possibility of the eu participating as an observer’ in the pacific alliance. the eu has already been invited to the high-level meetings of the pacific alliance, including the summit in cali (27-30 june), as a special guest. we will look into the possibility of becoming an observer as the pacific alliance continues to consolidate itself. let me also mention our relations with mercosur, which have been galvanised by resuming the negotiation of an association agreement. our goal is to finish the negotiations in the coming months, but beyond the regional and sub-regional organisation, our bilateral relations with almost all countries of the continent are going through a particularly dynamic phase. let me just mention a few concrete examples. the negotiations to modernise the eu-mexico association agreement are advancing at a good pace. via meetings, videoconferences and negotiation rounds, the agreement is taking shape and we aim to conclude negotiations in the coming months. the council is currently discussing the mandate to negotiate the update of the eu-chile association agreement. this negotiation will allow us to deepen our relations with a close ally with whom we share a rich common agenda, including peace and security. another partner in defence and security is colombia, where we have supported the peace agreement from the moment it was signed with a dedicated trust fund. let me pay tribute to the role the european parliament has been playing to support an active contribution by the european union to the peace process in colombia. the bilateral ceasefire announced by the government and the eln on 4 september constitutes a further step forward for peace in colombia. the european union, also through the high representative’s special envoy mr eamon gilmore, will continue our work to help the peace process overcome all remaining obstacles. peace in colombia was not the only historic event taking place in the region over the past few months. our political dialogue and cooperation agreement with cuba constitutes a landmark for the eu’s policy towards the region. in a sign of a new era in latin america and the caribbean, we are looking forward to the launch of the provisional application of an agreement that will allow us to strengthen our relations in a wide array of areas, including human rights. human rights is precisely one of the areas where we cooperate the most with our partners in the region, including in central america and the caribbean, where we are also strengthening our support to fight against climate change. the situation in venezuela makes for a striking exception after such a long list of positive developments. the political violence and the economic crisis risk destabilising not only the country, but the entire region. this crisis encourages us to seek even closer cooperation with all countries in latin america and the caribbean to support any attempt for regional mediation between the venezuela government and the opposition. our regions may be geographically distant, but there is so much that we share. we have a direct interest in seeing latin america and the caribbean prosper, with peace, development and social justice for all. our commitment is here to stay. our friendship is here to stay, and our partnership can only get deeper and stronger in time.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, as this report points out, we must strengthen and modernise our cooperation and relations with latin america and the caribbean, and a good way to do this if not the best is to cooperate with them in achieving the sustainable development goals. the latin america and caribbean area has grown in recent years and has lifted millions of people out of poverty, but still today 175 million live below the poverty line, live in exclusion and live in inequality. measuring our cooperation by a single indicator - gross domestic product - and excluding middle-income countries from it is a bad solution, it is unfair and it is discriminatory. because gdp is blind to territorial inequalities, it is blind to generational inequalities, and it is blind to the specific risk of climate change. a good way of cooperating with them is to support the latin american countries which, together with the united nations, are proposing a way of restructuring sovereign debt in a sustainable and at the same time supportive manner.

the rapporteur. mr president, very quickly, i want to thank my colleagues for the work done to have a report that tries to strengthen, promote and give a more coherent framework to our relations with latin america, in defense of the same values: multilateralism, open societies or human rights; and for sharing an agenda, which is the agenda of the fight against climate change, gender equality or having an inclusive growth that governs globalization.
when some people talk about the need to include agriculture and therefore forest management and land use in the strategy to combat climate change, they are not talking about including it in the global emissions trading. we are talking about the need for a change in our relationship with the environment; for a change in the global food system; for the earth to be seen again as a common good that belongs to all of us and that its care benefits all of us. we are talking about instituting the right to use instead of the right to own. we are talking about something which is far from the subject of this report: the avoidance of measures which market and market the environment.
i voted in favour of this proposal because it sets out a binding commitment for each member state to ensure that accounted emissions from land use are offset by an equivalent removal of co2 from the atmosphere through measures in these sectors. climate change is a transboundary and global problem that cannot be solved by national or local action alone. the paris agreement includes a long-term objective and states that the contribution of land use, land-use change and forestry to achieving long-term climate mitigation objectives will be critical. the european union and the member states are currently required to take account of this sector under the kyoto protocol, which imposes limitations on the european union and each of the member states to ensure that they do not generate additional emissions. in addition, forest management plays a crucial role in the fight against climate change, as all these sectors must contribute to the overall eu emission reduction target.
the arms trade has reached the highest volume since the cold war, which is very bad, but europe is the second largest arms supplier in the world, which should be a shame. we have therefore voted in favour of this report, which calls on the member states to comply with the common position and the arms trade treaty. the sale of arms to countries such as saudi arabia is contrary to human rights and, in the same vein, the resolution of this parliament of 25 february 2016 calls on the commission to impose an embargo on the sale of arms to saudi arabia. but on 13 march, in the port of bilbao, more than 4 000 tonnes of arms were being shipped to saudi arabia, a scene which, tragically, is being repeated all the time. in such an action, the guard corporal of the fire department alleged reasons of conscience to not participate in that operation. now he's facing disciplinary action that could result in disqualification. what this fireman has done is nothing more than to defend human rights, which mr juncker has spoken so much about this morning. that is why it deserves our support and solidarity.
there are many countries in latin america that are experiencing an alarming deterioration of human rights; argentina: we keep asking where santiago maldonado is; mexico: hundreds of journalists killed for denouncing the complicity between the government and drug trafficking; brazil: a coup government that wants to change the constitution to attack the rights of indigenous peoples to their lands. i think of all those people, just as this report only thinks of interfering in venezuela. human rights must be defended throughout latin america, and the european union must demand that they be respected, not take advantage of their absence. when we approve and commit ourselves to fair international trade, among equals, which puts people, peoples and the environment before the interests of transnational corporations, then we will vote in favour.
if someone outside this parliament were to read the report, they might think that corruption is only a problem in the countries of the south; that there is no corruption here; that there is no corruption in europe or that, for example, multinational companies, most of them based in europe, have nothing to do with corruption in the countries of the south. it is obvious, for example, that these multinationals are responsible for 70 per cent of the tax evasion cases in the world. it is obvious, for example, that in my country the prime minister has had to go to court to testify about corruption or that his party is now being sued for illegal funding. i would even like to mention the transnational corruption, that of mr pedro agramunt, who is the president of the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe and is directly linked to a case of corruption in azerbaijan and money laundering. from here we must demand accountability, understand that corruption is an evil that pervades the international elites and their multinationals and demand the resignation of mr agramunt.
corruption is a drag. it is a drag on the economy, on democracy and on social equity. there can be no disagreement on that. there are some paragraphs in this report which are pure common sense. however, as a spaniard and a member of this parliament, i can only feel ashamed when we try to lecture third countries. the report points to the countries of the south, but it forgets that 70% of tax evasion in the world comes from multinationals, those great friends of the european union's trade policy. i am reminded that there is a commissioner in this parliament who is involved in one of the biggest corruption cases in the world: the panama papers. we are not here to lecture anyone and we should be much less hypocritical.
mr president, commissioner, we have been with the committee of inquiry into the measurement of emissions in the automotive sector for a year. experts from all over europe have been through it and we have been able to know clearly what has happened. at this point we have a clear idea of what has happened and the text of the conclusions also gives us guidelines and solutions to the questions raised. the priority must be to preserve the environment and the health of consumers, but also to establish and promote legislation on less polluting fuels and to restrict the installation of deactivation devices. what we cannot and should not do is demonize diesel vehicles, or ban them immediately, because we have boosted their development to reduce co2 emissions and because they are a very important part of our european production. but, yes, perhaps we should reflect on whether we have gone too far and adopted too soon an environmental legislation which has given rise to these manipulations to enforce it. the european union legislation must of course offer greater protection and redress to consumers in cases like the one we have seen, but it must also be rational and capable of being enforced and, above all, capable of being monitored. the text we are voting on tomorrow clearly points the way forward.

member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, and the rapporteurs from the other committees. the commission has been working hard to foster social inclusion in europe and this parliament has been one of our strongest supporters. but we will never achieve our goals as long as everyday life remains as inaccessible as it is today for 80 million europeans with a disability. the solutions exist to make accessibility happen and demand for accessible products and services will only increase as europe’s population is ageing. but the gap between what is possible and what has actually been achieved in reality remains large. the european union is committed to the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities and its obligations on accessibility. we celebrated the convention’s 10th anniversary last year. people with a disability are expecting us to act – now. last year’s adoption of the web accessibility directive constituted an important step forward and i welcome that parliament is now ready to set out its position on the commission proposal for a european accessibility act. the accessibility act aims at using the full potential of our single market to trigger real change in people’s lives. it puts forward a common european approach to accessibility, instead of having 28 national ones. this common approach will maximise opportunities and minimise costs for european businesses and consumers. the experience from the us has shown very well how accessibility policies can be a catalyst for economic growth and inclusion. i welcome the fact that parliament’s report supports the commission’s objective to improve accessibility. it brings a number of useful clarifications, also concerning the relation with existing eu legislation. but i would like to take this opportunity to highlight the commission’s position on some of the main points under debate. first, preservation of the integrity of the internal market. about 95% of eu companies are either microenterprises or smes. many of them have to deal with new accessibility requirements, for instance due to the new ‘buy accessible’ obligations in public procurement legislation. but, they do not have the same resources or capacities to deal with changing regulatory requirements. the commission has therefore introduced strong safeguard clauses and light rules in terms of conformity assessment, in particular for microenterprises. however, a blanket exclusion of microenterprises would not only put at risk the objective of the proposal, it would seriously distort the functioning of the internal market. for instance, a microenterprise might be allowed to import non-accessible products from third countries, such as smartphones, while eu producers have to comply with accessibility requirements. secondly, public procurement and eu funds. we want public money to be invested in accessible products, services and buildings. buying accessible is already a general obligation in the eu public procurement directives, but more is needed to ensure a proper internal market in this area. the accessibility act puts forward a list of functional requirements so that industry knows what to deliver, users know what to expect and public authorities know what to ask for. this brings me to the last point. the accessibility requirements will determine the level of accessibility of our products and services in the internal market for the coming decades. so, indeed, we need to be flexible as technological possibilities are constantly changing. that is why the accessibility act puts forward functional accessibility requirements instead of prescribing the detailed technical solutions to achieve them. but we also need to ensure that our laws are effective and enforceable, and provide legal certainty both for industry and consumers. in light of the still ongoing work in the council, the commission will stand ready to support the co-legislators in clarifying and further detailing the accessibility requirements. we have a chance here to make a real difference, both for citizens and for business. the commission counts on your support.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment. mr president, the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, the european disability strategy 2010-2020 itself, and so many other instruments call for freedom, the rule of law and equality. this was stated by our president juncker today in the debate on the state of the european union. we are, in essence, the defence of freedom, equality and the rule of law. we have the opportunity, with the adoption of this european accessibility act, to show that europe has a soul and to show that europe believes in equality. accessibility is participation; accessibility is equality; accessibility is removing obstacles to free movement; accessibility is supporting the right to the integrity of persons; it is supporting the right to the dignity of persons, the right to education, to work, to free movement and residence. that's why the vote tomorrow is important. we must be more ambitious than the text adopted by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and we must stick to the line proposed by the commission: support the amendments of the committee on employment and social affairs and the committee on transport and tourism so that all micro and small businesses can also take part. the dignity of the people is at stake, democracy is at stake. human values have to be above economic values.
i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr løkkegaard, on the foresight and prudence he has shown in this report, and i would like to thank him sincerely for the effort he has made to integrate the proposals. they better balance the needs of people with disabilities and the possibilities for public and private sector responses. the commission is also preparing a proposal to make innovation the best tool for the integration of disability, and is planning to take steps to ensure that this removal of barriers benefits other types of functional diversity, although an exact definition of this term has yet to be finalised. finally, this text is an example of how to resolve problems of legislative collision before they occur and to fill some gaps that are not covered by sectoral and national legislation. that is why i shall be supporting some amendments which seek to solve some of the black holes which need to be solved urgently. for example, to require that renovations and new works in environments and complementary infrastructure of basic services, such as transport, must incorporate accessibility.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank colleagues for this substantial debate. the european accessibility act is a priority file for this year under the joint declaration of the three institutions. indeed, accessibility is one of the eight key pillars of our european disability strategy 2010-20. the un committee on the rights of persons with disabilities mentioned it as a priority action in their last concluding observations to the european union. we know that our member states have started to legislate on accessibility independently and in an uncoordinated way. divergence in national rules will make it more difficult for industry to sell products and services across borders. it also does not benefit those citizens who are most in need of accessible products and services. accessibility will be vital to ensure inclusive societies, especially against the background of demographic ageing and the digital transition. the accessibility act will create a better functioning and a more competitive internal market, leading to a wider choice of accessible products and services for consumers, and also at lower prices. it will facilitate the access of persons with disabilities to education, enhance their job opportunities and give them more freedom and opportunities in their everyday choices in life. it is the commission’s firm intention to enhance social fairness in europe. nobody should be left behind. the accessibility act underlines the european union’s commitment to ensure that economic growth and social progress go hand in hand. we look forward to tomorrow’s vote and to continuing the work with you on this important file.

mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to thank president gualtieri and the other members for their work. for a job well done. and i want to welcome this proposal to extend the european statistical programme to the period 2018-2020. reliable and relevant evidence based on european statistics is absolutely essential for measuring the progress and evaluating the efficiency of union policies and programmes, especially in the context of the europe 2020 strategy and the agenda for jobs, growth, equity and democratic change. european unity faces challenges in many policy areas and the demand for european statistics remains very high. the need for a policy response to the deep economic crisis and its social impact has driven the demand for better economic and social policies based on robust and comparable evidence. the european commission has identified among its ten policy priorities the importance of meeting the growing demand for statistics and the need to make them available much more quickly. the implementation and monitoring of european union policies are based on high-quality, comparable statistical information on the economic, social and environmental situation in the european union and its components at national and regional level. the agreement reached has ensured that three of the fundamental objectives have been met. first, high quality statistical information, ensuring that no statistical gaps are left and focusing on a number of priority areas reflecting the commission's ten policy priorities. second, to be able to respond more rapidly to the statistical needs of the union by adapting the statistical infrastructure to take advantage of the potential of new data sources. and thirdly, to improve the productivity of the european statistical system and to ensure its global prominence. european statistics are also essential for the general public to understand europe and for citizens to participate in the democratic process and the debate on the present and future of the european union. this new system will be able to meet the growing demand for statistics and the need to make them available more quickly, guaranteeing reliable, objective, comparable and coherent european statistics despite what has been said here.
