on behalf of the enf group. mr president, i believe that this plan for the north sea has two advantages. the first is, of course, the multiannual nature, which will make it possible to give fishermen more visibility. it is important that the fishing opportunities for a given stock do not change drastically from one year to the next. the second advantage is that the plan is designed to remedy the problems caused by quota-limited stocks. the demersal stocks, i.e. the stocks of species living on the seabed, are often exploited in mixed fisheries. this means that when the nets are lifted, there may be different species of fish caught: cod, haddock, black spot, whiting, sole, plaice and lobster. for fishermen, the problem is that they have to stop their campaign as soon as they have reached their quota on one species even if they still have quotas on other species. the landing obligation now makes it illegal to discard any catch in excess of a quota. this plan should therefore address this problem by introducing possibilities for trading quotas between member states, but also with third countries. similarly, fishing opportunities will be allocated by bands in order to be more flexible. all these measures therefore converge towards greater flexibility and greater visibility for the benefit of fishermen. that is why we will vote in favour of this plan.
mr president, dear commissioner, i remember well what we approved with the council in 2013: the reform of the cfp, which some people today want to ignore. and when that happens, we politicians lose all credibility in the eyes of society, and operators lack legal certainty, which is a basic requirement for any business. we therefore supported multiannual plans and regionalisation, and we worked with the fishermen to convince them that regionalised measures through multiannual plans would bring them much closer to decision-making. however, when enthusiasm turns to frustration, it is very difficult to rebuild trust. the fishermen are feeling frustrated today, as am i. they expected something else from this plan. they hoped that the ranges within which the council could fix the total allowable catch would be set on sound scientific grounds. that is precisely what the basic regulation states in article 9 (1) of the basic regulation, but ranges have been proposed in this plan without any scientific basis. the fishermen also trusted that the measures would take into account their socioeconomic impact, as provided for in article 9 (4) of the cfp. here again they were deceived. i will not refer to the chances of capture, which have also been deceived in this case. i sincerely hope that these points will be changed tomorrow. i would not want to be associated in any way with a mandate from parliament which would mislead those who have to implement what we have decided here, since the operators themselves would have no motivation to comply with these requirements. the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs for their contributions and their willingness to engage in dialogue, which have made it possible to produce a very good report. i also congratulate the european external action service and the commission, headed by commissioner malmström, for their excellent work in strengthening relations between the european union and latin america, and particularly with chile, a stable and reliable partner of the union and a necessary partner in the achievement of fairer global governance. i would also like to take this opportunity to greet the ambassador of the republic of chile to the european union, who has had the pleasure and interest of being here with us today. the agreement on bilateral trade in organic products is the first such agreement signed by the european union with a view to contributing to the development and expansion of organic farming. it is based on a strict mutual recognition and certification procedure with high control and safeguards, providing for the creation of a joint committee to monitor its implementation, as well as a unilateral suspension clause in the event of non-compliance. chile recognizes all certified european products, but the european union excludes chilean animal and feed products, as well as unregulated aquaculture. we support this agreement, commissioner, but i ask you to undertake to keep this parliament duly informed on its implementation, and i also ask you to carry out an evaluation before the end of the period of application and, if necessary, every three years thereafter. as regards croatia's accession to the current association agreement, i would just like to point out that it follows the ordinary adjustment procedure following new accession, following the procedure of the world trade organisation. finally, i would like to refer to the most relevant report, the future modernisation of the association agreement with chile. it is true that the current agreement has worked very well since it came into force in 2003. however, it needs to be modernised because it is out of date, because it does not meet the new requirements of trade policy and because both sides have concluded more ambitious agreements with third countries. the framework for trade relations between the european union and chile cannot be left behind. the modernisation of the chile agreement is also a great opportunity to implement a more ambitious trade policy which is conducive to sustainable development. we share the same principles and values. and in this report - which, by the way, was approved by a very large majority in the committee on international trade, the largest majority achieved in a trade agreement in this parliament - what are the recommendations of this parliament? first, we demand more transparency and involvement of parliamentarians and civil society and demand the immediate publication of the negotiating mandate as soon as it takes place. we call for ambitious improvements in market access, but protecting sensitive agricultural and industrial products and putting the defence and welfare of the people first. we call for the right and the capacity of the parties to regulate in the general interest, including, of course, public services, and for this to be explicitly and unequivocally ensured throughout the agreement. we call for a modern investment policy which must take into account both the protection and the obligations of investors; preserve the right of governments to regulate; avoid unfounded litigation and, of course, replace the private arbitration system with a public, transparent, guaranteeing system, which seeks the commitment of the parties to give priority to recourse to the competent courts while progress is being made in the creation of the multilateral investment tribunal. and of course we demand an ambitious chapter on sustainable development with binding, enforceable provisions, subject to dispute resolution mechanisms and considering the imposition of sanctions while promoting corporate social responsibility. we want firm commitments on the fight against tax evasion, against corruption and, of course, we are asking for a specific chapter on smes and on something that i know you are firmly committed to, as is chile, which is that, finally, the european union will sign a trade agreement with a specific gender chapter. i therefore ask all the members of this parliament to support this report by a majority tomorrow and i ask the commission and the council to take these recommendations into account because they are good, they are necessary and because, moreover, it is this parliament which will have to have the last word.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, i welcome the political agreement reached in the tripartite dialogues on the transposition into european union law of the recommendations on management, conservation and control measures applicable in the iccat convention area. i think it is fundamental, although, after listening to some of the previous speeches, one wonders whether it is really worthwhile to continue talking about law, about laws, when some people absolutely ignore them, they transgress them without any problem. in any case, i will not go into the content of the report, but i do want to highlight some very clear messages. first of all, i would naturally like to thank the council, the commission and the shadow rapporteurs who have made this agreement possible. the agreement provides for a level playing field for all operators, both eu and non-eu, operating in the same area. ensuring a level playing field in the same area where european fleets compete with foreign fleets is crucial if we are to have the confidence of fishermen. the eu fleet often applies much stricter measures than those adopted by regional fisheries management organisations. we must convince third countries, through our action in the rdps, to follow the european union's rules in these cases. for example, transhipment at sea, which is prohibited for eu vessels in eu waters. transhipment at sea is one of the main causes of lack of transparency in fisheries worldwide and facilitates iuu fishing. and this is often done by foreign fleets, always the same ones on a global level - and needless to say - with low social or no environmental considerations. it is important to continue to make every effort to export our sustainability standards to third country fleets. the final agreed text calls on the european commission to take all necessary steps to extend the union ban to all waters. it is something that our sector has been asking for many years - and rightly so - and i think we should be grateful for it. the agreed text also stresses the need to pay particular attention to traditional and artisanal fisheries and to provide incentives for eu bluefin tuna and swordfish fishermen using fishing gear and techniques to reduce environmental impact and that this be taken into account when allocating quotas at national level. that was a battle we had with the member states and we negotiated very well then for bluefin tuna, and now that commitment is confirmed. however, i am very concerned that the commission, almost a year after the adoption by iccat of a multiannual recovery plan for mediterranean swordfish - an iconic species whose stocks are in very poor condition - has not sent the european parliament any proposal transposing this plan. and that is the commission's general approach: more delay than would be desirable. i am convinced that the commissioner does not agree with this either and he views this very negatively. in fact, we are going to adopt, we are going to transpose, a number of measures of the iccaa which are now obsolete and outdated. we're talking about measures from ten years ago. these measures were put on the table ten years ago and we are going to adopt these recommendations now: there is no justification for them. this leads to legal uncertainty for operators and to legitimate criticism from interested parties. this situation is legal and, more importantly, politically unacceptable. that is why we have submitted a statement to the final text expressing our concerns. i know, commissioner, that you will accept this gladly, and there must be a commitment from the commission to ensure that these rules are not born dead. today we are approving recommendations that were already exceeded a year ago by a plan for swordfish. i must also say that i am dissatisfied with the latest decision taken by the iccat on the fixing of swordfish quotas in the mediterranean, which does not take into account the fact that the vessels fishing for swordfish are the same as those fishing for bluefin tuna, and that whilst they reduce swordfish quotas, which is probably right, they do not increase those for bluefin tuna, when it has been shown that, after a very well-executed plan, the stock has been fully and absolutely restored. i simply hope that now, commissioner, in the month of november in marrakesh, where there is a new meeting of the iccat, that recovery will be clearly reflected in a very significant increase in quotas and, moreover, in a more equitable distribution and that account will be taken - as i said at the beginning - of small boats, craft boats and boats which are more respectful of the environment. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you again for your willingness to think and to take up the challenge - which i am sure the commissioner will accept - that the implementation of the recommendations should not take ten years: if it is ten months, much better.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, i regret that it took ten years to translate into european law these iccat recommendations for atlantic tuna, which is completely out of line with the will and usual diligence of the rapporteur, mr mato, whom i would like to thank for his excellent work. the commission has also been asked to provide information on the implementation of the new rules on the conservation of fishery resources. in this way we can create legal uncertainty, such as that affecting swordfish, with a conservation plan that applies to operators but has not yet been transposed into community legislation despite the fact that it is a simple process. at least, thanks to the contributions of the committee on fisheries, we have added to the protection and conservation measures some considerations which better connect them with the criteria of the common fisheries policy for the management of fish stocks. we are thus obliged to apply more transparent criteria when allocating catch quotas between member states. we will also support small-scale fleets because of their lower environmental impact and their decisive contribution to maintaining sustainable economic activity and the possibility of obtaining resources to diversify sources of income in coastal areas. it is also essential to give priority to the use of low-impact selective gear and not to impose additional obligations on european vessels to those of third countries; member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank all those who participated in the debate. it has shown a very broad criticism of the delay but broad support for the approval of this proposal and i am very happy that the negotiations have concluded. many have stressed the issue of the delayed transposition, which i fully understand. i have already commented on the delay in my introductory remarks. i stress again that the european union has been complying with its international obligations all along, in spite of the delay in transposition. the eu was never in breach of any law. the adoption of this proposal will also contribute to reducing such delays in the future. this is a milestone that will contribute to a quicker procedure to transpose international obligations, acquired by the union under regional fisheries management organisations (rfmo), into eu law in a timely manner. i want to stress the fact that the eu fishing industry was never exempt from any measure of the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas (iccat). the european union is a contracting party to iccat since 1997; as such the eu is under international obligation to ensure that the provisions of the iccat recommendations are effectively complied with, but pursuant to article 216(2) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu) this international obligation also lies with member states. they are bound to comply with the provisions of rfmos and take necessary measures to this end, even in the absence of transposition of the said measures into eu law. in fact, the commission was continuously monitoring to ensure that all member states were adhering to iccat obligations and measures. with regards to the use of data, i can assure you all that we are not using ten year old data as was said. i want to assure everyone that all fishing opportunities are evaluated by scientists on the latest data given by all contracting parties. one comment regarding mr marias’ question on what support could be given to fishermen affected by an oil spin – i will take note of this and will revert directly to you to see whether support measures are available under the european maritime and fisheries fund (emff). with regards to this regulation, the commission sees it as an inspiration for future transpositions. it was led by the principle of fair and strict transpositions and it allows for quick implementation of new iccat recommendations. as i said, the proposal transposing the management plan for swordfish is expected to reach you during the next months. the issue of quota distribution, which was raised by some meps, is not part of this regulation. this has been discussed extensively with members states both before the iccat meeting and also after. we have found a good solution. madam president, i would like to thank again mr mato and madam renata briano for their support and the debate. i am looking forward to a very positive vote in the future.

member of the commission. – madam president, first of all, i would like to thank anna hedh, the rapporteur of this report. women’s equal participation in the labour market and in economic decision-making are preconditions for women’s empowerment. the commission’s strategic engagement for gender equality 2016-2019 identifies five priority areas for action. 1: increasing female labour market participation and the equal economic independence of women and men; 2: reducing the gender pay earnings and pension gaps and thus fighting poverty among women; 3: promoting equality between women and men in decision-making; 4: combating gender-based violence and protecting and supporting victims; and 5: promoting gender equality and women’s rights across the world. in this context, let us focus on two important aspects. first, closing the gender employment gap. women remain significantly under-represented in the labour market. in 2016, women’s employment rate was still more than 10 points lower than men’s employment rate. if you look at the full-time equivalent employment rate, the gap reaches 18 points. this gap is not related to professional qualifications or academic achievement, where women more and more out-perform men. it is first and foremost related to the way women and men share caring responsibilities in our society. the commission has developed an extensive package of measures contributing to the economic empowerment of women. the main objective of our proposal for a directive on work-life balance of working parents and carers is to address women’s under-representation in the labour market. the proposed directive aims at modernising the current eu legal and policy frameworks for family-related leave and flexible working arrangements. the proposed directive is complemented with non-legislative measures with the objective to promote the development of formal care services; the enforcement of the rules with regard to dismissal; protection for pregnant women; and removing economic disincentives for second earners to work. we are also developing the relevant indicators in order to be able to measure progress in all these areas. the second aspect to focus on when it comes to the economic empowerment of women is closing the gender pay gap. the gender pay gap has been decreasing only slowly and seems to have stabilised at 16% over the last years as a result of pervasive segregation on the labour market, persistent stereotypes fuelled by inadequate work-life balance policies, and discrimination, all of this combined with a lack of transparency. the effective application of the existing legal framework on equal pay remains a challenge in all member states. the commission constantly monitors whether eu law on equal pay is applied correctly and supports member states and other stakeholders in the proper enforcement of the existing rules. we are now finalising – and intend to propose – an action plan to tackle the gender pay gap from all possible angles. it will aim, in particular, at improving the application of the equal-pay principle, combating segregation in occupations and sectors, combating vertical segregation, and recognising women’s skills, efforts and responsibilities.
in writing. although the eu is a world leader in women's rights and gender equality, we have not yet achieved full equality in terms of women's participation in the labour market, wages and pensions, political and economic representation, etc. the eu needs to take concrete action to boost women's empowerment as soon as possible, because only when we achieve economic independence for all women can we achieve gender equality. there is a need to improve work-life balance, achieve a more balanced distribution of unpaid work between men and women, improve wage transparency and wage mapping through binding provisions to achieve equal pay for equal work of equal value, require companies to negotiate gender equality plans to strengthen equal opportunities and combat discrimination, ensure equal representation on collective bargaining teams, increase women's participation in decision-making, promote the use of gender quotas and cremation lists in policy-making and eradicate gender-based violence.

the rapporteur. madam president, this is an own-initiative report of great importance for civil society in developing countries and also for the european institutions. before i go into the main points of this report, i would like to stress the unanimous position that all the political groups have taken on the situation of civil society in developing countries. i have also seen the importance of working together and of consensus in order to achieve a good result, and thanks to that good will, because of the importance of this report, we were able to adopt it with 22 votes in favour, one abstention and one vote against. it is a very timely and relevant report, reflecting the reality of civil society in many developing countries that receive aid from the european union. i have had the opportunity to meet the ngos working on the ground, to hear the problems and difficulties they face. i have also had the opportunity to meet with representatives of the european commission and the european external action service and they have also allowed me to see another perspective of the challenges that need to be addressed in the european union in order to help the most disadvantaged. we all agree that human rights, the rule of law and democracy must be respected. civil society in developing countries is so weak that it needs all of our action and attention. i have seen the difficulties faced by workers, journalists and human rights defenders, situations which are unacceptable and which often lead to their death. there are also very desperate situations in countries in conflict. i am thinking of africa, where the cooperatives and civil society suffer daily from the scourge of terrorism. throughout this text, i have tried to underline the value of civil society in preserving a more democratic, dignified and just society, by working positively with both the public and private sectors. the report also stresses the importance of recognising the european union's action, since it defends and strengthens the role of civil society in development cooperation. the initiatives could be grouped into two parts. the first is political support, where various measures are proposed, such as regular meetings with members of civil society in the framework of official visits. 'when members go on delegation, i personally have the presidency, to a country, i always reserve a space to attend to all ngos'. also regularly include this issue in the agenda of the foreign affairs councils. the commission also proposes to promote policy coherence in the areas of human rights, development, justice and security. the creation of a monitoring and early warning mechanism in relation to the shrinking space in civil society. the second initiative concerns financial support. it is recalled that the european union is the main donor of aid to civil society organisations in developing countries, but we call for increased funding for dedicated instruments such as the european instrument for human rights and the instrument for development cooperation. the need for greater synergies between all instruments is also stressed, with a call for country-by-country monitoring of all civil society support activities funded by the european union. in conclusion, i would like to stress once again to this house the unity of opinion in the work carried out in committee. certainly some of the parts do not meet the expectations of those who have worked on it, but i believe that in the dialogue that has been held common sense and willingness to do a good job have prevailed. that is why i ask for the support of this house, because i believe that we must send an important message, loud and clear, to this civil society which is threatened in many countries of the world.
in writing. – restrictions on civil society have become increasingly repressive. to counterbalance this fact the report brings forward positive proposals to guarantee the role ngos play in fostering democracy and the well-being of citizens worldwide. however, in order not to jeopardise the development of free and diverse civil societies, and in line with policy coherence for development, we believe it is fundamental for the eu to establish legal human rights obligations for business. in addition, we believe in free and independent civil societies, but deplore the strong reference the report makes to religion or faith-based movements. we will therefore abstain from supporting this resolution.

the rapporteur. mr president, improving the safety of passengers in maritime transport by providing uniform data to emergency services in the event of an accident throughout the union, and doing so with the utmost respect for privacy and european data protection rules, is the objective of this report. we have here an agreement which has had from the beginning the best will on the part of all, an attitude which i want to acknowledge and i want to thank especially itxaso and mae for the work they have done, the alternative rapporteurs and also the commission. but let me stress in particular the role of the maltese presidency, which deserves public recognition for the commitment with which it has carried out its six-month presidency. the report also seeks to contribute to the shared objective of better legislation and the elimination of obstacles through simpler rules, because in this particular aspect of passenger data, the dispersion of regulations, the organisational constraints and the distance between what the rules envisaged and what technology allows were already unacceptable today: a gap which, in addition to penalizing efficiency in a possible rescue operation, contributed to legal uncertainty. the agreement with the council focuses on new rules to digitise the register of passengers on ships and provide full data to rescue services to improve their operational efficiency. we are thus protecting the right and also responding to the need of family members to have verified and reliable information in emergency and distress situations. the purpose is to make the exact number of passengers and other useful information immediately available to search and rescue services in the event of an accident. precious minutes can now be lost because the data on the people on board is stored by a shipping company. the search and rescue centre has to ask the company's contact person for the necessary information, and in digital form the information will be directly accessible. in order to facilitate assistance to victims and their relatives, the data recorded shall include the nationality of the passengers. the rules in force oblige the shipping company to record the name, date of birth, sex and, if the passenger so wishes, the need for special assistance in case of emergency. the new rules also provide for the possibility of voluntarily providing a telephone number for emergency contacts. under the new requirements, the data shall be sent to the competent authority in electronic format within 15 minutes of the vessel's departure. two means of transmission may be used: the national single window or the automatic identification system, subject to certain conditions. the progress made in developing national one-stop shops will hopefully serve as a basis for promoting a european one-stop shop in the future. the agreement is also characterised by its ability to offer solutions and flexibility and provides for specific situations for short crossings affecting germany, denmark and sweden. in such cases, data transmission shall be accepted until one hour after the start of the journey. privacy and data protection are ensured by the immediate destruction of these passenger lists, automatically and without undue delay, as soon as the journey is completed and the data are no longer needed to support rescue services in an accident, emergency or for use in legal proceedings. member states will have four years to make the necessary technological and organisational transition and another two years from the entry into force of the directive to be able to incorporate the new rules into their national legislation.
mr president, i would like to thank mrs aiuto for the work she has done on this difficult report, because this proposal adds safety guarantees to maritime transport passengers and because it clarifies the requirements that ships must respect during their construction process. it also details the stability conditions and improves fire protection measures. the agreement, which will apply to ships over 24 metres in length, strengthens the effectiveness of the legislation because the new standards it defines favour uniform interpretation. the logical consequence is a reinforcement of the security guarantees and more control possibilities. the agreement also solves the problem of the initial deadline for repealing the directive in respect of aluminium ships, a serious problem for one of the member states. the solution found allows this requirement to be waived only for ships currently under construction or for orders available to shipyards for which financing contracts already exist. in any event, these vessels shall be subject to national rules without prejudice to their safety.
member of the commission. – mr president, on behalf of commissioner bulc, i would like to thank the parliament and, in particular, all three rapporteurs and the shadow rapporteurs for their work on these files and for their constructive approach which facilitated reaching an agreement with the council. thank you so much. on safety rules and standards, we are sending a clear signal to our citizens travelling on board passenger ships in eu waters that their safety is our priority. i wish to reiterate that the commission’s services, with the assistance of the european maritime safety agency, are currently focusing on developing guidelines for small passenger ships. we will also duly respond to the parliament’s call to assess the need for common european requirements for sailing ships and ship carrier tenders. concerning the legislation proposal, we are ensuring that the competent authorities have immediate access to accurate data on persons on board in case of emergency, and that they can therefore deal with any accident more effectively. i am sure that you will continue to fully support our efforts to further digitalise maritime transport and to enhance the single window for reporting formalities. this is where the commission is committed to proposing revised legislation on reporting formalities by next april, which will establish a harmonised european maritime single window environment. the new rules on inspections will ensure that the respective regime brings value for money for all parties concerned. besides the cost savings, it removes the unnecessary duplication and complexity of existing regimes, which had developed over time and resulted in overlapping requirements spread across different pieces of legislation. the new rules will facilitate implementation, monitoring and enforcement. i am sure that you will continue to fully support our efforts to further improve, simplify and modernise maritime legislation, and commissioner bulc looks forward to our future cooperation.
the rapporteur. mr president, we are aware that these are three very important reports, but they must not have generated much enthusiasm in the house. in any case, i will respond to the comments of our colleague who said that the safety of ships is not achieved by registering them. we are obviously talking about a directive which will improve the collection of data so that search and rescue can be effective in the event of an accident. we must therefore focus our arguments on this directive and its content. as for your fear, you spoke about the possible misuse of this information, i must tell you that regulation (eu) 2016/679 will be applied here, which is about the protection of personal data and privacy. in addition, i have made a reference in my speech to the fact that data will be deleted, that is, all information, when it is no longer necessary for the purposes for which it was retrieved. and it will be deleted automatically and without undue delay. so, all the fears you might have are covered in this report. nothing more to say, other than express my gratitude to all of you. and a final message on the problem we always have: we have made the effort; i hope that parliament will indeed vote with a large majority tomorrow, but what we need is for the member states to comply with the directives within the time limits that are set, because this will contribute to the improvement and safety of the entire maritime sector.

member of the commission. – mr president, first of all i would like to express my thanks to parliament for its strong support for the proposed fertilising products regulation. in particular, i thank the rapporteur and shadow rapporteurs for all their valuable input. the regulation is in many ways ground-breaking and also very complex. being here today gives me a chance to recall its core principles. first of all, with regard to the potential of the circular economy, the proposed regulation is the first deliverable of the circular economy action plan. it is a very ambitious contribution to that. i say very ambitious because, for the first time, this regulation will open up the single market for products needed by european farmers in the 21st century. the products i am talking about are innovative agro-chemicals produced from organic materials present in by-products and waste. those products have enormous potential to make european agriculture more efficient and sustainable and to create jobs and opportunities for innovative businesses in europe. when organic materials available in europe are recycled, european farmers get an outlet for agricultural by-products that would otherwise have been wasted. european fertiliser manufacturers become much less dependent on imported, scarce raw materials, such as phosphate, from other regions in the world and, in between, a market is created for innovative european recycling operators and technology providers. so this is a win-win for european farmers, fertiliser producers and innovative businesspeople. in terms of a free market for responsible actors, we are trying with the proposed new regulation to free up the market as much as possible for products that can reform the european agro-industry. gone are the days when fertilisers had to comply with narrow definitions set by the legislator, or when they had to be halted at every border between member states for new certification. nowadays, manufacturers have real freedom to adapt their products to farmers’ needs, using a mix of conventional and innovative raw materials. farmers understand their own needs much better than any legislator. that is why we have proposed legislation which keeps farmers’ choices as wide as possible. but this presumes that manufacturers take all responsibility for product safety. spreading products on farmland can pose a risk to health and the environment. known and unknown toxic contaminants can end up in our water, food and animal feed. so we have proposed that all agro-chemicals covered in the legislation must be subject to a chemical safety assessment under the general registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals (reach) legislation. if this proposal is amended, nobody – neither the legislator nor the manufacturer – will be responsible for assessing the safety of using agro-chemicals on land, and crops. that could have dramatic impacts on the environment and on the safety of the food chain, so i urge the european parliament not to water down our proposal on this point. european fertiliser producers are more than able to take on the responsibility that the new market freedom requires and european farmers and citizens have the right to expect. finally, this proposal not only provides new opportunities for the european agro-industry, it also provides you with an opportunity to limit emissions of toxic contaminants to farmland, drinking water and food. i would like to thank you for your general support for this part of our proposal. together, we will raise environmental standards in an area in which europeans are lagging behind the rest of the world. future generations of europeans will have their health better protected. a particular concern for health and the environment is cadmium in phosphate fertilisers. as far back as 1988, a council resolution called for a strategy to reduce cadmium in phosphate fertilisers, and the problem has far from disappeared since then. there are a few marginal scientific differences, but the overall picture is clear: the european environment and people are too exposed to cadmium, and the only remaining major polluter of food in the environment is the phosphate fertilisers industry. so it is time for phosphate fertiliser manufacturers make sure that some of the dirtiest phosphate rock is cleaned before it is used in fertilisers, or for them to replace it with cleaner recycled phosphates sourced from europe. and they can do that. the market is already developing and we are ready to support it further. please remember that the limit values will also apply to imported phosphate fertilisers sold in the single market with the ce mark. this gives the european industry a golden opportunity to lead the world, not only as manufacturers of clean fertilisers with access to the single market, but also as technology providers to importers. so the industry should work with us, not against us. it is in their interest. it will help them to get a competitive advantage by developing clean technologies in innovative ways. to conclude my opening remarks, let me thank you again for your support. i look forward to hearing your views.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, i welcome this legislation, which is part of the circular economy package, because it proposes organic and recycled fertilisers, thus reducing inorganic raw material. in addition, harmonized environmental and food safety criteria are established to promote trade in these products. all of that is very good and very commendable. these are great objectives and we must pursue them, but sometimes the end does not justify the means, especially if the means available are not feasible or economically and practically acceptable to the sectors which have to take them on and apply them. favouring the expansion of organic matter is very positive. however, we cannot pretend to substitute mineral products, at least not until we are sure that they provide the same level and efficiency in terms of soil fertilization. it should not be forgotten that fertilisers are essential and ensure that farmers get enough nutrients for their crops. moreover, although it is important to promote the use of manure as organic fertilisers, i do not think this is the regulation to try, as it would directly affect the nitrates directive. i would also like to refer, of course, to the maximum cadmium content. the limits on cadmium have been the subject of much debate and have a great deal to do with the competitiveness of industry and agriculture, as well as other geopolitical connotations, as has just been said here. i think the limits proposed by the commission are too narrow. i would even say that they are unacceptable and that the proposal should be made more flexible: 80 milligrams, as the scientific reports indicate, would be a reasonable figure, especially as we now have no limit. in any case, we must push this regulation to support industry to make it more sustainable and more competitive and to promote sustainable economic growth and employment. but if we go too far on some issues, we'll have to vote against it.

the rapporteur. mr president according to the latest european drug report 2017, presented by the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction, overdose deaths have increased considerably due to a lack of knowledge about the dangers of these new psychotropic substances. in 2015, there were a total of 8 441 overdose deaths among the 28 eu member states plus norway and turkey, mostly related to heroin and other drugs. the most widely used illicit stimulant drugs in europe are cocaine, ecstasy and amphetamines. in my country, spain, a total of 455 drug-induced deaths were recorded in 2015 15 per million inhabitants, compared to the eu average of 21.3 per million citizens. apart from the conventional drugs already mentioned - such as cocaine and heroin - the use of new psychotropic substances is increasing every year. in june this year, commissioner avramopoulos expressed concern about young people being exposed to new and dangerous substances. these new psychoactive substances that are legal, also known as designer drugs, are a group of synthetic or semi-synthetic chemical compounds that are produced in industrial laboratories, most of them in china or india, and are circulating in a legal market. the popularity of these substances has been increasing in europe and the rest of the world due to their availability on the internet and their easy sale in shops. each year, many young people - particularly men - die from taking new psychotropic substances. the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction in lisbon detected 540 new psychotropic drugs in the union last year, and the trend continues to increase each year. the growth of internet sales of these types of drugs and the ease of their manufacture have made it more difficult for the european union to stop their production. the 2014 framework decision was no longer effective and therefore a new legislative instrument was needed. the commission drew up a new regulation in 2013 - mr boni is the rapporteur for the report on that regulation - and, as a consequence, a new directive to overcome this legal challenge. almost five years later, we've finally reached an agreement. the aim of the legislative package is to reduce the availability of new psychotropic substances that present risks, which will be achieved through faster and more effective action at union level compared to the instrument we had in 2005, which did not include information exchange, early warning, risk assessment or control of new psychotropic substances. the directive aimed in particular to amend framework decision 757/2004 in order to be able to criminalise new psychotropic substances. from now on, member states can take the necessary measures to ensure that those who manufacture, produce and distribute 'this designer drug' are punished with maximum sentences of five to ten years' imprisonment. i have to remind you that this directive does not penalise the consumption of this drug, but the trafficking of it. these two instruments - directive and regulation - have come a long way. parliament approved the proposal in 2014 but, to date, we have not been able to find a satisfactory compromise. both reports are a success, because we have reached an agreement that will help all european citizens. finally, i would like to thank the maltese presidency for its excellent work in finding a balance between parliament and the council. i would also like to thank the commission for its supporting role during all the meetings of the tripartite dialogues. finally, i would like to express my gratitude to mr boni for the fruitful cooperation we have had.

first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, a renowned and brave journalist died in the most brutal and shocking manner in malta last week. a wife, a mother, a mother-in-law, a friend, a neighbour, a colleague. daphne caruana galizia appears to have been killed because someone wanted to stop her from reporting. and it happened right here, in the european union! let me first express my deepest condolences to her family and loved ones. your loss, i cannot imagine. i did not have the privilege to know daphne personally but a few things stand out – her courage and doggedness in the pursuit of the truth, her readiness to ask the questions that really matter about politicians of all colours. the very heart of democracy is that those who the people choose to lead them are also accountable to them. journalists such as daphne represent us all when they ask the difficult questions and when they keep digging even if it becomes uncomfortable and dangerous to find the truth. when i attended the spontaneous vigil last wednesday in brussels, when i stood here in silence with you earlier today in the presence of daphne’s family, to whom i have had the chance to express my condolences in person this morning, my deep concerns about what this tragic event represents in terms of our democratic values were dwarfed by the immediate human tragedy: the three sons and a daughter-in-law suddenly and violently losing a mother, and a husband prematurely and painfully losing his beloved wife. at the european council last week and again this morning, president tajani made a strong call for a detailed in-depth international investigation. on behalf of president juncker and all my colleagues in the college, i can say that the commission very much agrees that ensuring an independent and thorough investigation of the facts and bringing those responsible to justice must be the top priority for now. prime minister muscat gave such an assurance to his fellow leaders on thursday and the eyes of europe and the world are now on malta to ensure this is the case. i welcome the fact that the maltese authorities have engaged with their counterparts in europe and beyond, including forensics experts from the netherlands, the united kingdom and the united states, and wherever useful, europol and eurojust are there to help. we know that good journalism can be a dangerous job. last year 72 journalists were killed worldwide and more than 50 others have died so far this year. but the targeted and brutal manner of daphne’s killing and the fact that it happened here on the soil of one of our member states profoundly shocks. even here in europe, too many journalists are threatened every day. the campaign ‘mapping media freedom’ has already reported more than 300 alerts of threats to journalistic freedom in the eu since the beginning of the year and more than 3 000 since the beginning of the project. i pay tribute to all those who have stood up and asked the tough questions. since – and i say this as a politician and democrat among politicians and democrats – since professional journalism is a necessary job because it ensures that all of us who are entrusted with certain responsibilities are also scrutinised for how we exercise them, that perhaps matters now more than ever, as we find ourselves in an era where anyone can publish their views online, where facts and fiction are sometimes mixed, where false information is repeated ever louder. i have said before in this house that everyone is entitled to her or his own opinions, but no one is entitled to their own facts. that is what journalists do. they are the human face of stubborn facts. that is their job, their mission. a free media is the watchdog in our democracies. healthy democracy requires a free and pluralistic media, free from state intervention and from undue political or commercial pressures. ed murrow put it well when he said that every healthy democracy needs a good dose of itching pills, and as president juncker said last week, the right of a journalist to investigate, to ask uncomfortable questions and report effectively is at the heart of our values and needs to be guaranteed at all times. under the treaties, the commission has limited powers in this area. we can, however, encourage and guide, which is why last year we chose to devote our annual colloquium on fundamental rights to the theme of media pluralism and democracy. three quarters of respondents to the public consultation covering all our member states in preparation for the colloquium said that they were aware of or have experienced limitations on journalistic activities by state measures, and more than two thirds of respondents said they have experienced or are aware of censorship and self-censorship. such findings are very worrying. if journalists have to fear for their lives just for doing their job, they cannot operate with a level of freedom and independence that is essential for the media in any democracy, in any rule-of-law based society. media freedom and pluralism are fundamental rights enshrined in article 11 of the eu charter on fundamental rights and constitute essential foundations of our democratic societies. it is the duty of the maltese state to investigate and prosecute this case in accordance with its constitution, its legal order and international human rights obligations. the maltese authorities and institutions must deliver on their commitment to do everything in their power to ensure that the perpetrators will be brought to justice. malta needs to show to europe and the world that its rules and regulations are healthy and robust. this is why it is important that the maltese government has indicated that the investigation and prosecution should be allowed to run their full course, that if problems of a more general or systemic nature are brought to light, they should also be addressed, regardless of the consequences. today’s debate proves once more that the eyes of europe stay firmly fixed on malta, because the murder of a brave journalist such as daphne is a direct concern for us all. we will, it is our duty, continue to stand up for our shared values. why? well, for the sake of daphne, her loved ones and everything she stood for, for the sake of the european union and everything it stands for.

the rapporteur. - madam president, first of all i would like to thank all the parties involved, especially commissioner avramopoulos, the maltese presidency, all the alternative rapporteurs and also the legal services. the european commission launched its final legislative proposal in april 2016, after the ground was set in 2013 in complementary areas of study, pilot projects, budget projections and studies of different alternatives, such as biometric data or system architecture. the legislative task is being tackled because technical gaps have been identified in the management of the union's external borders. at present, external borders are controlled by border guards who check the authenticity of passports and visas for those third-country nationals who want to enter the european union for 90 days in any 180-day period, but there is no procedure to control those who, after the authorized period has expired, remain on european territory irregularly. our regulation thus establishes a centralised management and control system, through which the authenticity of third-country nationals' travel documents is verified by recording alphanumeric data, biometric data and information on the date, time and place of entry and exit. a calculator is also created for the actual calculation of the 90 days allowed. as regards the objectives of the regulation, they are twofold: firstly, to improve the management of the external borders and to prevent irregular immigration and facilitate the management of migratory flows; and secondly, to contribute to the prevention, detection and investigation of terrorist offences and other serious criminal offences. this second objective is also crucial, as it will help to detect criminals with multiple false identities, as was the case with the terrorist who attacked the christmas market in berlin, who had entered and left our borders with fifteen different identities. but access to information on entries and exits by the police authorities of the member states and europol will be under strictly defined conditions. this is essential because the interinstitutional agreement ensures full respect for human rights, such as those relating to privacy, the protection of personal data and the principles of necessity, proportionality and legality. in order to ensure this, the european data protection supervisor shall be responsible for monitoring the data processing activities of the system. in addition, the central access point is created, which is the technical support of the eu-lisa agency its responsible, under the supervision of the european data protection supervisor. and, in addition, there will be a website where passengers can check their period of stay. the retention period shall be three years for bona fide passengers and five years for those who have exceeded the legal period of stay. i would also like to highlight the territorial scope of the system, which is the external borders of the member states applying the schengen acquis and also those countries which, although not applying it, have passed the evaluation. i am referring specifically to bulgaria and romania: this parliament has advocated from the outset the need to include these two countries. and i would point out that, of course, as soon as possible, croatia will also be included. this required giving passive access to the vis to bulgaria and romania, and was voted by an overwhelming majority in the last plenary. interoperability between the ees and the vis is also necessary, ladies and gentlemen, so that the system can verify that the visa with which you are trying to enter the european union is a legal and authentic visa. after three years of use of the system, the commission shall make an assessment of its use. finally, i would like to stress that the regulation will enter into force in 2020 and, in order to reach that date, many procedures are necessary which from the point of view of implementation must be fulfilled - we are talking about tenders, contracts, programme development, tests, etc. in conclusion, i think it is essential that we approve the entry/exit system today and not later. why would you do that? because it will improve the identification and authenticity of travel documents and therefore make it easier to identify criminals with false identities; it will replace the stamp; we will know in real time who has been staying at our borders irregularly; we will better protect freedom of transit in the schengen area; it will improve the facilitation of entry and exit - that is, fewer queues - and it will contribute to more protection and better management of the union's external borders. in conclusion, it will be faster and safer to enter.
madam president, in view of the recent serious errors in the exchange of information on third-country nationals travelling to the schengen area, the entry/exit system is an important instrument for improving the protection of the external borders and contributing to the prevention and investigation of terrorist offences and other serious criminal offences. the entry/exit system will replace the traditional passport stamping system with one adapted to the use of new technologies. it shall also retain personal data of third-country nationals travelling to the union on a short-stay visa, including facial image and fingerprints. during the retention period of personal data, law enforcement agencies will have access to that information, provided that certain established criteria are met. the report is therefore a positive outcome, the result of consensus and the need to strengthen border controls in the current context of the fight against terrorism.
member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the honourable members for their contributions to this debate and their comments. our external border management is the nexus of our policy on security and migration and the european union is implementing several initiatives in this domain. i therefore welcome the negotiations starting today – indeed now – between this house and the council, and i hope a compromise will be reached soon. the compromise on the entry/exit system will modernise and strengthen the schengen area’s external management. it will help member states to deal with increasing traveller flows without having to increase the number of border guards. it will also promote mobility between the schengen area and third countries in a secure environment, while contributing to the fight against terrorism and serious crime, and safeguarding fundamental rights. i want to be clear on a point that was mentioned earlier. the court of justice opinion on the eu-canada passenger name record (pnr) agreement does not have any direct and binding legal effect on the entry/exit system. the court ruled on a specific legal situation, which cannot be automatically extrapolated to other situations. there are significant differences between pnr and the entry/exit system. the legal basis, the purpose and the scope of data gathered, and the basis and rationale in respect of retention periods are not comparable. i am glad that this long process is now coming to an end and that we can soon start developing the system. i therefore encourage the honourable members to support these important pieces of legislation when they vote later today.
the rapporteur. madam president, thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen, for such a rich debate. the fact that there were 44 interventions gives you an idea of what i mean: i thank all of them. i thank all those who have supported the report, who have supported my work, who have expressed their eloquent silence. in short, everyone has contributed to enriching this debate. i would like to conclude, madam president, by quoting the legal services of the three institutions verbatim, so that it can be clearly and unequivocally stated that there has been no ambiguity in the pronouncements of the three legal services with reference to the judgment of the court of justice in case 1/15 concerning the international convention between the european union and canada on pnr. the report of our interinstitutional legal services says it verbatim: 'judgment 1/15 has no direct or automatic impact on the ees because of many differences between the system and the pnr, in particular in terms of the objectives, the scope and the personal data collected.'

mr president, commissioner, one of the main pillars of the capital markets union is the effort to revitalize the securitisation market in order to improve the financing of our economy. the regulatory package we are going to adopt tomorrow sets common rules for all securitisations and provides a framework for securitisation products to be, despite the doubts of some, safe, simple and transparent, and to be standardised and sufficiently supervised. these new rules will help investors to better assess the risks associated with securitisation, both in the products themselves and in the different product categories. in 2014 we saw the securitisation market shrink by almost 50% from its 2007 peak, and this led to many smes not getting the funding they were seeking. this agreement contributes to creating new investment opportunities across the union and provides an additional source of financing for the economy, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups. the reactivation of the securitisation market will lead to more diversified sources of financing and less dependence on the banking sector, thus contributing to the overall stability and resilience of the financial system. the commission's forecasts show that if the volume of securitisation in the european union reached the average level before the crisis, it could generate between eur 100 and eur 150 billion more in funding. the main beneficiaries would be small and mediumsized enterprises, which are the engine of the european economy. in conclusion, a well-structured securitisation market will contribute to improving the efficiency and stability of the financial system, providing investment opportunities and creating benefits for citizens and businesses, with cheaper and more accessible loans. i welcome this proposal and congratulate the negotiating team on their great work.

mr president, we appreciate the implementation of the environmental liability directive which was adopted in 2004 and then transposed a few years later. the aim was, of course, to prevent and repair any environmental damage under the 'polluter pays' principle. everything that is prevention and repair is, of course, key to being able to have sustainable growth and to be able to make economies work and societies be healthy. in this respect, the directive sought to work in three areas: halting the loss of biodiversity, both in relation to protected species and habitats; the quality and quantity of water 'could somehow stop the deterioration'; and also the protection of soil. the rapporteur, mrs laura ferrara, looks at the shortcomings in the implementation of this directive, and one that has been noted throughout the session is the different implementation by the member states. in fact, there are many differences in the number of incidents of environmental damage triggering the application of this directive between member states. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. the commission has said so. we will have to compare and study all the member states with comparative data to see what is really happening and from there to see how we can improve the legal text. the proposal is to extend the scope of the directive beyond 'technological and medical research' to include environmental damage which may affect human health and therefore also to cover this subject, and also to cover all matters relating to air pollution. in short, it is a matter of complying with the 2020 strategy of having integrated but also sustainable growth, and therefore of supporting the commission in this study, in this collating of data, in this looking at exchanges to see how we can improve the application of this directive, which will, without a doubt, make our economy work and we will have a healthy society.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, europe is based on different philosophical, legal and moral pillars, but its history and identity are still difficult to understand without christianity, even in the midst of a secular age. no other part of the world has been more influenced by christianity and no other can do more now to defend its survival and freedom in the face of persecution. i would simply like to stress two facts in connection with the persecution of christians. the first is that this persecution is global in nature and various indicators point to it being increasing, even in its most lethal dimensions. christians are the most persecuted religious group in most countries. and according to studies, christians are the target of 60 to 80 percent of religious discrimination worldwide, both by states and by social groups. the second is that the persecution of christians continues to receive the coverage it deserves from the media, the major human rights associations and political institutions, including the european union. we should be particularly concerned about the destruction of historic christian communities that is taking place among our mediterranean neighbours, a ordeal that threatens to spread to refugees who manage to reach europe. the european union is obliged to protect this valuable moral and cultural heritage. and this we can understand, believers and non-believers, as a citizen like myself. let us use this debate to ensure that this issue is firmly on the european agenda.

author. mr president, commissioner, i am speaking on behalf of the chairman of the committee on fisheries, mr alain cadec, and i will also be joining my speech to the one i had scheduled, thus adding up the two times, with the presidency's permission, to a maximum of five minutes which i will not be able to meet. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not left behind. and you know why? because the fisheries sector is always the first to have an interest in maintaining optimum environmental conditions, and the defence of posidonia is a common element of all the political groups in the committee on fisheries. as is well known, posidonia oceanica is an endemic plant of the mediterranean, one of the most productive and resilient species in the biosphere, capable of forming underwater meadows of great ecological importance, within which many animal and plant organisms live and which provide food and protection. it is also an excellent bioindicator of the quality of coastal marine waters. today, there are doubts about the conservation of these habitats, but sometimes the fishermen are always blamed, and it is not fair that the fishing industry is accused of causing a negative impact on the environment. there are many other factors, such as dredging practices, coastal development, eutrophication and climate change - among others - that have plunged this mediterranean lung into a serious regression process in recent years, making the slow-growing and difficult-to-regenerate posidonia one of the most endangered seaweeds at the moment. given the importance of this fact, we ask the commission to explain to us whether it has envisaged any additional measures that can be taken, not only to protect the posidonia oceanica stocks but also to restore their stocks. in this regard, some member states - including spain, with six mediterranean marine reserves with grasslands of this species - have taken concrete measures to curb the impact of human actions and ensure the conservation and preservation of the marine ecosystem. the routine of marine reserve services includes the recognition of the health status of these grasslands, and in particular their flowering and fruiting, whose increased interannual frequency and longer seasonal duration seem to be related to global change. also the specific collaboration in projects such as posimed, in collaboration with different ecology institutes, or the prohibition of diving in the integral reserves, or the elaboration of specific content on values of this species that forms underwater forests of fisheries interest. the inclusion of content on the need to protect marine habitats, with grasslands being a preferred habitat in national fisheries and biodiversity legislation. finally, the inclusion of content on this species in the educational strategy of marine reserve networks, school campaigns and school outreach, because we cannot forget that environmental education and awareness are fundamental if we want to stop the deterioration of the posidonia oceanica and also protect coastal marine habitats. in this connection, and in order to avoid the enormous pressure on these habitats which are essential for the conversion of carbon dioxide into oxygen, the productivity of marine resources and the protection of the coast, this house would like to know firsthand what data the commission has and what its assessment is of the investments made through its programmes. i would like to inform you that i am pleased that the level of protection provided for in the habitats directive, which is an instrument for the protection of posidonia meadows, is maintained. marine habitats provide great ecological services for humanity and in this context, posidonia is an important part of maintaining that biodiversity. i'm aware of this importance, but it's not enough to be aware. what is needed at european union level is the promotion of similar actions in other member states, as i said is happening in spain. it is the commission's task to coordinate these actions throughout europe. and finally, when we talk about the mediterranean, it is also important that the neighbouring third countries participate in a joint effort. the european union has a duty to help the countries of the mediterranean to achieve their goals.
mr president, the surface of posidonia oceanica has decreased by 50% in the mediterranean over the last 20 years. the decline of this plant is caused by dredging practices, pollution, poor anchoring practices or uncontrolled anchoring linked to mass tourism, among many other reasons. the malfunctioning, the inadequate or non-existent treatment of waste water and the pollution of rivers is something that is constantly being denounced by sectors such as shellfish and shallow-water fisheries, a situation which i have repeatedly brought to the commission's attention. and, commissioner, the answers often reflect passivity or the lack of decisive action to reverse this situation, both in terms of the deficiencies in the water treatment systems and in terms of pollution linked to mass tourism or different infrastructures in these areas. and i ask you, commissioner, will you take it seriously this time? will you protect the posidonia and the rest of the coastal marine habitats by tackling the pollution that is destroying them? and the last question: what are the limits to blue growth to preserve these habitats?
in writing. the grasslands of posidonia oceanica are the most important mediterranean forest by extension, co2 fixation functions, great biodiversity hosting more than 400 species of mostly fishy fry or for their great oxygenation capacity. the big problem with this ecologically valuable aquatic plant forest is that it's not in sight, and its positive effects on the coast are only appreciated when they disappear. the population of the riverine is constantly increasing, negatively impacting this prairie so important for the maintenance of the good state of our sea. but, nevertheless, this growth and development is not accompanied by protective measures. the simple act of anchoring any recreational craft, increasingly frequent, irreversibly destroys a portion of up to one square meter of poseidon surface, which will take 100 years to cover, growth rate impossible to compete with the use that the human being makes of the coast. the measures to be promoted by the commission, such as ecological foundations that reconcile recreational use with the preservation of biodiversity, should be included in the review of environmental and land use legislation in the mediterranean coastal strip.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, we have before us a report on the demographic challenges which, in my view, are an essential issue for the european union project: the demographic challenges, because we are the continent with the world's oldest population and because we must take into account a question which i think reflects very well the radiography of what these demographic challenges are. 80% of the european population lives on 20% of the surface of our europe. that means we have very large rural areas, with depopulation processes that are really worrying. i would like to thank the commissioner, mrs crețu, for being here today, because it is a reflection of the european commission's commitment to this very important issue, and i would also like to thank, in this first speech, the work done by the various alternative rapporteurs, the various political groups and the staff of our committee in contributing to the improvement of this report which we are debating today. europe has important demographic challenges and next year, 2018, is a year where we will face fundamental negotiations, and this parliament will have to take a political position on this. we will be faced with debates such as the new budgetary framework of the union and what the new structural fund regulations are. on both these issues it is essential that there be a political position of this parliament to determine how we deal with the processes of depopulation in the european union. and i am pleased with the outcome of the debate and the vote in the committee on regional development on this report, because it raises fundamental issues and we have managed to take a position on issues which i believe are important in dealing with the processes of depopulation. firstly, the establishment of a legal framework. it is essential that we have the possibility of a legal framework defining which areas of depopulation need to be addressed as a matter of priority in order to solve the problems we are facing at the moment. we also propose in this report that there should be budget headings in all the structural fund regulations to meet the challenges faced by regions in the process of depopulation. there is one fundamental question which we have been raising for some time, and which is important to have reflected in this report, and that is that gdp, gross domestic product, should not be the sole criterion for taking into account or for determining the allocation of funds. and this is a fundamental question. and i say this is a fundamental question because gdp, being a fundamental and important criterion, cannot be the only one. other criteria must be taken into account, such as the processes of depopulation, ageing, dispersion, the rural environment, which are fundamental issues, because if not, we will find ourselves with european regions which are the richest in all of europe, but which have no population on which to implement the operational programmes of the structural funds. and coordination between the different funds is necessary. the coordination between the structural funds, the common agricultural policy, the investment funds and so on is a fundamental question. we have to deal with the masculinization of the countryside. we need to put public service policies in place in rural areas, which are fundamental. the austerity policy has done a lot of damage to our society, but especially to the rural environment, because when we remove a teacher from a school in a city it is important, but when we remove him from the rural environment we are closing schools. that is why it is essential to make rural areas attractive places where young men and women can decide to create their future. we do not have much time: the countryside is dying; we are closing down villages, they will disappear if we are not able to implement policies committed from the european union to fight against the processes of depopulation.
mr president, commissioner, i thank the rapporteur for this excellent report, which shows that the problem of depopulation is a european problem which we must solve by means of a great deal of agreement in our institutions. because, in the end, the consequences of depopulation are known to all of us: there are consequences from environmental to social. but what we have to go to is to solve the cause. the reason is the lack of equal opportunities, because of insufficient investment, because of a lack of public services and because of a lack of companies that will create jobs. and so we need an effort, a positive discrimination from the community budget for those regions, for those regions where there are greater problems of depopulation. it cannot be that the percentage of gdp alone is the yardstick for allocating community funds. cohesion, which is ultimately at the heart of community policy, has to start by seeking internal cohesion between the urban and the rural. we need your help, commissioner, to create more investment, to make more public effort, to ensure equal opportunities in our towns.

in writing. the leaks known as the paradise papers have once again highlighted the scandalous phenomenon of tax evasion and avoidance, by concealing the wealth of the richest in shell companies with no real economic activity, located in jurisdictions where they do not in practice comply with the standards for automatic exchange of information between tax administrations or where non-residents are exempt from taxation. these revelations, which are in addition to those in the 'panama papers', require the commission to publish the european list of tax havens as soon as possible, given that the oecd list does not correspond to the actual practices of many states, which manage not to be nominally classified as such. we also call on the member states to prohibit the opening of bank accounts by non-residents who do not carry out commercial activities in the states included in the future list of the european union, since the purpose of this can only be tax evasion. we spanish socialists reiterate that the unremitting fight against the great social injustice of tax fraud is an absolute priority of our political action.
